teile.einleitung: The solar wind is a stream of tiny particles that the Sun constantly blows into space. It is not a wind made of air, and we cannot feel it. Even so, it creates one of the most beautiful shows in the sky: the aurora.
wichtigste: The solar wind is made of tiny, electrically charged particles.
It blows in space, not in the air.
You cannot feel it on your skin.
The Earth's magnetic field protects us from a large part of it.
The particles fly much faster than any aeroplane.
The solar wind makes auroras glow and can disturb satellites.

abschnitte.text: The solar wind is **not a wind made of air**. It consists of **tiny particles**, mainly electrons and protons. They stream out of the outermost layer of the Sun, the **corona**, in all directions into **space**. There is no air in space that you could feel as wind. That is why you cannot feel the solar wind on your skin.

The particles of the solar wind are **much faster than any aeroplane**. Usually they fly several hundred kilometres per second. An aeroplane cannot even manage one kilometre per second. So the particles reach the Earth in a few days. The solar wind blows far out beyond the planets.

The Earth has a **magnetic field** that works like an invisible protective shield. It steers a large part of the solar wind around the Earth. Without this protection, the solar wind would slowly strip away the atmosphere. Only near the poles can some particles get further in.

When the particles hit the air above the poles, they make it **glow**. This creates **auroras**, the northern and southern lights, in green, red or purple. You usually see them in the far north, for example in Norway or Iceland. When the solar wind is very strong, you can occasionally even see them in Switzerland in the northern sky.

Sometimes the Sun flings a particularly large number of particles into space all at once. This is called a **solar storm**. It can disturb **satellites**, interfere with radio and in rare cases put a strain on power grids. That is why researchers watch the Sun closely, so that they can give warning in time.

gewusst: During the Moon landings, researchers from the University of Bern caught real particles of the solar wind with a sheet of foil.
Because of the solar wind, the tails of comets always point away from the Sun.

teile.einleitung: Mars is often called the Red Planet because it shines reddish in the sky. It is the fourth planet from the Sun and one of the Earth's neighbours. Many space probes and rovers have already explored it.
wichtigste: Mars is named after the Roman god of war.
Its red colour comes from iron oxide, a kind of rust in the dust.
A Martian year lasts 687 days, almost two Earth years.
A Martian day lasts 24 hours and 37 minutes.
Mars has two small moons: Phobos and Deimos.
There are white ice caps at its poles.

abschnitte.text: There is a lot of fine **dust** on Mars. It contains **iron oxide**, which is a kind of **rust**. That is why the planet shines reddish. In the past the colour reminded people of blood and war. So it was given the name of the Roman **god of war, Mars**.

Mars is about **6800 kilometres** across, while the Earth is almost 13,000 kilometres. So it is about **half as wide**. Because it is further from the Sun, it is very **cold** there. Its **air** is very thin and consists almost entirely of carbon dioxide. People could not breathe it.

Mars turns once on its own axis in **24 hours and 37 minutes**. So a Martian day is only a little longer than an Earth day. But it needs **687 days** for one lap around the Sun, almost **two Earth years**. Like the Earth, Mars has **seasons**. At its North Pole and South Pole there are **white ice caps**.

On Mars stands **Olympus Mons**, the highest known volcano in the whole solar system. A huge system of canyons is called **Valles Marineris**. Sometimes **dust storms** rage that cover the whole planet for weeks. Then you can hardly see the surface. At **sunset** the sky around the Sun glows **bluish**, because the fine dust scatters the blue light that way.

Mars has two small, oddly shaped moons: **Phobos** and **Deimos**. Their names mean “fear” and “terror”. Many **rovers** have explored Mars. In February 2021 the rover **Perseverance** landed. It carried the small helicopter **Ingenuity**, the first aircraft to fly on another planet.

gewusst: On Mars you weigh only about 38 per cent of what you weigh on Earth.
Olympus Mons is more than twice as high as Mount Everest.

teile.einleitung: Going to the toilet is not that easy in space. Without gravity nothing falls down, so a space toilet works with a stream of air, a bit like a vacuum cleaner.
wichtigste: A space toilet **sucks** everything away with a stream of air.
Before use, the **air suction** has to be running.
For a wee there is a **funnel with a hose**.
Astronauts hold on with **handles and foot loops**.
In the space station, urine is turned back into **drinking water**.
At launch, astronauts often wear a special **nappy**.

abschnitte.text: On Earth gravity pulls everything down into the toilet. In space everything floats. That is why the toilet in the space station needs a **stream of air** that sucks everything away. Before using it, you have to switch on the **suction**. Only then is everything safely pulled into a container, and nothing floats around.

For a wee there is a **funnel** hanging on a hose. A stream of air sucks the urine in. For a poo there is a small seat with an opening. So that they do not float away, the astronauts hold on to **handles** and put their feet into **loops**.

Water is very precious in the space station, because otherwise every litre has to be brought up from Earth. That is why urine is collected and **cleaned** very thoroughly by a machine. After that it is clean **drinking water** again. Sweat and moisture from the air are also collected and reused.

The solid waste goes into containers. These are later loaded into a **cargo spacecraft**. The cargo spacecraft leaves the station and enters the Earth's atmosphere. It **burns up** there together with the waste. So nothing is left behind in space.

The space toilet is very different from an ordinary toilet. That is why astronauts practise on a **training toilet** on Earth before the flight. During launch and landing they sit strapped into their seats for hours. Because they cannot go to the toilet then, they wear a special **nappy**.

gewusst: A large part of the water that astronauts drink in the space station was once urine or sweat.
On the first space flights there was no toilet at all, only bags and hoses.

teile.einleitung: SETI stands for “Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence”. Researchers listen, mainly with radio telescopes, for artificial signals from space. So far no definite signal has been found.
wichtigste: SETI means searching for signals from extraterrestrial intelligence.
In 1959 Cocconi and Morrison suggested searching at the 21 cm line of hydrogen.
In 1960 Frank Drake carried out the first SETI experiment with Project Ozma.
The puzzling Wow! signal from 1977 was never received again.
In 1974 the Arecibo message was sent towards the globular cluster M13.
Breakthrough Listen has been the largest search programme since 2015.

abschnitte.text: In **1959** the physicists **Giuseppe Cocconi** and **Philip Morrison** suggested using radio telescopes to search for messages from space. As the frequency they recommended the **21 cm line** of hydrogen at about **1420 MHz**. Hydrogen is the most common element, and every technical civilisation would know this frequency. The quiet range between the lines of hydrogen and hydroxyl is called the **water hole**, because together the two make water. There the cosmic noise is low.

The first SETI experiment was **Project Ozma** by **Frank Drake** in **1960**. With a radio telescope he listened to two Sun-like stars: **Tau Ceti** and **Epsilon Eridani**. Both are only just over ten light years away. Drake did not find an artificial signal. He also became known for the **Drake equation**, which tries to estimate how many civilisations there might be.

In **1977** the radio telescope **Big Ear** in Ohio picked up a striking signal. The astronomer **Jerry Ehman** circled the data on the printout and wrote “**Wow!**” next to it. The signal was strong and narrow, as you would expect from an artificial source. But it was **never received again**. Where it came from is still unexplained today.

People have also sent out messages themselves. In **1974** the **Arecibo** radio telescope sent a message towards the **globular cluster M13**. It consisted of **1679 bits**, which can be arranged into a picture. It shows, for example, numbers, building blocks of the genetic material DNA and the outline of a human. It will take about 25,000 years for the message to arrive.

The project **SETI@home** started in **1999**. Millions of people let their **home computers** analyse radio data when they were not being used. It is seen as a pioneer of **distributed computing**. Since **2015**, **Breakthrough Listen** has been running with about 100 million dollars and large radio telescopes such as Green Bank and Parkes. As early as 1960 **Freeman Dyson** suggested looking for a **sphere** around a star that catches the starlight and would give off a lot of heat in the infrared.

gewusst: The number 1679 in the Arecibo message is the product of the prime numbers 23 and 73, which gives a picture of 23 by 73 dots.
The question of why we have not yet found any aliens despite all the stars is called the Fermi paradox.

teile.einleitung: During re-entry, a spacecraft comes back from space into the Earth's atmosphere. It is extremely fast and gets very hot. That is why re-entry is one of the most dangerous parts of a space flight.
wichtigste: The heat comes mainly from the strongly **squashed air** in front of the vehicle.
A **plasma sheath** cuts off radio contact for a few minutes.
From low Earth orbit a vehicle arrives at about 7.8 km/s, from the Moon at about 11 km/s.
The angle of entry has to lie within a narrow **corridor**.
In 2003 the Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart during re-entry.
Old space stations are deliberately crashed into the South Pacific near **Point Nemo**.

abschnitte.text: During re-entry a spacecraft races into the atmosphere at many kilometres per second. In front of the vehicle a **shock wave** forms, in which the air is strongly squashed. It heats up to several thousand degrees and passes the heat on to the vehicle. A **heat shield** protects the crew. On capsules it slowly burns away, while on the Space Shuttle it was made of special tiles.

The extremely hot air becomes **ionised**, which means it becomes electrically charged. It surrounds the vehicle as **plasma**. This swallows or reflects radio waves. That is why radio contact breaks off for a few minutes. For the ground station these are always especially tense minutes.

From a low Earth orbit, a vehicle hits the atmosphere at about 7.8 km/s. The **Apollo capsules** coming back from the Moon even arrived at about 11 km/s. The angle of entry has to lie within a narrow **corridor**. If it is too shallow, the capsule can bounce back into space. If it is too steep, the heat and braking become too strong. NASA sets the start of re-entry, the “entry interface”, at a height of about 120 km.

During re-entry the **Space Shuttle** flew wide S-shaped curves. By banking to the left and right, it made its path through the air longer and so lost speed in a controlled way, without any engines. Then it landed like a glider. Capsules, on the other hand, are slowed down at the end by **parachutes** and land in the sea or on land.

On 1 February 2003 the Space Shuttle **Columbia** broke apart during re-entry, and the seven astronauts died. At launch a piece of insulating foam had damaged the leading edge of the left wing, and during re-entry hot gas got in there. Old space stations are deliberately crashed into the **South Pacific** near Point Nemo, the point in the ocean furthest from any land. The space station Mir came down there in 2001.

gewusst: Shooting stars are small particles from space that burn up as they enter the atmosphere.
When returning from the Moon, the Apollo capsules were almost as fast as the Earth's escape velocity.

teile.einleitung: In the past a rocket was thrown away after every launch. Reusable rockets are meant to land and fly several times. This makes space flights much cheaper.
wichtigste: The main aim of reusable rockets is to reduce **launch costs**.
The **Space Shuttle** flew a total of 135 missions from 1981 to 2011.
With the Shuttle, only the large **external tank** was lost each time.
The Soviet space shuttle **Buran** flew only once, in 1988 without a crew.
In November 2015 **New Shepard** became the first rocket to land vertically after a flight above 100 km.
In 2024 the arms of a launch tower caught a Starship booster in mid-air for the first time.

abschnitte.text: A **rocket stage** is the most expensive part of a launch. If it is thrown away after the flight, a new one has to be built for every launch. If it can land and fly again, the building costs are spread over many flights. It is similar to an aeroplane, which you do not scrap after one flight either.

NASA's **Space Shuttle** was the first partly reusable spacecraft. The orbiter landed like a glider, and the **solid rocket boosters** were recovered from the sea. Only the large **external tank** burned up after every launch. From 1981 to 2011 the five orbiters flew 135 missions. Two were lost: Challenger in 1986 and Columbia in 2003. The Soviet space shuttle **Buran** flew only once, in November 1988, fully automatically and without a crew.

In November 2015 Blue Origin's rocket **New Shepard** landed vertically in Texas after a flight above 100 km. However, it was not a flight into Earth orbit. Then in December 2015 the first stage of a SpaceX **Falcon 9** landed for the first time after a flight into orbit. Today such stages regularly land on land or on ships at sea and fly many times.

On 13 October 2024 a Starship **Super Heavy booster** flew back to the launch tower. Two large arms caught it in mid-air, so it did not need landing legs. In November 2025, on its second flight, the first stage of Blue Origin's **New Glenn** also landed on a ship in the Atlantic. On that flight the rocket launched NASA's Mars probes ESCAPADE.

Reuse also has disadvantages. **Fuel** has to be left over for the flight back and the landing. Landing legs and control surfaces are extra weight. This mass is missing from the **payload**, that is, from satellites or cargo. That is why a reusable rocket can carry a little less than a single-use rocket of the same size.

gewusst: In 1988 Buran landed on a runway by itself, with no people on board at all.
Some Falcon 9 first stages have already flown more than twenty times.

teile.einleitung: Planetary protection means that space probes should not carry germs from Earth to other celestial bodies, and that possible alien life forms should not reach the Earth without being checked. There are international rules for this.
wichtigste: The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 requires harmful contamination of celestial bodies to be avoided.
The guidelines are set by the organisation COSPAR.
Forward contamination means that germs from Earth reach other celestial bodies.
Back contamination means that possible extraterrestrial organisms reach the Earth.
The Viking landers were heated for many hours before their launch in 1975.
In 2003, the Galileo probe was deliberately crashed into Jupiter to protect the moon Europa.

abschnitte.text: The **Outer Space Treaty** of 1967 is an important treaty under international law. In Article IX it requires states to avoid harmful contamination of other celestial bodies and harmful changes to the Earth's environment. The detailed guidelines are set by **COSPAR**, the Committee on Space Research. It divides missions into **categories**, depending on where they go and what they do.

In **forward contamination**, microbes from Earth reach another celestial body. They could settle in alien environments there or spoil the search for life. That is why probes are built in **clean rooms** and in some cases sterilised. To check, mainly **bacterial spores** are counted, because they survive dryness, cold and radiation particularly well.

In 1975, before their launch, the two **Viking landers** for Mars were dry-heated as a whole for about 40 hours at about 111 °C. Viking is still regarded as the standard for sterilisation. The Jupiter probe **Galileo** had delivered clues to an ocean beneath the ice of the moon **Europa**. So that it would never crash onto Europa out of control, NASA let it plunge into Jupiter in 2003.

On Mars there are possible **Special Regions**. These are areas where liquid water and suitable temperatures might be possible at times. Microbes from Earth could multiply there. That is why probes visiting such areas have to meet stricter requirements.

**Back contamination** is about protecting the Earth. If a mission brings back samples from a body that might have life, such as Mars, it falls into **Category V** with restricted return. The samples must stay safely sealed until they are considered harmless. The first **Apollo astronauts** were also put into quarantine as a precaution after returning from the Moon.

gewusst: The Saturn probe Cassini was also deliberately steered into Saturn in 2017 to protect the moons Titan and Enceladus.
Bacterial spores can survive extreme conditions that would kill most living things.

teile.einleitung: At the equinox, day and night are almost the same length, about 12 hours each. This happens twice a year, in March and in September. According to the calendar, spring and autumn begin with them.
wichtigste: There are **two** equinoxes a year.
The spring equinox is around **20 March**.
The autumn equinox is around **22 or 23 September**.
On these days, day and night each last about **12 hours**.
The Sun rises almost exactly in the **east** and sets in the **west**.
Between March and September, our days are longer than our nights.

abschnitte.text: A whole day with its night has 24 hours. At the **equinox**, day and night share this time almost equally. So both last about 12 hours. The scientific word **equinox** comes from Latin and means equal night. Day and night are usually not exactly the same length, but almost.

The Earth's axis is **tilted**. So on its way around the Sun, sometimes the Northern Hemisphere and sometimes the Southern Hemisphere is tilted more towards the Sun. In between there are two moments when neither hemisphere is favoured. The Sun is then exactly above the **equator** at midday. These are the equinoxes.

Around **20 March**, spring begins according to the calendar. From then on, the Sun rises earlier and earlier here and sets later. Until autumn, the days are longer than the nights. The longest day is in June, at the summer solstice.

Around **22 or 23 September** is the second equinox. Autumn begins with it. After that the Sun sets earlier and earlier, and the **nights** become longer than the days. This stays the same until the next spring. The longest night is in December, at the winter solstice.

At the equinoxes the Sun rises almost exactly in the **east** and sets almost exactly in the **west**. In summer it rises more in the north-east here, in winter more in the south-east. That is why on these days you can easily work out the points of the compass using the Sun.

gewusst: In the Southern Hemisphere it is exactly the other way round: there autumn begins in March and spring in September.
At the equinoxes, day and night are about the same length everywhere on Earth.

teile.einleitung: The Sphinx Observatory stands on a rocky peak above the Jungfraujoch. It is one of the highest research stations in Europe. Here researchers measure the weather, the air and radiation from space.
wichtigste: The Sphinx Observatory is at 3571 metres above sea level.
It stands in the canton of Valais above the Jungfraujoch.
The first researchers moved into the research station in 1931.
In 1937 a telescope with a diameter of 76 centimetres started work in the Sphinx.
From the Jungfraujoch you go up in a lift through the rock.
The weather station is the highest permanently staffed station in Europe.

abschnitte.text: The **Sphinx Observatory** stands on a rocky peak above the **Jungfraujoch**, at **3571 metres above sea level**. It is in the **canton of Valais**, right on the border with the canton of Bern. All around you can see glaciers such as the Great Aletsch Glacier. From the Jungfrau Railway station you go up in a **lift through the rock**. Tourists can also visit the viewing terrace.

As early as **1931**, the first researchers moved into the **High Alpine Research Station** on the Jungfraujoch. A few years later the observatory on the Sphinx was added. Scientists from many countries work here. They study, for example, the weather, glaciers, radiation from space and how the body reacts to high altitude.

In **1937** a telescope with a diameter of **76 centimetres** started work in the Sphinx. In the thin, clear mountain air, the Sun and the stars could be observed well. The dome of the Sphinx can be seen from far away. Today, measuring the air and the climate is more important at the station.

The Sphinx is often **above the polluted air of the valleys**. That is why it is particularly well suited to measuring **what the air is made of**. Here, for example, greenhouse gases, fine dust and pollutants that come from far away are measured. Sometimes even dust from the Sahara blows in. The series of measurements help us to understand climate change better.

On the Sphinx there is also a weather station run by MeteoSwiss. It is said to be the **highest permanently staffed station in Europe**. Up here it is cold almost all year round, and strong winds are common. The measurements are used in weather forecasting. In this way the Sphinx also helps with the weather report for the whole of Switzerland.

gewusst: The Jungfraujoch is also called the “Top of Europe”, because its railway station is the highest in Europe.
In fine weather you can see from the Sphinx far across the Alps as far as the Vosges and the Black Forest.

teile.einleitung: A sundial shows the time with a shadow. It needs no electricity or batteries, just sunshine. Sundials are among the oldest clocks in the world.
wichtigste: A sundial shows the time with a shadow.
It only works when the Sun is shining.
A sundial needs no electricity.
In Switzerland you often see sundials on house walls and churches.
On a sundial on the ground, the shadow moves clockwise.
When the Sun is at its highest, the shadow points roughly to the 12.

abschnitte.text: A sundial has a rod or a point, the **gnomon**. The Sun casts its **shadow** onto a surface with numbers. Because the Sun moves across the sky, the shadow moves too. Where it points, you read off the **time**. If there is no sunshine, for example at night or when there are thick clouds, the sundial does not work.

In the morning the Sun is in the east, and the shadow points west. At midday the Sun is in the south, and the shadow points north to the **12**. In the evening it points east. That is why on a sundial on the ground, the shadow moves **clockwise**. People even say that clock hands turn this way because they copy sundials.

In Switzerland you can see many sundials on **house walls** and **churches**. They are often beautifully painted, sometimes with a saying about time. There are particularly many in the Engadine, for example. These wall sundials usually face south, so that the Sun shines on them for a long time.

Sundials are **much older** than wristwatches. In ancient Egypt and Greece people already measured time with shadows. The Romans put up sundials in their squares. Mechanical clocks with gearwheels only came much later. A sundial needs no **electricity** and can therefore last a very long time.

You can measure time yourself. Push a **stick** into the sand or into a lawn. Every hour, mark where its **shadow** ends. And there you have a simple sundial. Careful: in summer, because of summer time, it shows about one hour less than your watch.

gewusst: A sundial shows local time, so it often differs a little from the time on your mobile phone.
In the Southern Hemisphere the shadow of a sundial on the ground turns the other way round.

teile.einleitung: Soyuz is a spacecraft that takes people into space and back again. It was developed in the Soviet Union and is built by Russia today. For decades, astronauts have been flying to the space station in it.
wichtigste: Soyuz comes from the Soviet Union and is built by Russia today.
The Russian word “Soyuz” means “union” or “alliance”.
There is room for three people in the descent capsule.
People have been flying into space in Soyuz spacecraft since 1967.
Today Soyuz usually flies to the International Space Station ISS.
The capsules land under parachutes in the steppe of Kazakhstan, with small braking rockets making the landing softer.

abschnitte.text: **Soyuz** was developed in the **Soviet Union**. Today it is built and flown by **Russia**. The Russian word “**Soyuz**” means “**union**” or “**alliance**”. The name is a reminder of the Soviet Union. The rocket that carries the spacecraft into space is also called Soyuz.

A Soyuz spacecraft has **three parts**. At the front is a living section where the crew can move around during the flight. In the middle sits the **descent capsule**. At the back is a section with **engines**, fuel and solar cells. Only the descent capsule comes back to Earth at the end. **Three astronauts** sit in it close together, wearing their **spacesuits**.

People have been flying into space in Soyuz spacecraft since **1967**. Since then the spacecraft has been **improved** again and again. Today Soyuz takes astronauts to the **International Space Station ISS**. It stays docked there and also serves as a **lifeboat**. After a few months it brings the crew back to Earth.

For the return, the descent capsule separates from the other parts. It races through the atmosphere and is slowed down strongly. Then large **parachutes** open. The capsule does not land in the sea but **on land**, in the vast **steppe of Kazakhstan**. Just above the ground, **small braking rockets** fire and make the landing softer.

After the landing, **recovery teams** are already waiting with **helicopters** and vehicles. They help the astronauts out of the cramped capsule. After months in weightlessness, the astronauts often cannot stand properly yet. So they are first put on chairs and examined by doctors. The launches also take place in **Kazakhstan**, from the **Baikonur** Cosmodrome.

gewusst: From 2011 to 2020 Soyuz was the only spacecraft that could take people to the ISS.
Soyuz is one of the spacecraft that has been in use for the longest time.

teile.einleitung: Recoil is a movement in the opposite direction: when something is pushed backwards, you yourself are pushed forwards. Rockets fly on this principle. But you can also see recoil in everyday life.
wichtigste: If a body pushes something backwards, it is itself pushed forwards.
Isaac Newton described that every force has an equal opposite force.
A rocket flies by recoil, pushing gases out backwards.
A rocket does not need air and so it can fly in space too.
Balloons, squid, fire hoses and lawn sprinklers also show recoil.

abschnitte.text: Blow up a **balloon** and let it go without tying it. It shoots off wildly! The air rushes **backwards** out of the opening. This pushes the balloon **forwards**. This is called **recoil**. The balloon keeps flying until there is no air left inside it.

Over 300 years ago the scientist **Isaac Newton** described an important law. It says: every **force** has an **equal opposite force** in the other direction. It is also called “**actio equals reactio**”, which is Latin for action equals reaction. If you stand on a **skateboard** and throw a heavy ball forwards, you roll backwards. If you throw a sack from a **rowing boat** onto the shore, the boat moves away from the shore.

A **rocket** burns fuel. This produces hot **gases** that stream out backwards with great force. The rocket pushes the gases backwards, and the gases push the rocket forwards. That is why a rocket does **not need air** to push against. It can fly even in the **airless vacuum of space**.

Animals use recoil too. A **squid** sucks water into its body. Then it squeezes it out powerfully through an opening. This makes it shoot off like a small rocket. **Jellyfish** also move by pushing out water.

When a lot of water shoots out of a **fire hose**, the hose pushes back hard. So the firefighters have to hold it tightly. A **lawn sprinkler** with arms bent at an angle also turns by recoil. The water sprays out at an angle and pushes the arms in the other direction.

gewusst: A jet aeroplane also flies by recoil: it pushes hot air out backwards.
Astronauts who work outside the space station have small jets on their spacesuit for emergencies, which they can use to move by recoil.

teile.einleitung: At full moon we see the whole lit-up side of the Moon as a round, bright disc. This happens about once a month, when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon.
wichtigste: At full moon the **Earth** is roughly between the Sun and the Moon.
The full moon rises in the **east** at about **sunset**.
On a clear night you can see it **all night long**.
A **lunar eclipse** only happens at full moon.
A second full moon in the same calendar month is called a **blue moon**.
The fact that the Moon looks huge on the horizon is an **illusion**.

abschnitte.text: The Moon does not shine by itself; it is lit up by the **Sun**. Depending on its position, we see more or less of its bright side. At full moon the Sun, the Earth and the Moon are almost in a line, with the **Earth** in the middle. Then we see the whole lit-up side. It takes about 29.5 days from one full moon to the next.

The full moon is **opposite** the Sun. That is why it rises when the Sun sets. Like the Sun, it rises roughly in the **east** and sets in the **west**. This is because the Earth turns. In the morning, when the Sun rises, the full moon sets. So it is in the sky all night long.

In a **lunar eclipse**, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. This can only happen when the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, that is, at full moon. But usually the Moon passes just above or below the Earth's shadow. In a total eclipse the Moon often turns **reddish**. Some sunlight is bent by the Earth's atmosphere and falls on it with a red colour. This is also called a **blood moon**.

Just above the horizon, the full moon often looks huge. In reality it is no bigger there than high in the sky. Our **brain** tricks us, because we compare it with houses, trees and mountains. This is called the **Moon illusion**. You can check with a photo that the disc stays the same size.

If there are two full moons in one calendar month, the second is called a **blue moon**. It is not actually blue; it is just a name. In stories, **wolves** howl at the full moon. In reality, wolves howl to communicate with their pack, not because of the Moon.

gewusst: The full moon is so bright that on a clear night you can cast a shadow outside.
We always see the same side of the Moon, even at full moon.

teile.einleitung: Eight planets orbit our Sun, each on its own path. If you know their order, you will find your way around the solar system much more easily. A funny memory sentence helps with this.
wichtigste: Starting from the Sun, the order is: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
Only Mercury and Venus orbit closer to the Sun than the Earth.
The Earth's neighbours are Venus on the inside and Mars on the outside.
Beyond the orbit of Mars there are four more planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
The first letters of the German memory sentence “Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unseren Nachthimmel” show the order.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is at the centre of our **solar system**. Eight **planets** orbit around it. Each planet takes a different amount of time for one lap: the further out it is, the longer its year lasts. Mercury completes a lap in only 88 days, while Neptune needs about 165 Earth years.

The first four planets are called **rocky planets** because they have a solid surface made of rock. First comes **Mercury**, the smallest planet. Then comes **Venus**, followed by our **Earth** as the third planet. The fourth is reddish **Mars**. Venus and Mars are the Earth's neighbours.

Between Mars and Jupiter lies the **asteroid belt**, a zone with many small chunks of rock. After that come four large planets: **Jupiter**, **Saturn**, **Uranus** and **Neptune**. Jupiter and Saturn are called **gas giants**, and Uranus and Neptune are also called **ice giants**. They do not have a solid surface like the Earth. Jupiter is the largest planet of all.

With the German sentence “**Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unseren Nachthimmel**” (“My father explains our night sky to me every Sunday”) you can easily remember the order. Each word begins with the same letter as a planet. “Mein” stands for Mercury, “Vater” for Venus and “erklärt” for Earth. “Mir” is Mars, “jeden” is Jupiter, “Sonntag” is Saturn. “Unseren” stands for Uranus and “Nachthimmel” for Neptune. In English, many people use “My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming” instead.

In the past, **Pluto** was also counted as a planet. In 2006 astronomers decided to classify it as a **dwarf planet**. Pluto is much smaller than the other planets and orbits far out beyond Neptune. That is why today there are officially eight planets.

gewusst: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth, but about 4 hours to reach Neptune.
From Switzerland you can see Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn in the sky with the naked eye.

teile.einleitung: The Big Bang is the beginning of the universe as we know it. About 13.8 billion years ago everything was unimaginably hot and dense, and since then the universe has been expanding and cooling. The Big Bang was not an explosion in one place, but the beginning of space and time themselves.
wichtigste: According to today's knowledge, the Big Bang happened about 13.8 billion years ago.
Since then the universe has been expanding.
The Belgian physicist and priest Georges Lemaître is regarded as the founder of the Big Bang theory.
In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that most galaxies are moving away from us.
Shortly after the Big Bang, mainly hydrogen formed, along with helium.
The cosmic background radiation is regarded as the “afterglow” of the Big Bang.
Science cannot yet answer what came before the Big Bang.

abschnitte.text: The **Big Bang** describes how the universe came from an extremely hot and dense state. This happened about 13.8 billion years ago. Since then space itself has been expanding, and everything has been cooling down. It was not an explosion into an empty space, because space and time also only began then. The name “Big Bang” was coined in 1949 by the British astronomer Fred Hoyle, who actually rejected the theory.

In 1927 the Belgian physicist and Catholic priest **Georges Lemaître** suggested that the universe is expanding and came from a “primeval atom”. In 1929 the American astronomer **Edwin Hubble** showed that most galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the faster they move. This fits exactly with a growing universe. If you calculate the motion backwards, everything was once together at one point. Today this is called the **Hubble-Lemaître law**.

In the first fractions of a second the universe was unimaginably hot. As it cooled, tiny particles such as **protons** and neutrons formed first. In about the first three minutes some of them fused into helium nuclei. In the end, ordinary matter consisted of about three quarters **hydrogen** and one quarter helium. Heavier elements such as carbon or iron only formed much later in stars.

About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe had cooled down enough for light to travel freely. This light still reaches us today from all directions, greatly cooled to about minus 270 °C. It is called the **cosmic background radiation** and is regarded as the “afterglow” of the Big Bang. In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered it by chance with an antenna. Satellites such as Planck later measured it very precisely.

abschnitte.titel: From the Big Bang to today
abschnitte.text: A few hundred million years after the Big Bang, the first **stars** lit up. They gathered into galaxies such as our Milky Way. About 4.6 billion years ago the solar system with the Earth formed. Since 1998 we have known that the universe is expanding faster and faster. Researchers call the cause **dark energy**; what exactly it is is still unknown.

The Big Bang theory is well supported, but many questions are still open. Nobody knows what came before the Big Bang, or whether this question even makes sense. It is also unclear what **dark matter** is made of, which can only be noticed through its gravity. Telescopes such as the James Webb Space Telescope are searching for the very first galaxies. At CERN in Geneva, physicists use particle accelerators to study conditions like those shortly after the Big Bang.

begriffe.erklaerung: Everything that exists: space, time, stars, galaxies and all matter and energy.
Faint radiation from all directions that is left over from the early, hot universe.
The light of distant galaxies is shifted towards reddish colours because they are moving away.
A still mysterious cause of the universe expanding faster and faster.

gewusst: A small part of the fuzz that old tube televisions showed when no channel was tuned in came from the cosmic background radiation.
The hydrogen in every drop of water you drink is almost as old as the universe itself.
Because the universe is expanding, the most distant galaxies we can see are now more than 13.8 billion light years away.

teile.einleitung: A pulsar is a fast-spinning neutron star that sends out radiation like a cosmic lighthouse. On Earth, extremely regular pulses are received from it.
wichtigste: A pulsar is a fast-spinning neutron star.
Its radiation comes out in beams at the magnetic poles and sweeps over the Earth like a lighthouse.
The first pulsar signal, in 1967, was nicknamed LGM-1.
In 1974, Antony Hewish received the Nobel Prize in Physics, partly for the discovery of pulsars.
Isolated pulsars spin more and more slowly over time.
In 1992, the first confirmed exoplanets were discovered around a pulsar.

abschnitte.text: A **neutron star** is the remnant of a massive star after a supernova. It is only about 20 kilometres across but heavier than the Sun. Many neutron stars spin very fast and have a strong magnetic field. Their radiation comes out in beams at the **magnetic poles**. When this cone of radiation sweeps over the Earth, we receive a pulse, like the light of a **lighthouse**.

In 1967, the student **Jocelyn Bell** in Cambridge discovered a strange, very regular radio signal. Because it was so even, people briefly thought of an artificial signal. Jokingly, it was called **LGM-1**, for “Little Green Men”. It soon became clear that it was a natural object. **Antony Hewish**, the leader of the group, received the Nobel Prize in 1974 together with Martin Ryle.

A single pulsar gives off energy and loses rotational energy as it does so. That is why its **rotation period** slowly gets longer. But there are also **millisecond pulsars**: old neutron stars collect matter from a **companion star** and are speeded up to hundreds of turns per second. The fastest known pulsar, PSR J1748-2446ad, turns about **716 times a second** (as of 2025).

Because pulsars tick so precisely, tiny deviations reveal a lot. In 1992, Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail found the **first confirmed exoplanets** around the pulsar PSR B1257+12. Today, **pulsar timing arrays** use networks of millisecond pulsars to detect very slow **gravitational waves**. In 2023, several research groups reported signs of such a background.

gewusst: In the Crab Nebula sits a pulsar, the remnant of a supernova that was observed in 1054.
Some pulsars tick as precisely as the best atomic clocks.

teile.einleitung: The launch pad is the place from which a rocket takes off into space. It has to withstand enormous heat, noise and forces. Around it there are many clever facilities.
wichtigste: A rocket takes off from a launch pad.
The rocket stands upright there.
People reach the rocket by a tall tower.
The flames are directed into a trench under the pad.
A lot of water dampens the noise and protects the pad.
Launch pads are made of thick concrete and steel because the fire is extremely hot.

abschnitte.text: On the **launch pad**, the rocket stands **upright**, with its tip pointing to the sky. This allows it to rise straight up at launch. Next to it stands a tall **tower**. People reach the rocket by it, for example technicians or astronauts. The fuel is also filled in through hoses on the tower. Shortly before launch, the arms of the tower swing back.

Large rockets are put together in an **assembly building**. Then a large **transport vehicle** slowly takes them to the launch pad. In the USA, huge crawler vehicles carried the Moon rockets out at walking pace. Other rockets are driven lying down on rails and only raised upright at the pad.

At launch, the fire from the engines is **extremely hot**. That is why launch pads are built of very **thick concrete and steel**. Under the pad there is a **trench**. The **flames** are directed into it so that they do not damage the rocket and the facilities. Huge clouds of exhaust billow out of it.

At launch, **a great deal of water** pours over the launch pad. It **dampens the noise**, which would otherwise be so loud that it could damage the rocket. At the same time the water **cools and protects** the pad. A large part of it turns to steam immediately. That is why you often see enormous white clouds of steam at launch.

After a launch, the launch pad is **checked and repaired**. Heat and pressure often leave damage. Only then can the next rocket take off. Europe launches its Ariane rockets from Kourou in French Guiana in South America. Swiss companies also work on these rockets, for example on the protective nose cone.

gewusst: Launch sites are often close to the equator, because there the Earth's rotation gives rockets the biggest boost.
Launch sites are often by the sea, so that falling rocket parts do not fly over inhabited land.

teile.einleitung: The Pierre Auger Observatory is a huge facility for measuring cosmic rays. It is in Argentina and searches for the most energetic particles that hit the Earth from space.
wichtigste: The observatory lies on the Pampa Amarilla near Malargüe in the province of Mendoza in Argentina.
The detectors are spread over about 3,000 square kilometres, about the size of the canton of Vaud.
About 1,600 water tanks measure particles on the ground, and fluorescence telescopes watch the glow of the air.
The tanks stand in a triangular grid about 1.5 kilometres apart.
The facility is named after Pierre Auger, who discovered extensive air showers in 1938.
According to the measurements, the most energetic particles come mainly from outside the Milky Way.

abschnitte.text: Tiny particles from space constantly rain down on the Earth: **cosmic rays**. Most of them are atomic nuclei, for example protons. When a very energetic particle hits the atmosphere, it collides with air molecules. This creates new particles, which collide again. In this way an avalanche of billions of particles forms, an **air shower**.

In 1938, the French physicist **Pierre Auger** made measurements in the Alps, including on the **Jungfraujoch**. He found that counters far apart from each other recorded particles at the same time. From this he concluded that a single particle from space can set off a large shower. This discovery of extensive air showers is the basis of today's observatory.

About 1,600 large **water tanks** stand on the ground. When fast particles from the shower fly through the water, a faint bluish light is produced. Light sensors in the tank measure it. Because the tanks are about 1.5 kilometres apart, a large shower hits several of them at once. From the arrival times, scientists calculate which direction the particle came from.

At the edge of the measuring area stand **fluorescence telescopes**. They see how the **nitrogen** in the air glows faintly in ultraviolet when a shower passes through. This light is so faint that the telescopes can only measure on clear, moonless nights, which is about a tenth of the time. When the tanks and telescopes are used together, it is called a **hybrid measurement**.

abschnitte.titel: Where do the particles come from?
abschnitte.text: The highest-energy particles are very rare. That is why such a huge area is needed to catch enough of them. In 2017, an analysis showed that particles above 8 · 10^18 electronvolts come slightly more often from a direction far from the centre of the Milky Way. This suggests that their sources lie in **other galaxies**. Exactly which objects accelerate them is still being researched.

gewusst: A single particle from space can hit an area of many square kilometres on the ground with particles.
Researchers from many countries work together at the facility.
The plateau was chosen because it is flat and thinly populated and usually has clear nights.

teile.einleitung: In the evening the Sun sinks below the horizon in the west. The sky then often glows red and orange. After that it slowly gets dark, and the night begins.
wichtigste: After sunset comes the night.
The time when it slowly gets dark is called dusk.
In Switzerland the Sun sets earliest in winter.
At the end of June it does not set until about half past nine in the evening.
Just before it sets, the Sun often looks red or orange.
It usually gets cooler after sunset.

abschnitte.text: In fact it is not the Sun that moves, but the **Earth that turns**. In the evening our place turns away from the Sun. Then the Sun sinks below the horizon in the **west**. Shadows become very long and point **east**. Shortly afterwards **dusk** begins, when it slowly gets dark. After that comes the **night**.

Just before it sets, the Sun often looks **red** or **orange**. Its light then has to take a long path through the air. On the way the blue light is scattered to the side. What is left is mainly red and yellow light. Dust and clouds can make the sky especially colourful.

In Switzerland the Sun sets earliest in **winter**: in December it is already before five o'clock in the afternoon. In summer it stays light much longer. At the **end of June** the Sun does not set until about **half past nine** in the evening. In the mountains it often disappears earlier behind a peak.

After sunset it usually gets **cooler**, because no more warmth comes from the Sun. Many animals now become active. The **bat** flies out and hunts insects. Hedgehogs, foxes and owls are also out and about at night. For other animals, such as many birds, it is time to sleep.

gewusst: When we see the Sun on the horizon, it is in reality already a little lower: the air bends its light slightly.
Sometimes, in the last moment of sunset, a green point of light flashes up, the “green flash”.

teile.einleitung: Titan is Saturn's largest moon. It is the only moon in the solar system with a thick atmosphere, and it has lakes, rivers and rain, though not made of water but of methane and ethane.
wichtigste: Titan was discovered in **1655** by **Christiaan Huygens**.
It is the only moon with a **thick atmosphere**, made mainly of **nitrogen**.
At about **minus 180 degrees Celsius**, it is icy cold on the surface.
Its lakes are filled with liquid **methane and ethane**.
The probe **Huygens** landed on Titan on 14 January 2005.
The largest sea is called **Kraken Mare**.

abschnitte.text: The Dutch scientist **Christiaan Huygens** discovered Titan in 1655 with a telescope he had built himself. Titan was the first known moon of Saturn. After Jupiter's Ganymede, it is the second largest moon in the solar system. With a diameter of just over 5000 kilometres, it is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

Titan is surrounded by a thick, orange **atmosphere**. It consists of over 90 per cent **nitrogen**, plus some methane. The Earth's air is also made mostly of nitrogen. The air pressure on the ground is about one and a half times as high as on Earth. A thick **haze** of organic substances hides the surface, which is why it could not be seen for a long time.

Titan is almost ten times further from the Sun than the Earth. At about minus 180 degrees it is so cold that **methane and ethane** are liquid. They form lakes and rivers and even fall as **rain**. The largest sea is **Kraken Mare**, near the North Pole. It is about the size of the Caspian Sea on Earth.

The space probe **Cassini** reached Saturn in 2004. It brought along the European landing probe **Huygens**, named after the discoverer. On 14 January 2005 Huygens landed on Titan and radioed back pictures of the surface. With radar and special cameras, Cassini was able to see through the haze and discover the lakes.

NASA is planning a new mission called **Dragonfly**. It is a kind of large **drone with rotors**. In Titan's thick air and low gravity, it can fly well. It is to fly from place to place and study the ground. According to current plans, the launch is due in 2028.

gewusst: Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury but has less mass.
To this day Huygens is the landing of a space probe on a celestial body furthest from the Earth.

teile.einleitung: The Schwarzschild radius tells you how small you would have to squeeze a mass for a black hole to form. It determines the size of the event horizon, from which nothing can escape, not even light. It is named after the German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild.
wichtigste: The Schwarzschild radius is r = 2GM / c².
It grows in a straight line with the mass: twice the mass, twice the radius.
For one solar mass it is about 3 km, for 10 solar masses about 30 km.
The boundary surface with this radius is called the event horizon.
Karl Schwarzschild found his solution in 1915 as a soldier in the First World War; it was published in 1916.
The photon sphere lies at 1.5 times and the innermost stable circular orbit at 3 times the Schwarzschild radius.

abschnitte.text: The Schwarzschild radius is **r = 2GM / c²**. Here G is the gravitational constant, M the mass and c the **speed of light**. The mass appears in the formula in a simple, linear way. So twice the mass gives **twice the radius**. For one solar mass it is about **3 km**, so for 10 solar masses about **30 km**. For a person weighing 70 kg, you get only about **10^-25 metres**, far smaller than an atomic nucleus.

In 1915 **Albert Einstein** published the field equations of the **general theory of relativity**. Shortly afterwards **Karl Schwarzschild** found an exact solution for a spherical mass. At the time he was serving as an **officer in the First World War** on the Eastern Front. In December 1915 he sent his solution to Einstein, and it was published in **1916**. Schwarzschild died in May 1916 of an illness he had caught at the front.

The boundary surface at the Schwarzschild radius is called the **event horizon**. There the **escape velocity** would be exactly the speed of light. That is why nothing can escape from inside. Events inside this surface can **never affect** observers outside. This is where the name comes from: you cannot see beyond this “horizon”.

For a black hole that is not spinning, the **photon sphere** lies at **1.5 times** the Schwarzschild radius. There, in theory, light can circle the black hole on a circular path, but these paths are unstable. At **3 times** the radius lies the **innermost stable circular orbit** for matter. Further in, matter quickly falls in. That is why the inner edge of an **accretion disc** typically ends there.

Because the radius grows in a straight line with the mass, the **volume** grows with the mass cubed. The **average density** inside the horizon therefore falls as 1/M². For small black holes it is unimaginably high. But for **supermassive** black holes with hundreds of millions of solar masses, it can be **lower than that of water**.

gewusst: If the Earth had to become a black hole, it would only be about the size of a marble: its Schwarzschild radius is about 9 millimetres.
The black hole Sagittarius A* at the centre of the Milky Way has a Schwarzschild radius of about 12 million kilometres.

teile.einleitung: Today Mars is a cold, dry desert planet. But many traces show that water once flowed there. There is still water on Mars today, but mainly as ice.
wichtigste: Liquid water can hardly exist on today's surface because of the **low air pressure**.
Dried-up **river valleys and deltas** show that water once flowed.
**Clay minerals** only form when rock is in contact with water for a long time.
In 2008 the probe **Phoenix** found water ice just under the ground.
In 2021 the rover **Perseverance** landed in Jezero Crater, which has an ancient delta.
The **solar wind** carried away a large part of the Martian air.

abschnitte.text: The air on Mars is very **thin**. At such a low air pressure, water quickly evaporates or freezes. So liquid water can hardly stay on the surface for long. But there is still water: as **ice** in the polar caps and under the ground. In 2008 the lander **Phoenix** dug in the north of Mars and uncovered bright ice. After a few days it had vanished into the air, a sign that it was water ice.

On pictures taken from orbit you can see dried-up **river valleys** and **deltas**. Such shapes only form when water flows for a long time and deposits sand. So Mars used to be warmer and wetter. Billions of years ago, **Jezero Crater** was a lake with a delta. In 2021 the rover **Perseverance** landed there; it is searching for traces of past life.

In **Gale Crater**, the rover **Curiosity** found layered mudstones. They had settled in a lake, so the crater was once filled with water. The rover **Opportunity** discovered small balls made of the iron mineral **haematite**. They usually form in rock that contains water. Because of their shape they were called “blueberries”.

Probes and rovers found **clay minerals** in many places. They form when rock is in contact with water for a long time. Their presence shows that there used to be a lot of water on Mars. Such minerals can also keep clues about the living conditions of the past.

Today Mars no longer has a global **magnetic field** to protect it. So over a long time the **solar wind**, a stream of particles from the Sun, was able to carry gas from the upper atmosphere off into space. A lot of water was lost along with the air. Part of the water is still locked up today as ice in the ground and in the polar caps.

gewusst: The polar caps of Mars contain so much water ice that you can see them from the Earth through a telescope as white patches.
Opportunity's haematite balls are only a few millimetres in size.

teile.einleitung: How far away is a star or a galaxy? To find out, astronomers use standard candles. These are objects in the sky whose true brightness is known.
wichtigste: A standard candle is an object with a known luminosity.
By comparing true and apparent brightness you can calculate the distance.
Brightness decreases with the square of the distance.
Henrietta Swan Leavitt discovered that brighter Cepheids have longer periods.
RR Lyrae stars in globular clusters also serve as standard candles.
Dust can distort distances if it is not corrected for.

abschnitte.text: Imagine lots of candles that are equally bright. The further away one is, the fainter it looks. If you know the **true luminosity** of an object, you can calculate its distance from its **apparent brightness**. Such an object is called a **standard candle**. With standard candles, distances far beyond the Milky Way are measured.

Brightness decreases with the **square of the distance**. If a standard candle looks **9 times fainter** than a similar one, it is **3 times as far** away, because 3 times 3 is 9. In astronomy, brightness is measured in **magnitudes**. A difference of 5 magnitudes means 100 times less light and therefore a distance **10 times** greater. So a star with an absolute magnitude of 0 and an apparent magnitude of 10 is 1000 **parsecs** away.

**Cepheids** are stars that regularly become brighter and dimmer. At the beginning of the 20th century the American **Henrietta Swan Leavitt** studied such stars in the **Small Magellanic Cloud**. Because all these stars are about the same distance away, she could compare their brightness directly. She discovered: **brighter Cepheids** have **longer pulsation periods**. So if you measure the period, you know the luminosity.

In **globular clusters** you find **RR Lyrae stars**. These variable stars all have roughly the same luminosity. For very distant galaxies, special star explosions are used: **Type Ia supernovae**. They are so bright that they can be seen across billions of light years. With them it was discovered that the universe is expanding faster and faster.

Fine **dust** floats between the stars. It swallows part of the light and makes objects look fainter. Then you would estimate the distance as **too great**. That is why researchers have to correct for the dust. It helps that dust dims blue light more than red light, so the object looks redder.

gewusst: Edwin Hubble used Leavitt's Cepheids to show that the Andromeda Galaxy lies far outside the Milky Way.
The Pole Star is also a Cepheid, but its brightness changes only a little.

teile.einleitung: Spiral galaxies are huge star systems with shining arms that wind like a whirlpool around a bright centre. Our Milky Way is one of these galaxies too. They are among the most beautiful objects in the sky.
wichtigste: A spiral galaxy has a flat disc with spiral arms and a bulge in the middle.
The arms shine bluish because many young, hot stars form there.
The density wave theory explains why the arms do not wind up.
The “B” in the Hubble classification stands for a bar through the centre.
Today the Milky Way is regarded as a barred spiral galaxy.
The Whirlpool Galaxy M51 is a famous spiral galaxy.

abschnitte.titel: How a spiral galaxy is built
abschnitte.text: A spiral galaxy consists of a flat **disc** of stars, gas and dust. In the middle sits a thicker part with mainly old stars, the **bulge**. Around it wind the **spiral arms**. The disc is very thin: in the **Milky Way**, thickness and diameter are roughly in the ratio **1 to 100**. All around lies a loose **halo** of old stars.

The spiral arms shine especially **bluish**. There a lot of gas is crowded together, and **many young, hot and massive stars** form. Such stars shine blue and very brightly. But they live only a short time and die before they move far out of the arm. There are stars between the arms too, but they are less striking.

A galaxy turns faster on the inside than on the outside. This is called **differential rotation**. So you would expect the arms to wind up tightly before long. The **density wave theory** explains why this does not happen. The arms are like a traffic jam on a motorway: stars and gas pass through, but the crowded zone stays in place. In the jam the gas is squeezed together, and new stars form.

The astronomer **Edwin Hubble** sorted galaxies by their shape. Spiral galaxies are called S, with the subtypes a, b and c. An **Sa** galaxy has a large bulge and tightly wound arms. An **Sc** galaxy has a small bulge and loosely wound arms. A **B**, as in “SBb”, stands for a **bar** through the centre. Today the **Milky Way** is also counted among these **barred spiral galaxies**.

The **Whirlpool Galaxy M51** is famous for its striking arms. It has a small companion galaxy that seems to hang on one arm. Our large neighbour, the **Andromeda Galaxy**, is also a spiral galaxy. On dark nights you can see it with the naked eye as a faint misty patch, including in the Swiss mountains.

gewusst: The Sun needs about 230 million years for one lap around the centre of the Milky Way.
The light from the Andromeda Galaxy has been travelling to us for about 2.5 million years.

teile.einleitung: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and our nearest neighbour in the solar system. It is almost as big as the Earth, but beneath its thick layer of clouds there is a scorching heat. In the sky it is the brightest object after the Sun and the Moon, which is why it is called the morning star or the evening star.
wichtigste: Venus is the second planet from the Sun.
It is the hottest planet in the solar system, hotter than Mercury.
A thick layer of clouds covers Venus completely.
When it shines brightly early in the morning it is called the morning star, in the evening the evening star.
Venus is named after the Roman goddess of love.
Venus is almost the same size as the Earth.
It turns very slowly and in the opposite direction to most planets.

abschnitte.text: **Venus** is the second planet from the Sun and about 108 million kilometres away from it. With a diameter of just over 12,100 kilometres, it is almost as big as the Earth. That is why it is sometimes called the Earth's sister. It is a **rocky planet** and has no moon. It is named after **Venus**, the Roman goddess of love.

Although Mercury is closer to the Sun, Venus is the hottest planet. Its surface is about 460 °C, hot enough to melt lead. This is caused by its extremely dense **atmosphere** of carbon dioxide. It traps the heat like a blanket; this is called the **greenhouse effect**. The air pressure on the ground is about 90 times as high as on Earth, like the pressure almost 1000 metres deep in the sea.

Venus is completely covered by a thick **layer of clouds**. These clouds are made of tiny droplets of **sulphuric acid**. They reflect sunlight strongly, which is why Venus shines so brightly. That is why you cannot see its surface from outside. Only with radar, for example from the space probe Magellan in the 1990s, was the landscape of volcanoes and lava plains mapped precisely.

Because Venus orbits closer to the Sun than the Earth, you always see it near the Sun. In the morning before sunrise it shines in the east as the **morning star**, and in the evening after sunset in the west as the **evening star**. In ancient times people at first thought the two were different stars. Through a telescope Venus shows phases like the Moon. Galileo Galilei observed these phases in 1610, and they helped to prove that the planets go around the Sun.

Venus turns on its axis extremely slowly. One turn takes about 243 Earth days, longer than its year of about 225 days. It also turns in a **retrograde** way, that is, in the opposite direction to the Earth. On Venus the Sun would therefore rise in the west and set in the east. But because of the thick clouds, you would hardly be able to see it from the ground.

With the **Venera programme**, the Soviet Union sent many probes to Venus. In 1970 Venera 7 was the first probe to make a soft landing on another planet, and in 1975 Venera 9 sent the first pictures from the surface. The landers usually only survived the heat and pressure for about an hour. Later NASA's probe **Magellan** mapped the planet, and from 2006 the European probe Venus Express studied the atmosphere.

begriffe.erklaerung: A name for Venus when it shines brightly in the eastern sky before sunrise.
Gases in the atmosphere trap heat, so that it gets warmer on the ground.
A very corrosive liquid; the clouds of Venus are made of its droplets.
The changing shape of a lit-up celestial body, for example as a crescent or a full disc.

gewusst: Venus is sometimes so bright that on a clear day you can even find it in daylight with the naked eye.
Almost all the mountains and craters of Venus are named after women: goddesses and famous women from history.
A day on Venus is longer than a whole Venus year.

teile.einleitung: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky. It is in the constellation Canis Major, the Great Dog, and so it is also called the Dog Star. The ancient Egyptians, Greeks and Romans already watched it closely.
wichtigste: Sirius has an apparent magnitude of about minus 1.46 mag.
It is about 8.6 light years away and one of the nearest stars.
Sirius shines about 25 times as strongly as the Sun.
It is a binary star; its companion Sirius B is a white dwarf.
Bessel predicted the companion in 1844, and Alvan Graham Clark saw it for the first time in 1862.
The dog days get their name from Sirius.

abschnitte.text: Sirius reaches an apparent magnitude of about **minus 1.46 mag**. Only the **Sun**, the **Moon** and some **planets** look brighter. It is so bright because it is **close** and at the same time shines much more strongly than the Sun. Sirius shines about **25 times** as strongly as the Sun. Its light takes only about **8.6 years** to reach us.

Sirius is **hotter than the Sun**. That is why it shines **bluish white**. When it is low on the horizon, it often **twinkles** in bright colours. This is caused by **turbulence** in the Earth's atmosphere, which keeps bending its light. In Switzerland you can see Sirius best on **winter nights**, low in the southern sky, to the lower left of the constellation Orion.

Sirius is a **binary star**. In **1844** the astronomer **Friedrich Bessel** noticed that Sirius moves across the sky in a slightly wavy line. From this he concluded that there was an invisible **companion**. **Alvan Graham Clark** discovered it in **1862** while testing a new telescope. This companion, **Sirius B**, is a **white dwarf**: the small, very dense remains of a star.

The ancient **Egyptians** called Sirius **Sothis**. Every year there was a time when the star could not be seen. Its first appearance in the **morning sky** before sunrise came at the same time as the start of the yearly **Nile flood**. The flood brought fertile mud to the fields. That is why Sirius was very important for the Egyptians' calendar.

Sirius is in the constellation **Canis Major, the Great Dog**, and is therefore also called the **Dog Star**. In ancient **Greece** and **Rome**, the hottest time of summer came at the same time as Sirius first appeared in the morning sky. That is why these days are still called the **dog days**. They fall roughly between the end of July and the end of August.

gewusst: A spoonful of material from Sirius B would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
Together with Procyon and Betelgeuse, Sirius forms the well-known Winter Triangle in the sky.

teile.einleitung: Every day the Sun reaches its highest point in the sky once. This is the Sun's highest point, also called solar noon. It happens around midday and depends on the season and on where you are on Earth.
wichtigste: The Sun is highest around midday.
In Switzerland it is then exactly in the south.
At midday your shadow points north and is at its shortest.
In summer the Sun is much higher at midday than in winter.
In Switzerland the Sun is never exactly straight above your head.
It is only straight above people near the equator.

abschnitte.text: In the morning the Sun rises in the east and climbs higher. Around **midday** it reaches its highest point. After that it sinks again and sets in the west. In Switzerland the Sun is exactly in the **south** at its highest point. Because of our time zone, this is usually not exactly at 12 o'clock but a little later, and in summer, because of summer time, even after 1 pm.

The higher the Sun, the shorter your **shadow**. That is why it is shortest at midday. Because the Sun is in the south, the shadow points **north**. With a stick and its shadow you can even find out the points of the compass this way. Sundials work in exactly the same way.

The Earth's axis is tilted. That is why in **summer** the Sun is much higher at midday than in winter. In Switzerland it reaches a good 65 degrees above the horizon in June, but only about 20 degrees in December. When the Sun is high, its rays hit the ground more steeply and warm it more. The days are also longer in summer. That is why it is warmer in summer.

In Switzerland the Sun is **never** exactly straight above your head. That only happens between the two **tropics**, that is, near the **equator**. There, on some days, you have almost no shadow at midday. The further north you go, the lower the Sun stays at midday.

abschnitte.titel: Watch out for the midday sun
abschnitte.text: Around midday the Sun is at its **strongest**. That is also when the invisible **UV radiation**, which causes sunburn, is greatest. So in summer it is best to stay in the shade over midday. A hat, sunglasses and sun cream give extra protection, especially in the mountains.

gewusst: Because Switzerland stretches from west to east, the Sun reaches its highest point in the Val Müstair more than a quarter of an hour earlier than in Geneva.
At the equator the Sun is exactly overhead at midday twice a year, in March and in September.

teile.einleitung: Star clusters are groups of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas. There are loose open star clusters and dense globular clusters. Some can be seen with the naked eye.
wichtigste: There are open star clusters and globular clusters.
The stars of a cluster formed from the same cloud of gas.
A globular cluster contains hundreds of thousands of stars.
Globular clusters are usually over 10 billion years old.
The Milky Way has about 150 known globular clusters; the largest is Omega Centauri.
Well-known open clusters are the Pleiades, the Hyades and the Beehive.

abschnitte.text: The stars of a **star cluster** formed from **the same cloud of gas**. That is why they are about the same age and the same distance from us. This is very useful for research. You can compare stars of different sizes and so learn how stars develop. There are two main kinds: **open star clusters** and **globular clusters**.

**Open star clusters** are loose and usually contain a few hundred to a thousand stars. They lie in the disc of the Milky Way and are often young. Over time their stars spread out. The **Pleiades** in Taurus are a well-known example. The **Hyades** form the face of the Bull. In the constellation Cancer, the Crab, you can see the **Beehive** with the naked eye as a misty patch.

**Globular clusters** are tightly packed balls of **hundreds of thousands** of stars. They are very old, usually **over 10 billion years**. They lie in the **halo**, a huge shell around the Milky Way. In our Milky Way **about 150** globular clusters are known. Because they are so old, they reveal a lot about the early days of our galaxy.

The largest globular cluster in the Milky Way is called **Omega Centauri**. It contains several million stars. To the naked eye it looks like a blurry star, which is why it was given a star's name. It is in the constellation Centaurus in the southern sky. You cannot see it from Switzerland, because there it never rises above the horizon.

gewusst: At the centre of a globular cluster the stars are so close together that the night sky there would shine with thousands of bright stars.
The Sun probably also formed in a star cluster whose stars spread out long ago.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is not always equally active. In a rhythm of about 11 years, it shows sometimes many and sometimes few sunspots. This rhythm is called the solar cycle.
wichtigste: A sunspot cycle lasts about 11 years on average.
After about 22 years the Sun's magnetic field has the same polarity again; this is the Hale cycle.
Heinrich Schwabe discovered the cycle in 1843.
In 1848 the Swiss Rudolf Wolf introduced the relative sunspot number.
From about 1645 to 1715 there were almost no sunspots, the Maunder Minimum.
Solar cycle 25 began in 2019.

abschnitte.text: The number of **sunspots** rises and falls regularly. A **sunspot cycle** lasts **about 11 years** on average, sometimes a little more or less. At **maximum** there are many spots, flares and auroras. At **minimum** the Sun is quiet. The total radiation output of the Sun changes by only **about 0.1 per cent**.

Behind the cycle is the Sun's **magnetic field**. In each 11-year cycle it reverses its polarity. Only after **about 22 years** does it have the same polarity as at the start. This double rhythm is called the **Hale cycle**, after the American astronomer George Ellery Hale. He discovered the magnetic fields in sunspots.

The German chemist and amateur astronomer **Heinrich Schwabe** observed the Sun for years. In **1843** he described the rhythm of the spots. The Swiss astronomer **Rudolf Wolf** introduced the **relative sunspot number** in **1848**. He also collected older observations and so reconstructed the cycles back into the 18th century. The numbering of the cycles goes back to him.

At the start of a cycle, new spots appear at **higher latitudes** on the Sun, far from the equator. During the cycle they appear closer and closer **towards the equator**. If you plot this on a graph, you get a pattern like butterfly wings. That is why it is called the **butterfly diagram**.

From about **1645 to 1715** almost no sunspots were observed. This period is called the **Maunder Minimum**, after the English astronomer Edward Maunder. It fell during the so-called Little Ice Age, when it was often colder in Europe. Whether the quiet Sun played an important part in this is still being researched. The current **solar cycle 25** began in **2019**.

gewusst: Rudolf Wolf later became the first director of the Federal Observatory in Zurich.
The cycles have been numbered since 1755, when cycle 1 began.

teile.einleitung: A Type Ia supernova is the explosion of a white dwarf in a binary star system. Because these explosions are almost always similarly bright, they serve as a measuring stick for huge distances in the universe.
wichtigste: In a Type Ia supernova, a **white dwarf** made of carbon and oxygen explodes.
It is approaching the **Chandrasekhar limit** of about 1.4 solar masses.
A typical feature is a strong absorption line of **silicon** in the spectrum.
The glow over weeks comes from the decay of **nickel-56** via cobalt-56 to iron-56.
At its peak it reaches an absolute magnitude of about **-19.3 mag**.
With distant Type Ia supernovae it was found in 1998 that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

abschnitte.text: A white dwarf is the dense remains of a star. It is held up by the **degeneracy pressure** of its electrons. When its mass approaches about 1.4 solar masses, the **Chandrasekhar limit**, this pressure is no longer enough. Then a **thermonuclear explosion** ignites and tears the white dwarf apart completely. Unlike other supernovae, no neutron star is left behind.

Two main ways in which they form are discussed. In one case the white dwarf sucks matter from a normal **companion star** until it becomes too heavy. In the other case two white dwarfs **merge**. Which way is more common is not yet clear. Perhaps both happen.

In its spectrum, a Type Ia supernova shows no hydrogen, but at its peak it shows a strong line of singly ionised **silicon** at about 615 nm. This is how it is told apart from types Ib and Ic. The explosion typically produces about 0.6 solar masses of **nickel-56**. It decays with a half-life of 6 days into cobalt-56, which decays with a half-life of 77 days into iron-56. This energy makes the supernova shine for weeks.

At its peak a Type Ia supernova shines as brightly as billions of Suns, at about **-19.3 mag**. That is why it can be seen across billions of light years. But the explosions are not all exactly equally bright. According to the **Phillips relation**, brighter supernovae fade more slowly. With this correction they become very precise **standard candles**: the distance can be calculated from the apparent brightness.

In 1998 two research teams studied distant Type Ia supernovae. They were fainter, and therefore further away, than expected if the expansion were slowing down. It followed that **the expansion of the universe is speeding up**. The suspected cause is **dark energy**. This discovery was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011.

gewusst: Tycho's Supernova of 1572 was confirmed as Type Ia in 2008: its light was reflected by clouds of dust and reached us as a light echo only centuries later.
A large part of the iron in the universe comes from Type Ia supernovae.

teile.einleitung: Venus is surrounded by an extremely dense and hot atmosphere. It is made almost entirely of carbon dioxide and makes Venus the hottest planet in the solar system, hotter than Mercury, which is closer to the Sun.
wichtigste: The atmosphere of Venus is about **96 per cent** **carbon dioxide**.
At the surface it is about **460 °C** day and night.
A strong **greenhouse effect** traps the heat.
The air pressure on the ground is about **90 times** as high as on Earth.
The clouds are made mainly of droplets of **sulphuric acid**.
In 1970 **Venera 7** was the first probe to make a soft landing on Venus.

abschnitte.text: About **96 per cent** of the atmosphere of Venus is **carbon dioxide**. Nitrogen makes up only about 3.5 per cent. The atmosphere is enormously dense. On the ground the pressure is about **92 bar**, while on Earth it is about 1 bar. That is like the water pressure about 900 m deep in the sea.

At the surface of Venus it is about **460 °C** day and night. That is hot enough to melt lead. The reason is a strong **greenhouse effect**: the dense atmosphere lets the Sun's energy in, but hardly lets any heat radiation back out. Mercury is closer to the Sun, but it has almost no atmosphere. That is why it cools down a lot at night.

Venus is completely covered in **clouds**. They are made mainly of tiny droplets of **sulphuric acid** and lie at a height of about 50 to 70 km. The clouds reflect a lot of sunlight. That is why Venus shines so brightly in our sky as the morning star or evening star.

Venus itself turns very slowly. Its upper atmosphere, on the other hand, is very fast. Strong winds drive the clouds once around the whole planet in about **4 days**. This is called **super-rotation**, because the clouds are much faster than the planet itself.

In December 1970 the Soviet probe **Venera 7** was the first to make a soft landing on Venus. Despite the heat and pressure, it radioed measurements back to Earth for about 20 minutes. ESA's probe **Venus Express** orbited Venus from 2006 to 2014. Among other things, it studied the winds, clouds and gases of the atmosphere.

gewusst: Venus needs longer to turn once on its axis than to go once around the Sun.
The air pressure on Venus would squash a submarine as if it were 900 m deep in the sea.

teile.einleitung: During the Cold War, the USA and the Soviet Union competed to see who could achieve the greatest successes in space. This space race lasted from about 1957 to 1975 and ended with the Moon landing and a joint flight.
wichtigste: The **space race** was run by the USA and the Soviet Union during the Cold War.
The launch of Sputnik in 1957 caused the **Sputnik shock** in the West.
In 1958 the US space agency **NASA** was founded.
In 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, followed shortly afterwards by Alan Shepard as the first American.
