President Kennedy wanted to put people on the Moon before 1970, and in 1969 it was achieved.
The joint flight **Apollo-Soyuz** in 1975 is seen as the symbolic end of the race.

abschnitte.text: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put the first artificial satellite into space with **Sputnik 1**. The USA was surprised and alarmed. This **Sputnik shock** led to large investments in research and education. Each side wanted to show that its technology and its political system were better.

In January 1958 the USA launched its first satellite, **Explorer 1**. Its instruments discovered zones with many charged particles around the Earth. They are called the **Van Allen belts**, after the scientist James Van Allen. In the same year **NASA** was founded, which later ran the Moon programme.

On 12 April 1961 the Soviet **Yuri Gagarin** became the first person to fly into space. On 5 May 1961 **Alan Shepard** followed as the first American; his flight lasted only about 15 minutes. In 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space. In 1965 **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to climb out of a spacecraft and floated on a tether for about twelve minutes.

In 1961 US President **John F. Kennedy** announced that he would land a man on the Moon and bring him back safely before 1970. In July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin became the first people to walk on the Moon with **Apollo 11**. Switzerland was there too: a **solar wind sail** from the University of Bern was the first experiment to be set up on the Moon.

In 1975 an American Apollo spacecraft and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked together in space. The crews shook hands. The **Apollo-Soyuz** project is seen as the symbolic end of the race. Today the USA and Russia work together with other countries on the International Space Station ISS.

gewusst: Sputnik 1 was a ball only about 58 cm across and sent out a simple beeping.
The solar wind sail from Bern was set up on the Moon even before the American flag.

teile.einleitung: Valles Marineris is a huge system of canyons on Mars. It is one of the largest canyons in the whole solar system and makes the Grand Canyon in the USA look tiny.
wichtigste: Valles Marineris is a **system of trenches** on Mars.
It is over **4000 km** long, almost a fifth of the way around Mars.
At its deepest points it is about **7 km** deep.
In places it is up to about **200 km** wide.
It lies just south of the **Martian equator**.
It is named after the space probe **Mariner 9**.

abschnitte.text: Valles Marineris runs in an **east-west direction** just south of the Martian equator. It stretches for more than **4000 km**. On Earth it would reach right across a whole continent. In some places it is up to about **7 km** deep. The Grand Canyon in the USA, on the other hand, is at most about 1.8 km deep.

In places the system of trenches is up to about **200 km** wide. So from one edge you often cannot even see the other edge. It is not a single canyon. Many **valleys** lie side by side and merge into each other. The Latin name means something like “valleys of the Mariner”.

NASA's probe **Mariner 9** went into orbit around Mars in November 1971. It was the **first probe** to orbit another planet. In 1971 and 1972 it photographed the system of trenches for the first time. That is why it was named after the probe.

Valles Marineris formed mainly through **cracks in the Martian crust**. Experts think the crust tore apart, probably in connection with the bulging up of the large **volcanic region** to the west of it. Later, **landslides** and probably water too shaped the canyons further. So unlike the Grand Canyon, it was not mainly carved out by a river.

gewusst: Valles Marineris is about four times as deep as the Grand Canyon.
Valles Marineris is almost ten times as long as the Grand Canyon.

teile.einleitung: A white dwarf is the small, very dense remains of a star that has used up its fuel. Our Sun will also become a white dwarf at the end of its life.
wichtigste: A white dwarf is about **the size of the Earth** but has about the mass of the Sun.
One cubic centimetre of its material weighs about **one tonne**.
It no longer carries out nuclear fusion and only gives off **leftover heat**.
A completely cooled white dwarf would be a **black dwarf**.
If it takes in too much gas from a partner, it can explode as a **supernova**.
Very heavy stars become **neutron stars** or **black holes** instead.

abschnitte.text: The Sun gets its energy from **nuclear fusion** inside it. In a few billion years its supply will be used up. Then it will swell up into a **red giant** and shed its outer layers. Only the hot, dense core will be left. This small remnant is called a **white dwarf**.

A white dwarf has about the mass of the Sun, but it is only roughly **the size of the Earth**. That makes it extremely **dense**. A piece the size of a sugar cube would weigh about one tonne, as much as a car. The matter is packed so tightly that the pressure of the **electrons** holds the star up.

A white dwarf no longer produces any new energy. It only gives off its stored **leftover heat**. Young white dwarfs are very hot at the surface and therefore shine **white**, even though they are faint. Over time they cool down. A completely cooled white dwarf would become a **black dwarf**. But that takes so long that there are none yet in today's universe.

abschnitte.titel: An explosion in a binary star
abschnitte.text: Many stars live in pairs in a **binary star system**. If a white dwarf takes in too much gas from its partner, it becomes too heavy. Then a gigantic explosion ignites, a **Type Ia supernova**. The limit is about 1.4 solar masses, the **Chandrasekhar limit**.

Not every star becomes a white dwarf. **Very massive** stars explode as a supernova at the end. Their core becomes a **neutron star** or a **black hole**. A well-known white dwarf is **Sirius B**, the small companion of the brightest star in our night sky.

gewusst: Most stars in the Milky Way will become white dwarfs at the end of their lives.
A white dwarf needs much longer to cool down than the universe has existed so far.

teile.einleitung: A red giant is a star that has swollen up hugely towards the end of its life. It is enormous, but cooler on its surface than the Sun. Our Sun will also become a red giant in the distant future.
wichtigste: A star becomes a red giant when the hydrogen in its core runs low.
Sun-like stars reach this phase towards the end of their lives.
Red giants shine reddish because their surface is cooler than the Sun's.
Even so, they give off much more light in total because their surface is huge.
Later, helium fuses into carbon in the core.
As a red giant, the Sun will very probably swallow Mercury and Venus.

abschnitte.text: Stars like the Sun fuse **hydrogen into helium** in their core. This produces the energy that makes them shine. This calm stage is called the **main sequence**, and it lasts for most of a star's life. When the **hydrogen in the core runs low**, the star changes. Its outer layers **swell up** greatly, and it becomes a **red giant**.

The colour of a star depends on the **temperature of its surface**. A red giant is **cooler than the Sun** on the outside and therefore shines reddish. Each square metre of its surface gives off less light. But because the surface is **enormously large**, the star gives off much more light in total than the Sun.

While the star swells up, its core shrinks and gets hotter and hotter. Once it is hot enough, a new kind of **nuclear fusion** starts there. Now **helium fuses into carbon**. In the end a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers. What is left is a small, hot **white dwarf**.

The Sun will also become a red giant, but not for about **five billion years**. It will then be **several hundred times larger** than today. Its edge will reach into the region of today's **Earth orbit**. The inner planets **Mercury** and **Venus** will very probably be swallowed. Whether the Earth will also disappear inside the Sun is uncertain.

There are many red giants in the sky. A well-known example is **Mira** in the constellation **Cetus, the Whale**. Its name means “**the wonderful one**”. Mira **pulsates** and changes its brightness greatly over about **eleven months**. Sometimes you can see it with the naked eye, sometimes only through a telescope.

gewusst: The bright, orange star Aldebaran in the constellation Taurus is a giant star.
Almost all the carbon in the universe, including the carbon in our bodies, was once made inside stars.

teile.einleitung: Albert Einstein's theory of relativity completely changed how we understand space, time and gravity. It shows, for example, that time passes more slowly for fast-moving bodies and that mass curves space. What sounds strange has been confirmed by many measurements and is even built into every GPS device.
wichtigste: The theory of relativity comes from Albert Einstein and has two parts.
The special theory of relativity appeared in 1905, the general theory in 1915.
For fast-moving bodies time passes more slowly; this is called time dilation.
According to the formula E equals mc², mass and energy are equivalent.
The general theory of relativity describes gravity as a curving of space and time.
During the solar eclipse of 1919, the bending of starlight by the Sun was measured.
Without relativistic corrections, GPS would be off by kilometres after just one day.

abschnitte.text: **Albert Einstein** developed his most important ideas in Switzerland. He studied at ETH Zurich and from 1902 worked at the patent office in Bern. There, in 1905, he published the **special theory of relativity** and the famous formula E equals mc². In his flat on the Kramgasse in Bern, today's Einstein House, you can get a feel for this time. He published the **general theory of relativity** in Berlin in 1915.

The special theory of relativity is based on the idea that the **speed of light** is the same for all observers. It follows from this that moving clocks run more slowly, which is called **time dilation**. If a spaceship flies at 0.8 times the speed of light and 6 years pass on board, then 10 years pass on Earth. In everyday life we notice nothing of this because we are far too slow. But with particles in accelerators such as at CERN in Geneva, the effect can easily be measured.

The formula **E equals mc²** says that mass and energy are equivalent. Here c stands for the speed of light, which multiplied by itself gives a huge number. Just 1 gram of mass corresponds to 9 times 10 to the power of 13 joules, as much energy as thousands of tonnes of explosives release. In the Sun, mass is turned into energy every second through **nuclear fusion**. Nuclear power stations also make use of this relationship.

The general theory of relativity describes gravity as a **curvature of spacetime**. You can imagine it like a stretched cloth into which a heavy ball presses a dip. It is based on the **equivalence principle**: gravitational mass and inertial mass are equivalent, which is why all bodies fall equally fast in a vacuum. The theory explained why the perihelion of Mercury shifts by an extra 43 arcseconds or so per century. It also predicts black holes and gravitational waves, which were measured directly for the first time in 2015.

During the solar eclipse of 1919, people observed that the Sun bends the light of stars, exactly as Einstein had predicted. This made him world famous. Today every **GPS** needs the theory of relativity. Because of relativistic effects, the atomic clocks of the satellites run faster than clocks on the ground by about 38 microseconds a day in total. Without correction, working out your location would get worse by about ten kilometres every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: Moving clocks run more slowly than clocks at rest.
Space and time thought of together as one single structure.
Gravitational mass and inertial mass are equivalent.
The highest possible speed, about 300,000 kilometres per second.

gewusst: On a high mountain such as the Jungfraujoch, time passes very slightly faster than in the valley because gravity is weaker.
Einstein did not receive the Nobel Prize in 1921 for the theory of relativity, but for explaining the photoelectric effect.
Einstein was a Swiss citizen for a long time and kept his Swiss citizenship until his death.

teile.einleitung: Sunspots are dark patches on the surface of the Sun. They are slightly cooler than their surroundings and therefore darker. Some are bigger than our whole Earth.
wichtigste: Sunspots look like dark patches on the Sun.
They are slightly cooler than the rest of the Sun's surface.
Sunspots move along as the Sun turns and disappear again after a while.
Many spots are bigger than the Earth.
The number of spots rises and falls in a rhythm of about 11 years.
You must never look at the Sun without a protective filter.

abschnitte.text: The surface of the Sun is about 5500 degrees hot. A sunspot is about 1500 degrees cooler. It still shines very brightly, but next to its hotter surroundings it looks **dark**. A spot has a dark core, the **umbra**, and a lighter edge, the **penumbra**. The cooling is caused by strong magnetic fields that slow down the flow of heat from inside.

From the Earth, sunspots look small. In reality, many are bigger than the **Earth**. Large groups of spots can be many times the Earth's diameter. Spots often appear in groups. Above them, strong outbursts sometimes occur, the **solar flares**.

Sunspots do not stay in the same place. Because the Sun turns, they **move** across the Sun's disc. After days or weeks they disappear again and new ones appear. The number is not the same every year. About every **11 years** there are especially many, and in between only a few. This rhythm is called the sunspot cycle.

Over 400 years ago, **Galileo Galilei** was already observing sunspots with a telescope. Today researchers use telescopes with a **solar filter** and satellites in space. Very important: never look directly at the Sun, and never look through binoculars or a telescope without a tested filter. This can badly injure your eyes immediately.

In the 19th century the Zurich astronomer **Rudolf Wolf** introduced a number with which sunspots can be compared. It is called the relative sunspot number or Wolf number. For a long time the spots were counted at the observatory in Zurich. Thanks to such records, we know the Sun's activity over many centuries.

gewusst: Sunspots often last only a few days, but large groups can last several weeks.
A sunspot only looks dark: seen on its own, it would shine more brightly than the full Moon.

teile.einleitung: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and an icy, blue-green giant. It was the first planet to be discovered with a telescope. What is particularly strange is that it lies almost on its side and so travels around the Sun like a rolling ball.
wichtigste: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun.
It was discovered in 1781 by William Herschel with a telescope.
Uranus shines blue-green because methane in its atmosphere swallows red light.
Its axis of rotation is tilted so much that it lies almost on its side.
It needs about 84 years for one lap around the Sun.
Uranus is one of the ice giants and has rings and many moons.
So far only one single space probe, Voyager 2, has visited Uranus.

abschnitte.text: Until the 18th century only six planets were known, up to Saturn. On 13 March 1781, the German-born musician and astronomer **William Herschel** discovered a new celestial body in England with a **telescope** he had built himself. At first he thought it was a comet. But it soon turned out to be a planet. At a stroke, the known solar system became twice as big.

Uranus has about four times the diameter of the Earth and about 14 Earth masses. It is counted among the **ice giants**, because inside it contains a lot of water, ammonia and methane in the form of hot, dense ice. Its outer atmosphere consists mainly of hydrogen and helium. The **methane** in it swallows red light, which is why Uranus looks blue-green. With temperatures of about minus 220 °C, it has the coldest atmosphere of all the planets.

The **axis of rotation** of Uranus is tilted by about 98 degrees. So it lies almost on its side and, so to speak, rolls around the Sun. A huge celestial body probably rammed it a long time ago. This creates extreme **seasons**: each pole has sunlight for about 42 years and then darkness for 42 years. That is because a Uranus year lasts about 84 Earth years.

Uranus has 13 known dark, narrow **rings**, which were discovered in 1977. In addition, almost 30 moons are now known. Unlike those of other planets, they are not named after figures from legends but after characters from works by **William Shakespeare** and Alexander Pope. The largest are called Titania, Oberon, Umbriel, Ariel and Miranda. Miranda has a particularly rugged surface with cliffs up to 20 kilometres high.

So far only one single space probe has flown past Uranus: **Voyager 2** in January 1986. It sent back pictures of the moons and rings and measured the tilted magnetic field. Since then Uranus has been observed mainly with the **Hubble Space Telescope** and the James Webb Telescope. NASA is planning its own Uranus mission for the future, with a probe that is to orbit it.

Uranus is at the limit of what you can see with the naked eye. Under a very dark sky it can be made out as a faint dot if you know exactly where to look. With **binoculars** it is easier to find. In a telescope it appears as a small greenish disc. It is named after **Uranus**, the god of the sky in Greek legend.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large planet that contains a lot of frozen water, ammonia and methane, like Uranus and Neptune.
The imaginary line around which a planet turns.
A gas made of carbon and hydrogen that gives Uranus its blue-green colour.
An uncrewed vehicle that flies through space and explores other celestial bodies.

gewusst: Herschel wanted to call the planet “George's Star” in honour of the English king George III.
A day on Uranus lasts only about 17 hours, even though a Uranus year is 84 Earth years long.
Since its discovery in 1781, Uranus has only gone around the Sun about three times.

teile.einleitung: Stars are huge, glowing hot balls of gas that shine by themselves. Our Sun is a star too; the others are just so unimaginably far away that they look like tiny points of light to us. On a clear night you can see several thousand stars with the naked eye.
wichtigste: Stars are hot balls of gas that shine by themselves through nuclear fusion.
The Sun is the star closest to the Earth.
You cannot see the stars during the day because the Sun is much brighter.
Very hot stars shine bluish white, cooler stars reddish.
Stars twinkle because the air in the Earth's atmosphere is moving.
The Milky Way is our galaxy, which contains several hundred billion stars.
A shooting star is not a star but a grain of dust burning up.

abschnitte.text: A **star** is a huge ball of gas, mainly hydrogen and helium. Inside it is millions of degrees hot. There, atomic nuclei fuse together; this is called **nuclear fusion**. This releases energy, which shines out into space as light and heat. Planets and moons, on the other hand, do not shine by themselves; they only reflect the light of their star.

Stars have different colours, and the colour reveals their **temperature**. Very hot stars shine bluish white, like Rigel in Orion. Medium stars like the Sun are yellowish, and cool stars like Betelgeuse reddish. There are small **dwarf stars** and huge **supergiants** that are hundreds of times bigger than the Sun. The brightest star in the night sky is Sirius in the constellation Canis Major, the Great Dog.

The distances to the stars are measured in **light years**. A light year is the distance that light travels in one year, almost 9.5 trillion kilometres. The nearest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, just over 4 light years away. So when we look at a star, we see light that set off years or thousands of years ago. Some stars that we see may not even exist any more.

The Sun belongs to a huge island of stars, the **Milky Way**. It is our **galaxy** and contains several hundred billion stars. On dark nights, for example in the mountains, you can see it as a bright, milky band across the sky. The universe in turn contains countless galaxies. The nearest large neighbouring galaxy is the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.5 million light years away.

Stars twinkle because their light has to pass through the restless **atmosphere of the Earth**. Warm and cold layers of air move and keep bending the light a little. That is why stars do not twinkle in space. During the day the stars are still there, but the bright sunlight is scattered in the air and outshines them. Only during a total solar eclipse can you see bright stars in the daytime.

A **shooting star** is really a tiny grain of dust from space. It races into the Earth's atmosphere at great speed and burns up high above. Experts call the trail of light a **meteor**. You can see a particularly large number of shooting stars around 12 August, when the Earth flies through the dust trail of a comet. This shower is called the Perseids.

begriffe.erklaerung: The joining together of atomic nuclei, which makes stars shine.
The distance that light travels in one year, almost 9.5 trillion kilometres.
A huge collection of billions of stars, gas and dust.
The trail of light of a particle burning up in the atmosphere.

gewusst: There are probably more stars in the universe than grains of sand on all the beaches on Earth.
The gold in your jewellery was probably formed when two neutron stars merged.
In a big city you often see only a few dozen stars because of all the lights, but in the mountains you can see thousands.

teile.einleitung: Astronauts need to sleep too, even when they are circling high above the Earth in the space station. In weightlessness this is very different from being in bed at home. There is no up and no down, and everything would float away.
wichtigste: Astronauts sleep in a sleeping bag in a small sleeping cabin.
The sleeping bag is fastened to the wall so that it does not float around.
The space station orbits the Earth in about an hour and a half, so there are about 16 sunrises a day.
Sleep masks and earplugs help against light and the humming of the machines.
About 8 hours of sleep are planned into the daily schedule.

abschnitte.text: On the **space station**, each astronaut has a small **sleeping cabin**. It is about the size of a **phone box**. Inside it hangs a **sleeping bag** that is fastened to the wall. Without this fastening, a sleeping astronaut would drift through the station. In the cabin everyone also has a little space for personal things such as photos.

In **weightlessness** there is no up and no down. So you can sleep on the wall or the ceiling just as well as on the floor. Without weight, your **arms** do not hang down but float forwards. That is why many astronauts tuck their arms into the sleeping bag. You do not need a pillow, because your head is not resting on anything.

The space station circles the Earth once in about **an hour and a half**. So the astronauts see about **16 sunrises** in one day. On top of that, many lamps shine in the station. To make it dark enough to sleep, they often wear a **sleep mask**. The time on board follows a fixed plan and not the Sun.

**Fans** and machines are always running in the space station. This is important: without moving air, the breathed-out air would collect around your head. But the machines **hum** all the time. That is why some astronauts sleep with **earplugs**.

People need enough **sleep** in space too. About **8 hours** of sleep are planned into the daily schedule. Only well-rested astronauts can carry out their difficult tasks safely. Even so, many sleep a little less in space than on Earth. That is why doctors on Earth keep a close eye on how well the crew sleeps.

gewusst: Some astronauts say that after returning to Earth they at first found it hard to fall asleep without floating.
The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier flew into space four times on the Space Shuttle and also slept floating there.

teile.einleitung: The Sun is a star, just like the many points of light in the night sky, only much closer to us. Every day it gives us light and warmth and so makes life on Earth possible at all. All the planets of our solar system orbit it.
wichtigste: The Sun is a star and the centre of our solar system.
It gives the Earth light and warmth; without it there would be no life.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth.
Over a million Earths would fit inside the Sun.
The Sun consists mainly of hydrogen and helium.
You must never look directly at the Sun, because it harms your eyes.
When the Moon covers the Sun, this is called a solar eclipse.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is a perfectly ordinary **star**, one of billions in the Milky Way. It is about 150 million kilometres from the Earth. Its diameter is about 1.4 million kilometres, which is about 109 times the diameter of the Earth. Over a million Earths would fit inside it. The Sun contains over 99 per cent of the total mass of the **solar system**.

The Sun consists mainly of **hydrogen** and **helium**. In its core it is about 15 million degrees hot. There, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium; this is called **nuclear fusion**. This releases an enormous amount of energy, which travels outwards and is given off as light and heat. At the visible surface it is about 5500 °C hot.

Without the Sun, the Earth would be an icy cold, dark lump of rock. Plants use its light for **photosynthesis** and so produce food and oxygen. The Sun also drives the weather, because it warms the air and seas by different amounts. Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach us. Today people use solar energy with **solar panels**, including on many Swiss roofs.

Sometimes you can see dark **sunspots** on the Sun; these are slightly cooler places. During outbursts the Sun flings particles into space, the **solar wind**. When these hit the Earth's magnetic field, they create auroras, which during strong storms can even be seen in Switzerland, as in May 2024. When the Moon moves in front of the Sun, there is a **solar eclipse**.

You must never look directly at the Sun, not even briefly, because this can permanently damage the **retina** in your eye. With a telescope or binoculars it is especially dangerous. Your skin needs protection too, because **UV radiation** can cause sunburn. In the mountains it is stronger than in the lowlands. Sun cream, a hat and sunglasses help.

The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and has lived about half of its life. In about 5 billion years the hydrogen in its core will run low. Then it will swell up into a **red giant**. In the end, a small, slowly cooling **white dwarf** will be left.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge, hot ball of gas that shines by itself.
The joining of small atomic nuclei into bigger ones, which releases a lot of energy.
A stream of tiny particles that the Sun constantly blows into space.
A darker, slightly cooler place on the surface of the Sun.

gewusst: The light that comes from the Sun today was made deep inside it many thousands of years ago and took a long time to reach the surface.
Through nuclear fusion the Sun loses about 4 million tonnes of mass every second, but it is so big that this hardly matters.
The Sun also spins on its axis, faster at the equator than at the poles.

teile.einleitung: The Aar Massif is a large block of ancient granite and gneiss in the heart of the Swiss Alps. It stretches from Valais through the Bernese Oberland into Central Switzerland and carries peaks such as the Finsteraarhorn.
wichtigste: The Aar Massif is an external massif made of European basement rock.
The Central Aar Granite formed about 300 million years ago during the Variscan mountain building.
To the south lies the Gotthard Massif, separated by the Urseren Valley.
The Finsteraarhorn, the highest mountain in the Bernese Alps, is made of its rocks.
Large rock crystals grew in Alpine fissures.
Large parts of the Jungfrau-Aletsch World Heritage Site lie in the Aar Massif.

abschnitte.text: The **external massifs** are bulges of the European **crystalline basement** on the northern edge of the Alps. Crystalline means that the rocks are made of crystals, like **granite** and **gneiss**. Unlike many other parts of the Alps, the Aar Massif was not pushed a long way as a **nappe**. It was deformed and lifted up where it was.

The **Central Aar Granite** crystallised about **300 million years ago**. That was at the end of the **Variscan mountain building**, long before the Alps existed. When the Alps formed, the granite was only lifted and deformed. To the south lies the **Gotthard Massif**. In between there is a narrow zone of soft rocks that has shaped the **Urseren Valley**.

At 4274 metres, the **Finsteraarhorn** is the highest mountain in the Bernese Alps, and it is built of rocks of the Aar Massif. Large parts of the UNESCO World Heritage Site **Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch** also lie in it. At the **Grimsel Pass**, the glaciers of the Ice Age ground the hard granite into smooth humps. These **roches moutonnées** shape the landscape around Lake Grimsel.

As the mountains rose, cracks opened up in the rock, so-called **Alpine fissures**. Hot solutions flowed through them. From these, **quartz** and other minerals crystallised. This is how magnificent **rock crystals** formed. In 2005 a particularly large group of crystals was found at the **Planggenstock** in the canton of Uri.

The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** begins in the north at **Erstfeld**. First it passes through the gneiss and granite of the Aar Massif. Further south come the Tavetsch intermediate massif, the Gotthard Massif and the Penninic gneisses. Before building it, geologists had to study these rocks carefully.

gewusst: Some of the crystals from the Planggenstock can be seen today in the Natural History Museum in Bern.
The name Aar Massif comes from the River Aare, which rises in the massif at the Grimsel.

teile.einleitung: On a spacewalk, an astronaut in a spacesuit climbs out of the spacecraft or space station. Outside in space they build or repair equipment. Experts also call this extravehicular activity.
wichtigste: A **spacewalk** is work done outside the spacecraft.
The first was made by the cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov** in 1965; he stayed outside for about 12 minutes.
Astronauts go out through an **airlock**.
They are fastened with **safety tethers**, and their tools are secured too.
Usually two astronauts go out together.
Today a spacewalk often lasts 6 to 7 hours.

abschnitte.text: On 18 March 1965 the Soviet cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to climb out of a spacecraft. He floated in space on a tether for about 12 minutes. His suit puffed up so much that he could hardly get back into the capsule. A few months later Ed White made the first American spacewalk.

An astronaut cannot simply open the door, or the air would escape from the station. First they go into an **airlock**, a small room with two doors. The air is pumped out there, and only then does the outer door open. Before that, the astronauts breathe pure oxygen for a while so that their bodies get used to the low pressure in the suit.

On the outside of the space station, equipment has to be fitted, replaced or repaired. Working in the thick gloves is slow and tiring. That is why a spacewalk often lasts **6 to 7 hours**. Usually **two astronauts** work together so that they can help each other. Colleagues in the station and on the ground support them by radio.

Without being secured, an astronaut could drift off into space. That is why they are attached to strong **safety tethers**, which are hooked onto handles on the station. Every **tool** is also fastened with a small tether, because anything you let go of floats away. The **spacesuit** is like a small spacecraft: it supplies oxygen, keeps the pressure and protects against heat, cold and radiation.

The space station does not circle far above the Earth. So outside, astronauts see seas, clouds and countries passing by beneath them. A Swiss astronaut has also been outside in space: **Claude Nicollier** went out in 1999 while repairing the Hubble Space Telescope.

gewusst: In 1984 Bruce McCandless flew freely in space with a backpack fitted with jets, without any tether at all.
The first woman to do a spacewalk was the cosmonaut Svetlana Savitskaya in 1984.

teile.einleitung: Saturn is famous for its magnificent rings. They look like a solid disc but are made of countless separate chunks. You can see them even with a small telescope.
wichtigste: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks, mostly of ice.
Each chunk orbits the planet on its own.
The bright rings are about 270,000 kilometres wide but very thin.
In 1655 Christiaan Huygens was the first to realise that Saturn has a ring.
The space probe Cassini orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017.
Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune have rings too, but only faint ones.

abschnitte.titel: What the rings are made of
abschnitte.text: The rings are not a solid disc. They are made of **countless chunks**, most of them of **water ice**. Some are as small as grains of dust, others as big as a house. Each chunk orbits Saturn on its own path. Because the ice reflects sunlight well, the rings shine brightly.

The bright rings are about **270,000 kilometres** wide from edge to edge. About **20 Earths** would fit side by side across them. At the same time, the rings are usually only about **10 metres to 1 kilometre** thick. Compared with their width, they are thinner than a sheet of paper. Every few years we look exactly at their **edge**, and then they are almost invisible. This happened in March 2025.

In 1610 Galileo Galilei saw with his simple telescope that there was something special about Saturn. But he did not yet understand what he was seeing. The scientist **Christiaan Huygens** from the Netherlands had a better telescope. In **1655** he was the first to realise that Saturn is surrounded by a ring. Today even a **small telescope** shows the rings, for example at an observatory.

From **2004 to 2017** the space probe **Cassini** orbited Saturn. It was a joint project of the American NASA and the European Space Agency ESA. For thirteen years it took pictures of Saturn, its rings and its moons. At the end of the mission it was deliberately sent crashing into Saturn.

Saturn is not the only planet with rings. **Jupiter**, **Uranus** and **Neptune** have them too. But these rings are dark and narrow and therefore hard to see. The rings of **Uranus** were not discovered until **1977**.

gewusst: The large gap between two bright rings of Saturn is called the Cassini Division, after the astronomer Giovanni Domenico Cassini.
Saturn has such a low density that it would float in a gigantic bathtub full of water.

teile.einleitung: A constellation is a group of stars that seems to form a figure in the sky. Thousands of years ago people already saw animals, heroes and objects in the stars and gave them names. Today there are officially 88 constellations, which divide up the whole sky.
wichtigste: A constellation is made of stars that together show a figure.
Officially there are 88 constellations.
The Plough looks like a cart with a shaft.
The Pole Star points almost exactly north.
Orion shows a hunter with a belt of three stars.
The stars of a constellation are often at very different distances from us.
Many constellations have names from Greek legends.

abschnitte.text: A **constellation** is a figure that you imagine between bright stars when you join them up with lines in your mind. In reality the stars do not belong together. Seen from the Earth, they just happen to lie in the same direction, and they are often at very different distances. Since 1922 the **International Astronomical Union** has decided which constellations there are. Since 1930 all 88 constellations have had exact borders, so that every point in the sky belongs to exactly one.

Many constellations come from ancient Mesopotamia and from Greece. The Greek scholar **Ptolemy** described 48 constellations about 1900 years ago. That is why many are named after figures from Greek legends, such as Perseus, Andromeda or Hercules. Constellations in the southern sky, which cannot be seen from Europe, were only named by seafarers from the 16th century onwards. That is why they have names such as Telescope, Compass or Toucan.

abschnitte.titel: The Plough and the Pole Star
abschnitte.text: The **Plough**, called the “Great Cart” in German, is the best-known group of stars in Switzerland, and you can see it all year round. It is made of seven bright stars and looks like a cart with a shaft. In fact it is part of the larger constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. If you extend the back edge of the cart about five times, you find the **Pole Star**. It stands almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole and so points almost exactly north.

In winter **Orion** is one of the most striking constellations. It shows a hunter with a **belt** of three bright stars in a row. At the top left shines the reddish giant star Betelgeuse, at the bottom right the bluish Rigel. Below the belt lies the Orion Nebula, a cloud in which new stars are forming. You can see it even with binoculars.

Over the course of a year the Sun seems to move through twelve well-known constellations, the **zodiac**. They include, for example, Aries, Taurus, Leo and Scorpius. In astronomy, Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, also belongs to it. The constellations are not the same as the star signs in horoscopes, which have no scientific basis.

Because the Earth turns, the constellations move across the sky from east to west during the night. Only the Pole Star stays almost in its place. Constellations close to the Pole Star, such as the Plough and **Cassiopeia**, never set in Switzerland. Others can only be seen at certain times of year, such as Orion in winter or Scorpius in summer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of stars that shows a figure and has a fixed area of the sky.
A bright star that stands almost exactly above the North Pole and shows the way north.
A well-known star pattern that is not an official constellation, for example the Plough.
The twelve constellations that the Sun seems to move through over the course of the year.

gewusst: The Pole Star is not the brightest star in the sky; it is only in about 48th place.
The largest constellation in the sky is Hydra, the Water Snake, and the smallest is the Southern Cross.
In a few thousand years, a different star will mark the north celestial pole instead of the Pole Star, because the Earth's axis slowly wobbles.

teile.einleitung: Voyager 1 is a NASA space probe that was launched in 1977. It flew past Jupiter and Saturn and today is the most distant object that humans have built.
wichtigste: Voyager 1 was launched in Florida in September **1977**.
It flew past **Jupiter** (1979) and **Saturn** (1980).
It studied Saturn's moon **Titan** close up.
In 1990 it took the photo **“Pale Blue Dot”** of the Earth.
In 2012 it was the first human-made object to reach **interstellar space**.
Its electricity comes from a **radioisotope battery**.

abschnitte.text: Voyager 1 was launched in Florida in September **1977**, about two weeks after its sister probe Voyager 2. Even so, it has the number 1. It flew on a **faster path**, overtook Voyager 2 and reached Jupiter and Saturn earlier. As of 2026 it is still sending data to Earth.

In 1979 Voyager 1 reached **Jupiter**, and in 1980 **Saturn**. It sent back many new pictures of the planets and their moons. The researchers steered it close past Saturn's moon **Titan**. But its thick orange atmosphere hid the surface. After this flyby, Voyager 1 left the plane of the planets.

The astronomer **Carl Sagan** persuaded NASA to turn the camera towards the Earth once more. In 1990 Voyager 1 photographed the Earth from a distance of about **6 billion kilometres**. In the picture “**Pale Blue Dot**”, it appears only as a tiny bluish point of light. Sagan later wrote a book about this “pale blue dot”.

The Sun constantly blows a stream of particles into space, the **solar wind**. It forms a huge bubble, the **heliosphere**. In 2012 Voyager 1 left this bubble. In doing so, it was the first human-made object to fly into **interstellar space**, the space between the stars.

So far from the Sun, **solar cells** supply far too little electricity. That is why Voyager 1 uses a **radioisotope battery**. It turns the heat from decaying **plutonium** into electricity. The power slowly decreases over the years, so instruments have been switched off one by one.

gewusst: On board Voyager 1 there is a golden record with pictures, music and greetings from Earth.
Radio signals from Voyager 1 travel for many hours before they reach the Earth.

teile.einleitung: An adiabatic process is a change in the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas without any exchange of heat with the surroundings. In meteorology it explains why rising air cools down and clouds form.
wichtigste: Adiabatic means: without exchange of heat with the surroundings.
Rising air expands, does work and cools down in the process.
Unsaturated air cools by about 1 °C per 100 m.
Saturated air cools more slowly, because heat is released during condensation.
The potential temperature stays the same during dry adiabatic movements.
The adiabatic index κ for dry air is about 1.4.

abschnitte.text: When a parcel of air rises, the air pressure around it falls. The parcel **expands** and in doing so does **work** against its surroundings. The energy for this comes from its **internal energy**. That is why its temperature falls, even though no heat is taken from it. The other way round, sinking air warms up, because it is compressed.

Unsaturated air cools by about **9.8 K per kilometre** as it rises, rounded to **1 °C per 100 m**. This is the **dry adiabatic lapse rate**. An example: a parcel of air is 25 °C at the ground and rises 1500 m. It cools by 15 °C and is then about **10 °C**.

If the air is saturated, water vapour **condenses** into cloud droplets. This releases **latent heat**, the heat of vaporisation. It slows the cooling to about **0.4 to 0.7 °C per 100 m**. In very cold air the difference is small. Cold air contains only a little water vapour, and hardly any heat of condensation is released.

The **potential temperature** is the temperature a parcel of air would have if you brought it dry adiabatically to **1000 hPa**. It stays the same during such movements and allows air from different heights to be compared. In physics, the **Poisson equation** describes adiabatic processes. The **adiabatic index κ** is the ratio of cp to cv and is about **1.4** for dry air.

gewusst: The warm föhn wind in Alpine valleys is caused, among other things, by the adiabatic warming of sinking air.
When you pump up a bicycle tyre quickly, the pump gets warm: an example of adiabatic compression.

teile.einleitung: A swing-by is a flyby of a space probe past a planet, in which the planet's gravity bends the probe's path. In this way the probe can speed up or slow down without fuel. It is also called a gravity assist.
wichtigste: The energy gained comes from the **planet's motion along its orbit** around the Sun.
Relative to the planet, the probe's speed stays the same; only its direction changes.
If the probe flies past behind the planet it speeds up; in front of it, it is slowed down.
In 1974 **Mariner 10** was the first probe to use a swing-by, at Venus.
In 1961 **Michael Minovitch** systematically calculated swing-by paths at JPL.
Voyager 2's **Grand Tour** is only possible about every 175 years.

abschnitte.text: A planet pulls on a passing probe with its **gravity**. The probe takes over a tiny part of the planet's **orbital momentum**. In return, the planet becomes very slightly slower. Because it is so much heavier than the probe, nothing can be noticed. But for the probe the difference can be huge.

Seen from the planet, the probe flies along a **hyperbola**. It leaves the planet at the same speed at which it arrived, just in a different direction. Only when seen from the Sun does this change of direction mean a gain or loss in speed. If the probe flies past **behind the planet**, the planet drags it along in its direction of motion. If it flies past in front, it is slowed down.

In 1961, as a student, the mathematician **Michael Minovitch** used the computers of the **Jet Propulsion Laboratory** in the USA. With them he systematically calculated paths using gravity assists. His work made flights to the outer planets realistic. Without swing-bys, such probes would need much more fuel.

**Mariner 10** flew past Venus in February 1974 and then reached Mercury. At the end of the 1970s the outer planets were lined up so favourably that **Voyager 2** was able to visit Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune one after the other. ESA's probe **Rosetta** flew past the Earth three times and past Mars once in 2007, before reaching the comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014.

A swing-by can also **slow** a probe **down**. This is needed when a probe is to get close to the Sun. The **Parker Solar Probe** gives up orbital energy during flybys of Venus. In this way it lowered its closest point to the Sun step by step, to about 6 million kilometres above the Sun's surface.

gewusst: With every swing-by the planet becomes a tiny bit slower, so little that it could never be measured.
The line-up of the planets for the Voyager probes' “Grand Tour” only happens about every 175 years.

teile.einleitung: The proton-proton chain is the chain of nuclear reactions with which the Sun produces energy. Hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, and a small part of the mass is turned into energy.
wichtigste: Overall, one helium-4 nucleus is made from four protons.
About 26.7 MeV of energy is released for each helium-4 nucleus.
About 0.7 per cent of the mass of the four protons is turned into energy.
The first step is extremely slow because it goes via the weak interaction.
In the Sun, the pp-I chain provides the largest share.
In 1939, Hans Bethe described how stars produce energy and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1967.

abschnitte.text: In the core of the Sun it is about 15 million degrees hot, and the pressure is enormous. There, **protons**, in other words hydrogen nuclei, collide so violently that they can fuse. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. The proton-proton chain is the most important way this happens in the Sun. In 1939, the physicist **Hans Bethe** described the fusion reactions in stars and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1967.

First, two protons collide. One of them has to turn into a **neutron**, which can only happen through the **weak interaction**. This produces a deuterium nucleus, a **deuteron**. A **positron** and an **electron neutrino** are also sent out. This step is extremely rare: a proton in the Sun's core waits on average for billions of years for it.

After that things happen quickly. The deuteron captures another proton, **helium-3** is formed and a gamma ray photon is given off. In the **pp-I chain**, two helium-3 nuclei then fuse into **helium-4**. Two protons are set free again. About four fifths of the helium nuclei in the Sun are formed this way. The branches pp-II and pp-III with beryllium and boron are rarer.

Four protons together have a mass of about 4.029 u, a helium-4 nucleus only about 4.002 u. The difference of about **0.7 per cent** becomes energy according to Einstein's formula E = mc². That is about **26.7 MeV** for each helium nucleus. A small part of it flies off with the **neutrinos**, which escape from the Sun almost unhindered. The rest warms the Sun and makes it shine.

gewusst: Every second, the Sun turns about four million tonnes of mass into energy.
Neutrinos from the Sun constantly fly through our bodies without us noticing.

teile.einleitung: Anthropocene means “age of humans”. The term describes the idea that humans are changing the Earth so much that you could speak of a separate epoch in the Earth's history.
wichtigste: Paul Crutzen made the term well known from the year 2000.
In 1995 Crutzen received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for research on ozone depletion.
The period around 1950 was proposed as the start, with plutonium as the marker.
Crawford Lake in Canada was proposed as the reference site.
In March 2024 the responsible expert commission rejected the Anthropocene as an official epoch.
Officially we live in the Holocene.

abschnitte.text: From the year **2000**, the atmospheric chemist **Paul Crutzen**, together with **Eugene Stoermer**, suggested seeing the present as an epoch of its own. Humans, he said, had become a **geological force**. Crutzen was well known: in 1995 he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** together with Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland. They showed how nitrogen oxides and **CFCs** damage the ozone layer.

Since about **1950**, population, energy use and pollution have risen steeply. This is called the **Great Acceleration**. That is why experts proposed 1950 as the start of the Anthropocene. New materials such as **plastics**, **concrete** and **aluminium** are now found in young deposits. These are called **technofossils**.

A new epoch needs a signal that can be measured at the same time everywhere on Earth. The proposal was **plutonium** from the above-ground **nuclear weapons tests** of the 1950s. This trace is found in sediments and ice worldwide. **Crawford Lake** near Toronto in Canada was proposed as the reference site. There, yearly layers settle undisturbed.

Official epochs are decided by the **International Union of Geological Sciences**. In **March 2024** its Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted against an Anthropocene epoch. So officially we still live in the **Holocene**, which began about 11,700 years ago after the last cold period. But the term Anthropocene remains widely used in science and by the public.

gewusst: In Crawford Lake you can count the layers almost like the rings of a tree.
Some experts see the Anthropocene more as an event that developed over a long time than as an epoch with a fixed starting year.

teile.einleitung: The rocket equation describes how much faster a rocket can become with its fuel. It is one of the most important formulas in space travel.
wichtigste: Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published the equation in 1903.
It calculates the possible change in speed, the delta-v.
The delta-v depends on the exhaust velocity and the mass ratio.
The mass ratio is the launch mass divided by the mass after burnout.
The delta-v only grows logarithmically with the mass ratio.
For a low Earth orbit, about 9 to 10 km/s are needed including losses.

abschnitte.text: The Russian teacher **Konstantin Tsiolkovsky** is considered one of the fathers of space travel. In 1903 he published the **rocket equation**. That is why it is also called the **Tsiolkovsky equation**. It is used to calculate the **delta-v**, the change in speed a rocket can achieve with its fuel. Gravity and air resistance are not taken into account.

The equation is: delta-v = exhaust velocity · ln(m0 / m1). The **exhaust velocity** tells you how fast the gases stream out of the nozzle. The **mass ratio** m0 / m1 compares the full rocket at launch with the rocket after burnout. It is always greater than 1. The symbol ln stands for the **natural logarithm**.

Because the delta-v only grows **logarithmically**, twice as much fuel gives much less than twice the delta-v. An example: for a delta-v of three times the exhaust velocity, you need a mass ratio of e to the power of 3, about **20**. Then about 95 per cent of the launch mass would have to be fuel. If a rocket is to reach 9,400 m/s and the gas streams out at 3,500 m/s, it needs a mass ratio of about **15**.

For a **low Earth orbit** you need an orbital speed of about 7.8 km/s. On top of that come losses through gravity and air resistance of about 1.5 to 2 km/s, so about **9 to 10 km/s** altogether. This can hardly be done with a single stage. That is why **multistage rockets** are built: empty tanks and engines are dropped and do not have to be accelerated any further. This improves the mass ratio of each following stage.

gewusst: Tsiolkovsky was already writing about space stations and spacesuits around 1900.
At launch, a large rocket consists by far mostly of fuel.

teile.einleitung: Sputnik 1 was the world's first artificial satellite. The Soviet Union launched it into space on 4 October 1957. With its beeping, the space age began.
wichtigste: Sputnik 1 was launched on 4 October 1957 as the first artificial satellite.
It was a metal ball with four long antennas.
The ball had a diameter of about 58 centimetres.
An R-7 rocket carried it into space.
It sent out a regular beeping that could be heard with simple radio receivers.
In January 1958 it burned up in the Earth's atmosphere.

abschnitte.text: On **4 October 1957** an **R-7** rocket was launched in the Soviet Union. It had originally been built as a military long-range missile. It was launched from Baikonur, which is in Kazakhstan today. At its tip it carried **Sputnik 1**. For the first time, an object built by humans orbited the Earth. The Russian word **sputnik** means **companion**.

Sputnik 1 was a polished **metal ball** with **four long antennas**. The ball had a diameter of **about 58 centimetres**, about the size of a large beach ball. It weighed about 84 kilograms. Inside were batteries, a radio transmitter and a small fan for cooling. Sputnik needed about 96 minutes to go once around the Earth.

Sputnik sent a **regular beeping** down to Earth. You could hear it with a **simple radio receiver**. Radio amateurs all over the world listened eagerly. In this way anyone could check that the satellite really was up there. After about three weeks the batteries ran out and Sputnik fell silent.

The Earth's atmosphere reaches thinly very high up and slowly slowed Sputnik down. It sank lower and lower. In **January 1958** it entered the thicker air and **burned up**. Altogether it was in space for about three months. Its orbit was so low that it could not stay up any longer.

The launch of Sputnik came as a surprise, especially to the **USA**. It was the time of the **Cold War**, a rivalry between the USA and the Soviet Union. The USA feared that it was falling behind in technology. That is why it founded the space agency **NASA** in 1958. This started the **space race**, which led to the Moon landing in 1969.

gewusst: Just one month after Sputnik 1, the dog Laika flew into space on Sputnik 2.
With binoculars you could not see the small ball at night, but you could see the larger rocket stage moving across the sky.

teile.einleitung: A shadow forms when an object blocks the light. Behind it there is a darker patch, because less light gets there. How long a shadow is and which way it points depends on the position of the Sun.
wichtigste: A shadow forms where an object blocks the light.
The shadow always lies on the side facing away from the light source.
At midday the Sun is at its highest, and then shadows are shortest.
In the morning and evening the Sun is low, and then shadows are long.
See-through things such as a clear pane of glass cast almost no shadow.
The closer an object is to the lamp, the bigger its shadow becomes.

abschnitte.text: Light travels in **straight lines**. When it hits an object that does not let light through, it is **blocked**. Behind the object there is a place where less light gets to: the **shadow**. That is why the shadow always lies on the side facing **away from the light source**. A shadow looks **dark grey to black**, whatever colour the object is.

At **midday** the Sun is at its highest. The light falls steeply, and your shadow is **short**. In the **morning** and **evening** the Sun is low. Then the light comes in at a shallow angle, and shadows become **long**. Because the Sun moves across the sky during the day, the shadow moves too.

Light passes almost completely through a **clear pane of glass**. That is why a clean pane of glass hardly casts a shadow. Such materials are called **transparent**. Frosted glass or paper let only part of the light through, so they cast a pale shadow. Wood, stones or your body let no light through and cast dark shadows.

In **shadow play**, you hold your hands in front of a lamp. Shapes such as a **rabbit** or a **bird** then appear on the wall. If you hold your hand **closer to the lamp**, it blocks more light, and its shadow becomes **bigger**. If you move your hand closer to the wall, the shadow becomes smaller and sharper. Many countries have an old tradition of **shadow theatre** with figures made of leather or cardboard.

No direct sunlight reaches the shade, so it is **cooler** there. On hot days **cows** in the pasture look for shade under trees. People also protect themselves from the heat with sunshades and hats. In the past, people read the time from a **sundial**: the shadow of a rod shows the hour there. Many old churches in Switzerland still have a sundial on the wall.

gewusst: During a lunar eclipse, the Moon moves through the Earth's shadow.
During a solar eclipse, the Moon's shadow falls on the Earth.

teile.einleitung: A spacesuit is like a small spacecraft that you can wear. It gives astronauts air to breathe and protects them from cold, heat and the vacuum of space.
wichtigste: Astronauts wear a spacesuit for trips outside the space station.
The backpack holds oxygen, power and cooling.
Suits for trips outside are usually white so that they do not get too hot.
A golden visor protects against glaring sunlight.
On Earth, a suit like this weighs over 100 kilograms.
Astronauts also wear a spacesuit during launch and landing.

abschnitte.text: Out in space there is **no air** to breathe. On top of that, it is very hot in the sunlight and icy cold in the shade. So for a trip outside the space station, an astronaut puts on a **spacesuit**. The suit is filled with air and keeps the necessary pressure. The **gloves** are firmly attached and protect the hands from cold, heat and the vacuum of space.

On their back the astronaut carries a big **backpack**. It works like a small life-support system. Inside are a supply of **oxygen**, batteries for **power** and a **cooling system**. Under the suit the astronaut wears special underwear with thin **water tubes**. Cool water flows through them so that the astronaut does not get too hot while working.

The suits for trips outside the space station are usually **white**. White reflects the glaring sunlight, so the suit does not get too hot. The helmet has a **golden visor**. The thin layer of gold blocks part of the sunlight, a bit like sunglasses. On Earth a suit like this weighs **over 100 kilograms**, but in space the astronaut does not feel this weight.

There are also spacesuits for **launch and landing**. They are lighter and protect the astronauts in case air escapes from the capsule. The first walk in open space was made in 1965 by the Soviet cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov**. The Swiss astronaut **Claude Nicollier** worked outside on the Hubble Space Telescope in a spacesuit in 1999.

gewusst: Putting on a spacesuit for a trip outside takes a long time and often needs help from other astronauts.
Claude Nicollier flew into space four times in total on the Space Shuttle.

teile.einleitung: A black hole is a place in space where so much mass is squeezed into such a small space that not even light can escape. That is why you cannot see it directly. Even so, researchers have proved that black holes exist and in 2019 even published the first picture of one.
wichtigste: A black hole has such strong gravity that nothing, not even light, can escape from it.
The boundary beyond which there is no way back is called the event horizon.
If you squeezed the Sun into a black hole, it would have a radius of only about 3 kilometres.
As a black hole, the Earth would have a Schwarzschild radius of about 9 millimetres.
At the centre of the Milky Way sits the black hole Sagittarius A*, with about 4 million solar masses.
In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first picture of a black hole, in the galaxy M87.
Many black holes form when very heavy stars collapse at the end of their lives.

abschnitte.text: A black hole is not really a hole, but an extremely dense collection of mass. Its **gravity** is so strong that you would have to be faster than light to escape. Since nothing is faster than light, everything that crosses the boundary stays trapped. This boundary is called the **event horizon**. Its radius is called the Schwarzschild radius, named after the German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild.

Very massive stars, which are much heavier than the Sun, often explode as a supernova at the end of their lives. Their core can collapse so much that a **stellar black hole** forms. Such black holes usually have a few to a few dozen solar masses. At the centre of almost every large galaxy, on the other hand, sits a **supermassive black hole** with millions or even billions of solar masses. How exactly these giants formed is still being researched.

Because black holes give off no light, they only reveal themselves through their effect on their surroundings. Gas falling into a black hole forms a hot, incredibly fast **accretion disc** that shines brightly, often in X-ray light. In this way, in the early 1970s, the binary star **Cygnus X-1** in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan, became the first convincing candidate. In the case of Sagittarius A*, stars were observed for years orbiting the invisible centre of the Milky Way very fast. Since 2015 it has also been possible to measure gravitational waves, which arise when two black holes merge.

In 2019 the **Event Horizon Telescope** published the first picture of a black hole. It shows the centre of the giant galaxy **M87**, about 55 million light years away. You can see a bright, orange ring of glowing gas around a dark shadow. For this, radio telescopes on several continents were linked together so that they worked like a single telescope the size of the Earth. In 2022 a picture of Sagittarius A* in our own Milky Way followed.

In 1974 the British physicist **Stephen Hawking** predicted that black holes give off very faint radiation. This **Hawking radiation** is caused by quantum effects at the event horizon. Its temperature is inversely proportional to the mass: the heavier a black hole is, the colder it is. Large black holes therefore give off so little radiation that it has not yet been possible to measure it. But over unimaginably long periods of time, black holes could slowly evaporate in this way.

According to Albert Einstein's **theory of relativity**, time runs more slowly close to a black hole than far away from it. An object falling in would be stretched out by the different strengths of the pull. Experts jokingly call this **spaghettification**. There is no danger to the Earth, because the nearest known black hole is more than a thousand light years away.

begriffe.erklaerung: The invisible boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing can escape.
The radius of the event horizon. It depends only on the mass.
A flat, glowing disc of gas that circles the black hole and slowly falls in.
A unit of mass in astronomy: as much mass as the Sun has.

gewusst: The Earth would have to be squeezed to the size of a marble about 2 centimetres across to become a black hole.
The picture of M87 was made from so much data that the hard drives were transported by aeroplane instead of being sent over the internet.
In 2020 the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for the prediction and discovery of Sagittarius A*.

teile.einleitung: The Alps formed when Africa, together with the Adriatic Plate, pushed against Europe. Over millions of years, layers of rock were pushed together, stacked and lifted up.
wichtigste: The formation of the Alps is part of the Alpine orogeny.
The Adriatic Plate was pushed against Europe as a spur of Africa.
The European Plate mostly dived beneath the Adriatic Plate.
About 35 million years ago the continental margins collided.
The Alps are a collision mountain range.
Flysch and the high-pressure mineral coesite tell the story of this.

abschnitte.text: The **Adriatic Plate**, also called the Apulian Plate, was connected to **Africa**. It pushed against the edge of **Europe**. At first there was an ocean in between. This was pushed down into the depths beneath the Adriatic Plate; this is called **subduction**. The **European Plate** dived southwards, and the Adriatic Plate formed the upper plate.

After the ocean had disappeared, the continental margins collided about **35 million years ago**. That is why the Alps are a **collision mountain range**. The layers of rock were stacked on top of each other as **nappes**, thickened and lifted. The formation of the Alps is part of the **Alpine orogeny**. The Pyrenees, the Carpathians and the Himalayas also belong to it.

In 1984 the mineral **coesite** was found in the **Dora Maira Massif** in the Western Alps. It is a form of SiO₂ that only forms under extremely high pressure. The find showed that crustal rock had gone down to **over 90 km deep** and then come back up to the surface. This was a big surprise at the time.

While the nappes were moving forward, alternating layers of sandstone, marl and clay were deposited in deep sea basins. They are called **flysch**. They were formed by **turbidity currents**, muddy currents on the sea floor. The term comes from the **Simmental** and was introduced into geology in 1827 by the Bern geologist **Bernhard Studer**.

In the **National Research Programme 20** (NRP 20), seismic profiles were measured right across the Swiss Alps in the 1980s and 1990s. For this, sound waves are sent into the ground and their echo is measured; this is called **reflection seismology**. The measurements showed how the European crust has been pushed under the Alps and forms a deep **crustal root**.

gewusst: On many Alpine peaks you can find rocks that once formed on the sea floor.
Africa and Europe are still slowly moving towards each other today.

teile.einleitung: X-ray astronomy explores space using X-rays. This radiation comes from very hot and energetic places, for example near neutron stars and black holes. Because the Earth's atmosphere swallows X-rays, you have to go into space to observe them.
wichtigste: X-rays from space do not reach the ground, so they are measured with rockets and satellites.
In 1962 the team led by Riccardo Giacconi found Scorpius X-1, the first X-ray source outside the solar system.
X-ray telescopes focus the radiation with mirrors at grazing incidence, often in the design by Hans Wolter.
Uhuru was the first satellite built only for X-rays, in 1970.
From 1990 the German satellite ROSAT found over 100,000 X-ray sources.
The Chandra observatory was carried into space by the Space Shuttle Columbia in 1999.

abschnitte.text: The Earth's **atmosphere** protects us from X-rays from space. So for measurements you need **sounding rockets** or **satellites**. In **1962** a team led by **Riccardo Giacconi** used a rocket to find a very bright X-ray source in the constellation Scorpius: **Scorpius X-1**. It was the first X-ray source outside the solar system. In **2002** Giacconi received the Nobel Prize in Physics for founding X-ray astronomy.

X-rays would simply pass into a normal mirror. They are only reflected when they hit it at a very shallow, **grazing angle**. That is why X-ray telescopes are made of almost tube-shaped mirrors **nested inside each other**. In 1952 the German physicist **Hans Wolter** described such arrangements made of a paraboloid and a hyperboloid. **Wolter telescopes** fly today, for example, in Chandra and XMM-Newton.

The first satellite built only for X-rays was **Uhuru**. It was launched from Kenya in **1970** on Kenyan Independence Day, and its name means “freedom” in Swahili. It produced the first X-ray catalogue of the whole sky. From **1990** the German satellite **ROSAT** surveyed the sky and found **over 100,000 sources**. In **1999** the Space Shuttle **Columbia** carried the **Chandra** observatory into space. In the same year the European telescope **XMM-Newton** was launched.

X-rays are produced where gas is **millions of degrees** hot. One example is close **binary star systems** with a **neutron star** or a **black hole**. Gas from the companion star spirals onto the compact object in an **accretion disc** and heats up strongly through friction. The hot corona of the Sun, the remains of exploded stars and the gas in **galaxy clusters** also shine in X-ray light.

In **2019** the X-ray telescope **eROSITA** was launched on the satellite **Spektr-RG**. It circles the **Lagrange point L2**, about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth. There the Earth hardly disturbs the observations. eROSITA was built by the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics in **Garching**, which had already looked after ROSAT. It has surveyed the whole sky several times.

gewusst: The mission STS-93, which carried Chandra into space, was led by Eileen Collins, the first woman to command a Shuttle mission.
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, after whom X-rays are named in German, studied at ETH Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Spectral analysis is a method of finding out from light which substances a light source is made of. To do this, you split the light into its colours, as in a rainbow. In this way astronomers can work out what very distant stars are made of without ever having been there.
wichtigste: In spectral analysis, light is split into its colours, the spectrum.
Each chemical element produces its own pattern of lines, like a fingerprint.
Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen founded spectral analysis in Heidelberg in 1859.
The Fraunhofer lines are dark absorption lines in the Sun's spectrum.
Helium was discovered first in the Sun's spectrum in 1868 and only found on Earth later.
From the shift of the lines you can measure how fast a star is moving.
From the colour of the light you can work out the temperature of a star.

abschnitte.text: White light is a mixture of many colours. A glass **prism** or a fine grating fans the light out into its colours, from red to violet. This band of colours is called a **spectrum**. Each colour belongs to a certain **wavelength**, which is measured in nanometres. Red light has a wavelength of about 700 nanometres, violet light about 400 nanometres.

In 1859 in Heidelberg, the physicist **Gustav Kirchhoff** and the chemist **Robert Bunsen** studied flames into which they held different substances. They found that each element gives off very particular bright lines. Sodium, for example, glows a strong yellow. With their **spectroscope** they even discovered new elements this way, namely caesium and rubidium. Bunsen's gas burner, which gives an almost colourless flame, was very helpful for this.

According to **Kirchhoff's laws** there are three kinds of spectra. A hot, dense body such as glowing metal gives off a continuous band of colour. A hot, thin gas in front of a dark background gives off an **emission line spectrum** with separate bright lines. If cooler gas lies in front of a hot light source, it swallows certain colours, and dark **absorption lines** appear. Joseph von Fraunhofer had already described such dark lines in sunlight around 1814, which is why they are called Fraunhofer lines.

The lines are produced in atoms. Electrons can only be at certain **energy levels**. When an electron jumps from a higher level to a lower one, it gives off light of one very particular colour. In hydrogen, the jumps of the **Balmer series** all lead to the level n equals 2, and their lines lie in visible light. Because every element has different levels, each also has its own pattern of lines.

From the lines you can tell which elements a star is made of. In 1868 an unknown yellow line was found in sunlight, and the new element was named after the Greek word for Sun: **helium**. From the colour at which a star shines most brightly, you can read its temperature; this is described by **Wien's displacement law**. A star of 5800 kelvin, roughly like the Sun, shines most strongly at about 500 nanometres.

If a light source moves away from us, its lines shift a little towards red; this is the **Doppler effect**. If it comes towards us, they shift towards blue. If a line at 600.0 nanometres appears at 600.6 nanometres, the source is moving away at about 300 kilometres per second. With this method it was discovered that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and many planets around other stars were found too. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz from Geneva found the first planet around a Sun-like star in this way.

begriffe.erklaerung: The band of colours you get when you split light into its parts.
A bright or dark line in the spectrum that belongs to a particular element.
The distance between two crests of a light wave. It decides the colour.
The change in light or sound when the source moves towards us or away from us.

gewusst: In 1835 the French philosopher Auguste Comte wrote that we would never find out what the stars are made of, and a few decades later spectral analysis achieved exactly that.
In 2019 Mayor and Queloz from Geneva received the Nobel Prize for discovering the first planet around a Sun-like star with the help of spectral lines.
Fireworks show spectral analysis in everyday life: strontium colours the sparks red, sodium yellow and copper green or blue.

teile.einleitung: The photosphere is the visible surface of the Sun. Most of the sunlight comes from this thin layer. The name comes from Greek and means something like “sphere of light”.
wichtigste: The photosphere has an effective temperature of about 5,800 kelvin.
It is only about 300 to 500 kilometres thick.
Its grainy granulation is caused by rising convection cells.
A granule is about 1,000 kilometres across and lasts about 8 to 20 minutes.
The edge of the Sun appears darker than the middle; this is called limb darkening.
Sunspots are cooler places with strong magnetic fields.

abschnitte.text: The Sun is a ball of hot gas and has no solid surface. Even so, we see a sharp edge. That is because of the **photosphere**, the layer from which most of the **visible light** comes. It is only about **300 to 500 kilometres** thick. Compared with the Sun's radius of about 700,000 kilometres, that is wafer-thin. Its **effective temperature** is about **5,800 kelvin**.

With special telescopes you can see that the photosphere looks **grainy**. This is called **granulation**. Hot gas rises in the middle of each **granule** and sinks back down, cooled, at the darker edges. Granulation is the top of the **convection zone**. A granule has a diameter of about **1,000 to 1,500 kilometres** and lasts only about **8 to 20 minutes**. In time-lapse, the Sun therefore looks like boiling porridge.

The Sun's disc is **darker** at the edge than in the middle. In the middle you are looking straight into the Sun and see deeper, hotter layers. At the edge the line of sight runs at an angle, so you only see as far as **higher, cooler layers**. These shine less brightly. This is called **limb darkening**.

**Sunspots** are dark places in the photosphere. There, strong **magnetic fields** of a few thousand gauss hold back the transport of heat from below. The gas there is about **1,500 kelvin cooler** and so shines less brightly. In fact, sunspots are still very bright and hot; they only look dark next to their surroundings.

How deep you can see into the Sun is decided mainly by the **negative hydrogen ion** H⁻. This is a hydrogen atom with an extra electron. It is only weakly bound and absorbs visible and infrared light very effectively. That is why the photosphere is **opaque**. Above it lie the **chromosphere** and the **corona**, which you can see mainly during total solar eclipses.

gewusst: The corona above the photosphere is more than a million degrees hot, much hotter than the photosphere itself.
Never look at the Sun without special protective glasses or filters, as this can damage your eyes permanently.

teile.einleitung: In films there are often bangs and booms in space. In reality, it is completely silent in empty space. The reason is simple: there is no air there that could carry the sound.
wichtigste: In empty space it is **completely silent**.
Sound needs air or another material to travel through.
You could see an explosion in space, but not hear it.
During a spacewalk, astronauts talk by **radio**.
There is air in the space station ISS, so fans and pumps hum there.
Light and radio waves travel through space even without air.

abschnitte.text: Sound is made when something **vibrates**, for example a guitar string. The vibration makes the air next to it vibrate. The air passes it on until it reaches our ear. Sound can also travel through water or wood. But without a material that vibrates along, there is no sound.

Space is almost empty. Between planets and stars there is so little gas that sound cannot travel. That is why it is **silent** there. If something exploded next to a spacecraft, you would see a bright flash. But you would not hear a bang.

During a **spacewalk**, astronauts wear a spacesuit with a helmet. Outside there is no air to carry their voice. That is why they have **radios** in their helmets. Radio waves are a kind of invisible light and do not need air. Space probes also send their messages to Earth with radio waves, even from billions of kilometres away.

It is not silent in the space station **ISS**. There is air to breathe there, so sound can travel. Fans, pumps and other machines run day and night. They make sure the air stays fresh. That is why many astronauts sleep with earplugs.

Light does not need air. It travels through empty space all the way to us. That is why we can **see** the Sun and the stars but not hear them. Inside, the Sun is very loud and restless. But none of the sound makes it through empty space to the Earth.

gewusst: On the Moon you could not talk to each other without radio, even if you were standing right next to each other.
An astronaut inside a spacesuit can still hear a knock on the suit, because the sound travels through the suit and the air inside it.

teile.einleitung: The Saturn V was the huge rocket with which the Americans sent people to the Moon. To this day it is one of the biggest and most powerful rockets ever built. It was developed in the 1960s.
wichtigste: The Saturn V was about 110 metres tall and weighed almost 3000 tonnes at launch.
It had three stages, with the Apollo spacecraft sitting right at the top.
The first stage had five huge F-1 engines.
The development was led by the rocket engineer Wernher von Braun.
The first flight took place in 1967, still without people on board.
The last launch carried the space station Skylab into space in 1973.

abschnitte.text: The **Saturn V** was about **110 metres** tall. That is about as tall as a tower block with 35 floors. When fully fuelled it weighed **almost 3000 tonnes**. Most of that was **fuel**. It was launched from the **Kennedy Space Center** in Florida.

The Saturn V was made of **three stages** stacked on top of each other. The **first stage** had **five** huge **F-1** engines. They lifted the whole rocket off the ground.
