When the fuel of one stage was used up, it was dropped and the next one fired. In this way the rocket kept getting lighter. Right at the top sat the **Apollo spacecraft**.

The development was led by **Wernher von Braun**, a German-American rocket engineer. His team worked for the American space agency **NASA**. Thousands of companies and specialists helped to build the rocket. The aim was to put people on the Moon before 1970.

The **first flight** of the Saturn V took place in **1967**, still without people on board. After that came the flights to the Moon. Each Apollo spacecraft carried **three astronauts**. During the Moon landings, two went down to the Moon and one stayed in lunar orbit. In July 1969 a Saturn V sent the **Apollo 11** mission on its way, the first Moon landing.

On its **last launch** in **1973**, the Saturn V did not carry astronauts to the Moon. It put the American space station **Skylab** into orbit. After that the rocket was no longer built. Today you can admire some leftover Saturn V rockets in **museums** in the USA.

gewusst: Altogether the Saturn V was launched thirteen times.
No Saturn V ever lost its crew.

teile.einleitung: When stars twinkle, their light flickers quickly brighter and dimmer. Experts call this scintillation. The twinkling does not come from the stars themselves but from the restless air above us.
wichtigste: **Scintillation** is the scientific word for the twinkling of stars.
Stars shine steadily; only our **air** makes their light tremble.
Stars twinkle most strongly close to the **horizon**.
When the air is windy and restless, the stars twinkle especially strongly.
**Planets** hardly twinkle, and this is often how you recognise them.
In space the stars do not twinkle.

abschnitte.text: The air above us is never completely still. There are warmer and colder layers of air that keep moving. Light is **bent** a little as it passes through such layers. So the light of a star does not reach us quite evenly. It becomes slightly brighter and dimmer very quickly and sometimes flashes in different colours.

When a star is high above us, its light only has to pass through a little air. Close to the **horizon**, the light goes at an angle through much more air. That is why stars twinkle most strongly there. On nights with **wind** and restless air, too, starlight is bent back and forth more. Then the sky twinkles especially strongly.

Stars are so far away that to us they are only tiny points of light. Even small disturbances in the air make their light flicker. **Planets** are much closer to us. They appear as tiny discs, not as points. The disturbances even out, so planets shine more steadily. This is how you can often tell a bright planet from the stars.

In space there is no air to disturb the light. So for astronauts the stars shine **steadily** and do not twinkle. Space telescopes such as Hubble have no problem with scintillation either. That is why they deliver especially sharp pictures.

For astronomers the twinkling is a nuisance, because it makes pictures blurry. That is why large telescopes are often on **high mountains**. There is less restless air above the telescope there. Modern telescopes can also partly correct the disturbances with moving mirrors. This is called **adaptive optics**.

gewusst: The nursery rhyme “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star” is really about scintillation.
A bright star low on the horizon can flash in colours so strongly that some people mistake it for an aeroplane or a UFO.

teile.einleitung: The zenith is the point in the sky that lies exactly straight above you. It is an important point of reference in astronomy. Because it depends on where you are, everyone has their own zenith.
wichtigste: The **zenith** lies exactly straight above the observer.
The opposite point beneath your feet is called the **nadir**.
The Sun can only be at the zenith between the **tropics**, so never in Switzerland.
The celestial meridian runs through the north point, the zenith and the south point.
The **zenith distance** is 90 degrees minus the height above the horizon.
The word “zenith” comes from Arabic.

abschnitte.text: Imagine a line pointing from your feet exactly straight up, like a plumb line. Where it meets the sky is the **zenith**. If you go to another place, your zenith is also at a different spot in the sky. The opposite point exactly beneath your feet is called the **nadir**. It cannot be seen from the Earth's surface.

Astronomers give the height of a star as an angle above the horizon. The horizon is 0 degrees, the zenith 90 degrees. The distance of a star from the zenith is called the **zenith distance**. It is 90 degrees minus the height. So a star 35 degrees above the horizon is 55 degrees from the zenith. The **celestial meridian** is the great circle from the north point over the zenith to the south point; the Sun crosses it every day at true midday.

The Sun can only be exactly straight overhead between the northern and southern **tropics**. Switzerland lies far to the north of them, so here the Sun is never at the zenith. In Bern, at about 47 degrees north, it reaches its greatest height of **about 66 degrees** at midday on 21 June. You calculate 90 degrees minus the latitude plus the tilt of the Earth's axis of just over 23 degrees. In winter it is only about 20 degrees high at midday.

Light from stars on the horizon has to pass at an angle through a great deal of air. Near the **zenith** the path through the atmosphere is shortest. This means the picture is disturbed less, and the stars look clearer. That is why astronomers prefer to observe celestial bodies when they are high in the sky.

The word “zenith” goes back to the Arabic “samt ar-ra's”, which means “direction of the head”. Many terms in astronomy came to Europe from Arabic in the Middle Ages. In everyday life people also say that someone is “at the zenith of their career”. This means at the high point.

gewusst: The word “nadir” also comes from Arabic.
At the equator the Sun is exactly at the zenith at midday twice a year.

teile.einleitung: Red dwarfs are small, cool and faint stars. They are the most common stars in the Milky Way, and yet you cannot see a single one with the naked eye. The nearest star after the Sun is also a red dwarf.
wichtigste: About three quarters of the stars in the Milky Way are red dwarfs.
At about 2500 to 4000 kelvin, their surface is much cooler than the Sun's.
Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf and the nearest star after the Sun.
Red dwarfs live for hundreds of billions to trillions of years, longer than the age of the universe.
Low-mass red dwarfs are fully convective and so use almost all their hydrogen.
Flare stars such as UV Ceti suddenly become much brighter because of magnetic outbursts.

abschnitte.text: Red dwarfs have only a fraction of the **mass** of the Sun. At about **2500 to 4000 kelvin**, their surface is much cooler than the Sun's, which is about 5800 kelvin. That is why they shine **reddish** and give off a lot of **infrared light**. They are so **faint** that not a single one can be seen with the naked eye. Yet about **three quarters** of all stars in the Milky Way are red dwarfs.

Red dwarfs use their **hydrogen** very sparingly. In addition, low-mass red dwarfs are **fully convective**: the gas is stirred around throughout the whole star. This means fresh hydrogen keeps reaching the core. They therefore live for **hundreds of billions to trillions of years**. The universe is only about **13.8 billion years** old, so no red dwarf has yet left the **main sequence**.

The nearest star after the Sun is **Proxima Centauri**, a red dwarf in the **Alpha Centauri system**. It is about 4.2 light years away. Another well-known red dwarf is **Barnard's Star**, only about 6 light years away. It has the **largest known proper motion** of any star and moves about **10 arcseconds per year** across the sky.

Many red dwarfs have strong **magnetic fields**. In so-called **flare stars**, the magnetic field suddenly releases energy. The brightness can multiply within **minutes**. A well-known example is **UV Ceti**. Such outbursts also send a lot of high-energy radiation into space.

**Planets** orbit many red dwarfs. Because the stars are so faint, their **habitable zone**, where liquid water would be possible, lies very close to the star. There, strong **tidal forces** slow down the planets' own rotation. That is why many of them are **tidally locked** and always show the same side to the star. Researchers are studying whether life is possible on such planets.

gewusst: In 2016 a planet was discovered orbiting Proxima Centauri in the habitable zone.
Seven roughly Earth-sized planets orbit the red dwarf TRAPPIST-1.

teile.einleitung: Space weather is the name for events between the Sun and the Earth that can affect technology and people. Outbursts on the Sun fling particles into space. When they hit the Earth, they create auroras, but sometimes also disruption.
wichtigste: The Sun constantly sends out the **solar wind**, much more strongly during outbursts.
Strong disturbances of the Earth's magnetic field are called **geomagnetic storms**.
The **Kp index** from 0 to 9 describes geomagnetic activity.
The NOAA scale goes from G1 to **G5** for extreme storms.
In 1989 a storm caused a big power cut in Quebec.
In May 2024 auroras could be seen all over Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Sun constantly sends a stream of charged particles into space, the **solar wind**. During large outbursts it also flings huge clouds of particles away. These **coronal mass ejections** usually take one to three days to reach the Earth. The Earth's magnetic field protects us but is shaken up strongly. The Sun's activity rises and falls in a cycle of about eleven years.

The worldwide disturbance of the Earth's magnetic field is described with the **Kp index**, from 0 to 9. It is calculated every three hours from measurements at several observatories. Values of 5 and above count as a **geomagnetic storm**. The US agency NOAA divides storms into five levels, from G1 for weak to **G5** for extreme. Probes such as SOHO or DSCOVR are at the **Lagrange point L1**, about 1.5 million kilometres towards the Sun, and give about 15 to 60 minutes' warning before the solar wind arrives.

When the Earth's magnetic field changes quickly, **geomagnetically induced currents** are produced in long conductors such as high-voltage power lines. They can overheat large transformers. On 13 March 1989 this caused the power grid of Hydro-Québec in Canada to collapse. About six million people were without electricity for about nine hours.

A storm heats the upper atmosphere, which then expands. In February 2022 this slowed down about 40 newly launched **Starlink satellites** more strongly, and they burned up. Space weather can also disturb radio links and GPS positioning. During strong outbursts, astronauts have to protect themselves from the increased radiation.

The beautiful side of space weather is the **aurora**. On the night of 10 to 11 May 2024 an extremely strong storm hit the Earth, and auroras glowed all over Switzerland too. The strongest known storm was the **Carrington Event** of 1859. At that time sparks flew from telegraph equipment, and some lines even worked without a battery.

gewusst: During the Carrington Event, auroras were seen as far south as the Caribbean.
The stronger a storm, the closer to the equator auroras can be seen.

teile.einleitung: Precession is a slow, top-like wobble of the Earth's axis. It takes so long that you hardly notice it in a lifetime, but over thousands of years it changes the sky.
wichtigste: The Earth's axis slowly traces out a cone, as with a spinning top.
One cycle takes about 26,000 years and is called the Platonic year.
The cause is the pull of the Sun and the Moon on the Earth's equatorial bulge.
Hipparchus discovered precession in the 2nd century BC.
In about 12,000 years, Vega will be near the north celestial pole.
The tilt of the axis stays at about 23.4 degrees; what changes is its direction.

abschnitte.text: A spinning **top** that is tilted does not fall over. Instead, its axis slowly moves round in a circle. This movement is called **precession**. The Earth is also a huge spinning top. Its axis slowly traces out a cone. One cycle takes about 25,800 years; this is called the **Platonic year**.

The Earth is not a perfect sphere; it is a little thicker at the equator. The **Sun and the Moon** pull on this **equatorial bulge** with their gravity. They try to set the tilted axis upright. But because the Earth is spinning, the axis does not tip over but moves off to the side. The **tilt** stays at about 23.4 degrees; what changes is the **direction** in which the axis points.

Today the Earth's axis points almost at the **Pole Star**. Because it moves, this will not stay so. In about 12,000 years, the bright star **Vega** will be near the north celestial pole. The **vernal equinox point**, where the Sun is at the start of spring, is also slowly moving backwards through the constellations of the zodiac.

In the 2nd century BC, the Greek astronomer **Hipparchus** compared his star measurements with older data. He noticed a slow shift and so discovered precession. Planetary orbits can also turn. The orbit of **Mercury** turns a little faster than Newton's law would lead you to expect. **Albert Einstein** explained this remaining difference in 1915 with the general theory of relativity.

gewusst: Because of precession, today's signs of the zodiac no longer match the constellations of the same names.
About 5,000 years ago, a star in the constellation Draco was the pole star.

teile.einleitung: A planetary nebula is a glowing shell of gas around a dying star. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets.
wichtigste: Planetary nebulae form when a star casts off its outer layers at the end of its life.
They form from stars with about 0.8 to 8 solar masses.
The UV radiation of the hot central star makes the gas glow.
William Herschel introduced the name in the 18th century.
A planetary nebula only glows for a few tens of thousands of years.
Well-known examples are the Ring Nebula M57 and the Dumbbell Nebula M27.

abschnitte.text: In small telescopes, these nebulae look like round, slightly greenish **little discs**. This was reminiscent of the discs of the planets Uranus and Neptune. That is why **William Herschel**, who observed many of these nebulae, called them “planetary nebulae” in the 1780s. Today we know that they have nothing to do with planets, but the name has stuck.

At the end of their lives, low-mass and medium-mass stars swell up into **giant stars**. In the last phase, they lose their outer layers, which slowly stream out into space. What remains is the hot, exposed core. It later becomes a **white dwarf**. Heavier stars with more than about 8 solar masses, on the other hand, end in a **supernova**.

The central star is extremely hot and gives off strong **UV radiation**. It tears electrons away from the atoms in the gas, and the gas is **ionised**. When the atoms capture electrons again, they give off light. The typical green colour used to be thought to come from an unknown element called “nebulium”. In 1927, **Ira Bowen** showed that it comes from doubly ionised **oxygen**.

The first planetary nebula to be discovered was the **Dumbbell Nebula** (M27) in the constellation Vulpecula, by Charles Messier in 1764. Also very well known is the **Ring Nebula** (M57) in the constellation Lyra, a popular target for small telescopes. Because the gas expands and becomes thinner and thinner, such a nebula only glows for a few tens of thousands of years. For the universe that is very short.

gewusst: According to current knowledge, our Sun will also cast off its outer layers in a few billion years and leave behind a white dwarf.
The green oxygen line only forms in very thin gas, which is why for a long time it could not be reproduced in the laboratory.

teile.einleitung: A space telescope is a telescope that orbits the Earth or the Sun in space. There no air spoils the view, and it can also measure radiation that the atmosphere swallows. Famous examples are the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes, which deliver breathtaking pictures from the depths of the universe.
wichtigste: Space telescopes observe space from above the troublesome atmosphere of the Earth.
X-ray telescopes such as Chandra have to be in space because the atmosphere absorbs X-rays.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990; at first its main mirror was ground wrongly.
The James Webb Space Telescope has a main mirror about 6.5 metres across.
James Webb is at the Lagrange point L2, about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth.
James Webb observes mainly in the infrared, because the light of early galaxies is strongly redshifted and infrared gets through dust.
ESA's Gaia mission measured the positions and movements of over a billion stars.

abschnitte.text: The **Earth's atmosphere** is a problem for astronomers. The air moves and makes stars twinkle, which makes pictures blurry. It also swallows large parts of the radiation from space, such as **X-rays**, much ultraviolet and much infrared. That is why X-ray telescopes such as Chandra have to be stationed in space. In space there is also no disturbing light from cities and no clouds.

The **Hubble Space Telescope** of NASA and ESA was carried into space by the Space Shuttle in 1990. It orbits the Earth at a height of about 540 kilometres and has a mirror 2.4 metres across. After the launch it turned out that its **main mirror** had been ground wrongly, and the pictures were blurry. In 1993 astronauts fitted correcting optics, rather like a pair of glasses. Among the astronauts was the Swiss **Claude Nicollier**, who took part in repair flights to Hubble in 1993 and 1999.

The **James Webb Space Telescope** was launched on 25 December 2021 on a European Ariane 5 rocket. Its main mirror is about 6.5 metres across and consists of 18 six-sided, gold-coated segments. It is at the **Lagrange point L2**, about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth, on the side facing away from the Sun. A sunshield the size of a tennis court keeps it cold, at about minus 230 °C. This cold is needed so that its own heat does not disturb the measurements.

Many space telescopes observe light that our eyes cannot see. James Webb works mainly in the **infrared**. The light of the earliest galaxies has been strongly shifted towards red by the expansion of the universe, all the way into the infrared. Infrared also gets through clouds of dust in which stars and planets form. From 2009 to 2013 the European telescope **Herschel** observed in the far infrared and, at 3.5 metres, had the largest mirror of any space telescope up to then.

Not all space telescopes take beautiful pictures. ESA's mission **Gaia** was launched in 2013 and measured the positions and movements of over a billion stars in the Milky Way. This produced the most precise three-dimensional map of our galaxy so far. From 2009 to 2018, NASA's **Kepler** space telescope searched for planets around other stars and found thousands of them. Together with the University of Bern, Switzerland built the telescope CHEOPS, which has been studying such distant planets more closely since 2019.

With Hubble, researchers were able to work out the age of the universe much more precisely. Its pictures of the **Hubble Deep Field** showed thousands of galaxies in a tiny patch of sky. James Webb finds galaxies that were already shining a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. It also studies the atmospheres of **exoplanets** and searches them for water and other substances. That is why space telescopes are among the most important tools of astronomy.

begriffe.erklaerung: An instrument that collects faint light and makes distant things visible.
Heat radiation that we cannot see but can feel as warmth.
A place in space where the pulls of the Sun and the Earth balance so that a satellite can travel along with the Earth.
A planet that orbits a star other than the Sun.

gewusst: At launch the James Webb Telescope was folded up and had to unfold in space over about two weeks, like origami.
The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier visited and serviced Hubble in space twice.
In over 35 years, Hubble has made more than a million observations, making it one of the most successful research instruments ever.

teile.einleitung: The Pole Star is the star that stands almost exactly above the Earth's North Pole. That is why it hardly seems to move in the sky and has always shown the direction of north.
wichtigste: The Pole Star lies almost exactly in line with the Earth's axis above the North Pole.
During the night it stays almost in the same place, while all the other stars seem to turn around it.
It is also called the North Star.
It is not the brightest star in the sky, only of medium brightness.
From Switzerland you can see it on every clear night about halfway up the northern sky.
It cannot be seen from Australia and the rest of the southern hemisphere.

abschnitte.text: To the north, the **Earth's axis** points almost exactly at the Pole Star. That is why it stands almost above the **North Pole**. Because the Earth turns, all the stars seem to move in circles at night. It is not the stars that are moving but we with the Earth. The Pole Star is almost at the centre of these circles and so stays almost in the same place.

Long ago, **sailors** already knew: where the Pole Star is, that is north. In this way they found their way even at night. Because of its position, it is also called the **North Star**. It should not be confused with the “evening star” or “morning star”. These are not stars at all but the planet **Venus**.

Many people believe the Pole Star is the brightest star in the sky. That is not true. It is only of **medium brightness**; many other stars shine more brightly, for example **Sirius**. You can find it with a trick: extend the back edge of the **Plough** about five times upwards. That is where the Pole Star is; it is the last star in the handle of the Little Dipper.

Switzerland lies roughly halfway between the **equator** and the North Pole. That is why here the Pole Star stands roughly **halfway up** between the horizon and the point directly overhead. It never sets and can be seen on every clear night. If you travel further south, you see it lower and lower. In the **southern hemisphere**, for example in Australia, it is below the horizon.

gewusst: The height of the Pole Star above the horizon is roughly equal to the latitude where you are standing.
Because the Earth's axis moves very slowly, in many thousands of years a different star will be the pole star.

teile.einleitung: Scorpius, the Scorpion, is a striking constellation in the summer sky. Its stars form a body with a long, curved tail like a real scorpion. Its brightest star is the red Antares.
wichtigste: The constellation Scorpius looks like a scorpion with a curved tail and sting.
Its brightest star is the red giant star Antares, the heart of the Scorpion.
Antares means something like “rival of Mars”.
Scorpius is a summer constellation and from Switzerland it is low in the south.
It is one of the twelve constellations of the zodiac, between Libra and Sagittarius.
In the Greek legend, a scorpion stung the hunter Orion.

abschnitte.text: The stars of **Scorpius** form a body with a long, curved **tail**. A long chain of stars makes up this tail. At the end it bends like a **hook** into the **sting**. Once you have found the constellation, you recognise the animal straight away. Scorpius is one of the few constellations that really look like their name.

The brightest star in Scorpius is called **Antares**. It shines clearly **reddish** and forms the **heart** of the Scorpion. Antares is a huge **red supergiant**, a particularly large giant star. Its name means something like “**rival of Mars**”. This is because it is red like the planet **Mars** and looks similar to it in the sky.

abschnitte.titel: When and where you can see it
abschnitte.text: Scorpius is a **summer constellation**. Here you can see it on **summer evenings**. It lies far to the **south** of the sky. From **Switzerland** it rises only just above the **southern horizon**. So you can only see the whole tail if the view to the south is clear, for example from a mountain. Further south, for instance by the Mediterranean, it stands higher in the sky.

Scorpius is one of the twelve constellations of the **zodiac**. The Sun, Moon and planets seem to move through these constellations over the course of the year. In the sky, Scorpius lies between **Libra** and **Sagittarius**. Planets such as Mars sometimes pass through Scorpius too. Then Mars and Antares stand close together, two red lights in the sky.

A **Greek legend** tells of the great hunter **Orion**. A **scorpion** stung him, and both were placed in the sky. There they stand far apart. When the Scorpion rises in the east, Orion sinks in the west. That is why you **hardly ever** see the two **at the same time**: Orion is a winter constellation, Scorpius a summer constellation.

gewusst: Antares is so big that, if it were put in place of the Sun, it would reach far beyond the orbit of Mars.
Very close to Antares lies a globular cluster, a gathering of a great many old stars.

teile.einleitung: The Sun sends us light and warmth. Without its radiation there would be no life on Earth. But part of it is invisible and can harm your skin.
wichtigste: The Sun sends visible light and invisible rays to the Earth.
Plants need sunlight to grow.
Invisible UV rays cause sunburn.
Solar cells turn sunlight into electricity.
Snow reflects a lot of light, so you need sunglasses in the mountains.
Black clothes get especially hot in the sun.

abschnitte.text: The Sun's rays bring **light** and **warmth**. That is why wet washing dries faster in the sun: the Sun warms it and the water evaporates. Animals use the warmth too. The **lizard** likes to lie on a warm stone. It cannot heat its body by itself, so it soaks up warmth for the day.

Plants need **light** to grow. In their green leaves they make their food from sunlight, water and air. This is called **photosynthesis**. It also produces oxygen, which we breathe. So almost all life on Earth depends on the Sun.

Part of the Sun's radiation is invisible. **UV rays** cause **sunburn** if you stay in the sun unprotected for too long. The higher up you are in the mountains, the stronger they are. **Snow** also reflects a lot of light. That is why you need **sunglasses** when skiing, so that your eyes are not dazzled and hurt.

With **solar cells** you can make electricity from sunlight. Many solar cells together make a solar panel. In Switzerland you can see such panels on more and more house roofs, barns and even on dam walls in the Alps. Other systems use the Sun to heat water for showers.

White sunlight is made of many colours. When it shines through **raindrops**, the colours are fanned out and a **rainbow** appears. Dark things absorb a lot of light and get warm. That is why **black clothes** get especially hot in bright sunshine. Light-coloured clothes reflect more light and stay cooler.

gewusst: Sunlight takes only just over eight minutes to reach the Earth.
Even on cloudy days, some of the UV rays get through the clouds.

teile.einleitung: The solar system is our home in space. At its centre is the Sun, which is orbited by eight planets, many moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets. The Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
wichtigste: The Sun is at the centre of the solar system.
Eight planets orbit the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
The solar system is about 4.6 billion years old.
The four inner planets are rocky planets, the four outer ones are giant planets.
Jupiter is the largest planet, Mercury the smallest.
Since 2006 Pluto has been classed as a dwarf planet.
A planet trail, like the one on the Uetliberg, shows the solar system on a smaller scale.

abschnitte.text: The centre is the **Sun**, which contains almost all the mass of the system. Eight **planets** orbit it, most of them with moons. On top of that there are **dwarf planets** such as Pluto and Ceres. Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt with countless chunks of rock. Right on the outside there is the Kuiper Belt and probably the huge Oort Cloud, where many comets come from.

Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are **rocky planets** with a solid surface. Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. Venus is the hottest planet, because its thick atmosphere traps the heat. The Earth is the only planet on which life is known so far. Mars is reddish because its ground contains a lot of iron oxide, a kind of rust.

Jupiter and Saturn are huge **gas planets**, made mainly of hydrogen and helium. Jupiter is so big that all the other planets together would fit inside it. Saturn is famous for its magnificent rings of ice and rock. Uranus and Neptune are called **ice giants**; they are bluish and very cold. Neptune needs about 165 years for one lap around the Sun.

The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a huge cloud of gas and dust. This cloud contracted under its own gravity. In the middle the Sun formed, and around it a flat, spinning disc. From dust and chunks in this **protoplanetary disc**, the planets gradually grew. That is why all the planets orbit in almost the same plane and in the same direction.

The distances in the solar system are huge and hard to imagine. A **planet trail** shows them on a smaller scale so that you can walk them. On the **Uetliberg** near Zurich, such a trail leads from the summit to the Felsenegg. Along the way there are models of the planets at the right size compared with the Sun. There are also planet trails in other places in Switzerland, for example on the Weissenstein near Solothurn.

The five bright planets that you can see with the naked eye have been known since ancient times. Uranus was discovered with a telescope in 1781 and Neptune in 1846. Since the 1960s **space probes** have been exploring the planets close up. The probes Voyager 1 and 2 were launched in 1977 and have since left the region where the solar wind blows.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large celestial body that orbits a star and has cleared its path.
A smaller, round celestial body orbiting the Sun that has not cleared its path, such as Pluto.
A small chunk of rock or metal that orbits the Sun.
The average distance between the Earth and the Sun, about 150 million kilometres.

gewusst: If the Sun were the size of a football, the Earth would only be the size of a pinhead and about 25 metres away from it.
A German memory sentence for the order of the planets is “Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unseren Nachthimmel” (“My father explains our night sky to me every Sunday”).
The solar system takes about 230 million years for one lap around the centre of the Milky Way.

teile.einleitung: A space capsule is a small spacecraft for people. In it, astronauts fly into space, to a space station or even to the Moon and back again.
wichtigste: At launch, the space capsule sits right at the top of the rocket.
It is very cramped inside a capsule, rather like a small car.
The Russian Soyuz capsule has been flying for many decades.
Astronauts flew to the Moon with Apollo in 1969.
A heat shield protects the capsule on the way back.
Since 2020, astronauts have also been flying in SpaceX's Crew Dragon capsule.

abschnitte.titel: Right at the top of the rocket
abschnitte.text: At launch, the **space capsule** sits right at the top of the rocket. Below it are the big fuel tanks and engines. This means the astronauts can be carried away from the rocket quickly if there is danger. It is **very cramped** inside the capsule, rather like a small car. The astronauts sit close together.

Astronauts flew to the Moon in the **Apollo** capsule in 1969. On **Apollo 11**, two of them walked on the surface of the Moon. The Russian capsule **Soyuz** has been flying for many decades, and a great many astronauts have flown to the space station in it. Since 2020, astronauts have also been flying in **Crew Dragon** from the company SpaceX. Dragon means “Drache” in German.

The capsule approaches the **space station** slowly and very precisely. Small steering thrusters help with this. Then it connects to a **docking port**. Once everything is sealed, the astronauts open the hatch and float across into the station.

On the way back, the capsule enters the Earth's **atmosphere** at very high speed. Friction with the air makes it extremely hot on the outside. The **heat shield** on the underside protects the astronauts. Then big **parachutes** open and slow the capsule down. Some capsules land in the sea, while Soyuz lands on solid ground in the steppe.

gewusst: After landing, a space capsule is often scorched black on the outside.
The first space capsule with a person on board carried Yuri Gagarin around the Earth in 1961.

teile.einleitung: Vostok 1 was the spacecraft in which Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space. The flight on 12 April 1961 was a great success for the Soviet Union and a milestone in space travel.
wichtigste: **Yuri Gagarin** was launched on Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.
The flight lasted about **108 minutes**.
Vostok 1 went around the Earth exactly **once**.
Gagarin landed using an **ejection seat** and a parachute of his own.
At launch he called out “Poyekhali!”, meaning something like “Let's go!”.
12 April is the International Day of Human Space Flight.

abschnitte.text: **Yuri Gagarin** was a military pilot in the Soviet Air Force. For the first cosmonauts, mainly young fighter pilots who were healthy and not too tall were chosen. Gagarin was selected from a small group. After his flight he became world famous and travelled to many countries.

On the morning of **12 April 1961** the rocket carrying Vostok 1 lifted off at Baikonur. At lift-off Gagarin called out “**Poyekhali!**”, which means something like “Let's go!”. The cry became very famous in the Soviet Union. The capsule was a ball in which Gagarin only just fitted. The flight was largely automatic.

Vostok 1 flew exactly **one lap** around the Earth. Then the spacecraft braked and returned into the atmosphere. The whole flight lasted about **108 minutes**, just under two hours. This made Gagarin the first person to see the Earth from space.

The capsule did not land with Gagarin inside it. At a height of a few kilometres he was shot out with the **ejection seat** and landed under a parachute of his own. The capsule also came down separately under a parachute. Gagarin landed in a field in the **Saratov region** on the Volga. Farm workers in the field were the first to see him.

In 2011 the **United Nations** declared 12 April the International Day of Human Space Flight. In Russia the day has long been known as Cosmonautics Day. Many streets, schools and even a crater on the Moon bear Gagarin's name.

gewusst: Yuri Gagarin's flight took place exactly 50 years before the UN declared the day of remembrance.
Yuri Gagarin was only 27 years old at the time of his flight.

teile.einleitung: Weather satellites watch clouds, storms and temperatures on Earth from space. Their pictures and measurements are essential for weather forecasts today, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: The first successful weather satellite was **TIROS-1**, launched in the USA in 1960.
The European weather satellites are called **Meteosat**.
They are run by **EUMETSAT**, based in Darmstadt; Switzerland is a member.
Geostationary satellites are about 36,000 km above the equator.
Polar satellites fly at about 800 km and gradually see the whole Earth.
Using **infrared**, weather satellites can see clouds at night too.

abschnitte.text: On 1 April 1960 **TIROS-1**, the first successful weather satellite, was launched in the USA. It sent the first television pictures of clouds from space back to Earth. For the first time, experts saw large weather systems from above. Since then many weather satellites have been added, delivering more and more precise pictures.

**Geostationary** satellites such as Meteosat orbit about 36,000 km above the equator. There one orbit takes exactly as long as one turn of the Earth. So the satellite seems to stand still above one point and can take a new picture of the same area every few minutes. But it only sees the polar regions at a steep angle at the edge of the picture.

**Polar** weather satellites fly much lower, at about 800 km, and cross the poles. Because the Earth turns beneath them, over time they see the whole Earth, including the polar regions. They deliver very precise measurements of temperature and humidity at different heights. These data are important for the computer models used in weather forecasting.

Clouds, land and sea give off **heat radiation**, even when it is dark. Infrared cameras measure this radiation without sunlight. This means cloud pictures can be made at night too. There are hardly any measuring stations over the sea, but satellites spot **tropical storms** there early on from their large spirals of cloud. This means people on the coasts can be warned in time.

The European weather satellites are called **Meteosat**. They are run by **EUMETSAT**, the European organisation for weather satellites, based in Darmstadt in Germany. Switzerland is one of the member states. **MeteoSwiss** uses the pictures and data for its weather forecasts and severe weather warnings.

gewusst: A geostationary satellite is almost three times as far from the Earth as the Earth is wide.
Weather satellites also measure water vapour in the air, which is invisible to the eye.

teile.einleitung: Space debris, also called space junk, is human-made parts that circle the Earth uselessly. They are extremely fast and can endanger satellites and space stations.
wichtigste: Space debris is old **satellites**, used rocket stages and wreckage.
In low orbit the parts fly at about **28,000 km/h**.
According to ESA, at the end of 2024 over 50,000 pieces larger than 10 cm were orbiting the Earth.
The **Kessler syndrome** describes a possible chain reaction of collisions.
The ISS dodges dangerous pieces using its engines.
Many pieces in low orbit burn up in the atmosphere after a while.

abschnitte.text: Since 1957 people have put thousands of satellites into space. Many of them no longer work but keep circling the Earth. On top of that there are burnt-out **rocket stages**, lost tools and countless **fragments**. All this is called space debris. According to the European Space Agency ESA, at the end of 2024 there were over 50,000 pieces larger than 10 cm up there, and there are far more smaller ones.

In low orbit everything has to move at about 7.8 km per second, which is about **28,000 km/h**. At this speed even a tiny piece can cause great damage. In February 2009, for the first time, two whole satellites collided above Siberia: the American **Iridium 33** and the old Russian **Kosmos 2251**. This produced over 2000 tracked pieces of wreckage.

In 1978 the scientist **Donald Kessler** warned of a dangerous development. Every collision creates new wreckage, which can cause further collisions. In the end a **chain reaction** could arise that makes some orbits unusable. Deliberate destruction makes the problem worse too: in 2007 China shot down its old weather satellite Fengyun-1C with a missile, creating over 3000 tracked pieces of wreckage.

Ground stations track larger pieces and calculate their paths. If a piece comes too close to the **International Space Station ISS**, the station raises or lowers its orbit a little with its engines. In low orbit, the thin air slowly slows the wreckage down. It sinks and **burns up** as it enters the atmosphere. Higher up, on the other hand, debris can circle for a very long time.

Today satellites are supposed to be deliberately brought down to burn up at the end of their work, or pushed into a graveyard orbit. Researchers are also developing satellites that are meant to catch debris. The company **ClearSpace** from Lausanne is working with ESA on such a mission. But tidying up in space is difficult and expensive.

gewusst: Even small flakes of paint have damaged the windows of space shuttles.
A piece of debris in low orbit goes around the Earth in about an hour and a half.

teile.einleitung: In a solar eclipse, the Moon moves between the Sun and the Earth and covers the Sun completely or partly. During the day it suddenly becomes dim or even dark. Total solar eclipses are among the most impressive natural spectacles of all.
wichtigste: In a solar eclipse, the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth.
The Sun is about 400 times bigger than the Moon but also about 400 times further away, so both look about the same size.
In a total eclipse you can see the Sun's halo of rays, the corona.
If the Moon is further away, it looks smaller and a bright ring remains: an annular eclipse.
A solar eclipse only happens at new moon.
You may only look at it directly with tested solar eclipse glasses.
On 11 August 1999 the Sun was almost completely covered in Switzerland too.

abschnitte.text: The Moon orbits the Earth about once a month. At **new moon** it is between the Sun and the Earth. Usually it passes just above or below the Sun, because its orbit is slightly tilted. Only when the Sun, Moon and Earth are exactly in a line does the **Moon's shadow** fall on the Earth. Then there is a solar eclipse, total or partial depending on where you are.

The Sun is about 400 times bigger than the Moon. But it is also about 400 times further away from us. That is why both look almost exactly the same size in the sky, and the small Moon can cover the huge Sun exactly. You can compare this **apparent diameter** with a coin that hides a ball far away.

In a **total solar eclipse**, the Sun is completely covered, but only in a narrow strip on the Earth. Outside that strip you see a **partial eclipse**, in which only a piece of the Sun is missing. The distance between the Moon and the Earth varies. If the Moon happens to be further away, it looks smaller and does not cover the Sun completely. Then a shining ring remains: this is an **annular solar eclipse**.

During totality it becomes almost as dark as night within a few minutes, and the temperature drops noticeably. Bright stars and planets become visible, and birds fall silent. Around the black disc of the Moon shines the **corona**, the delicate halo of rays of the Sun. At the edge you can sometimes see reddish clouds of gas, the **prominences**. Totality lasts at most a little over seven minutes, but usually only two to four.

Even when only a small part of the Sun can be seen, its light is dangerous for your eyes. Ordinary sunglasses do not protect you. You need tested **solar eclipse glasses** or a telescope with a special solar filter. A simple method is a **pinhole camera**: you let sunlight fall through a small hole onto a sheet of paper and see a picture of the covered Sun there.

On 11 August 1999 the Moon's full shadow passed over southern Germany, very close to Switzerland. In Switzerland the Sun was almost completely covered, and many people travelled to the neighbouring country to see totality. Partial eclipses happen in Switzerland every few years. The next total solar eclipse visible in Switzerland will not take place until **3 September 2081**. On 12 August 2026 a total eclipse could be seen in Spain, and a partial one in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outer, very hot halo of rays of the Sun, which can only be seen well during a total eclipse.
The phase of the Moon when it is between the Earth and the Sun and invisible to us.
The short time during which the Sun is completely covered by the Moon.
The opposite: the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and the Moon lies in the Earth's shadow.

gewusst: In 1868, during a solar eclipse, researchers discovered a new element in the light of the corona, which was later called helium.
The Moon moves about 3.8 centimetres further away from the Earth every year, so in the distant future there will be no more total solar eclipses.
During the solar eclipse of 1919, researchers confirmed that the Sun bends the light of stars, as Einstein had predicted.

teile.einleitung: Space medicine studies what happens to the human body in space. Without gravity, bones, muscles and balance change. Doctors look for ways to keep astronauts healthy.
wichtigste: Without countermeasures, astronauts lose about 1 to 1.5 per cent of their **bone mass** per month.
In weightlessness, body fluid shifts towards the head and the face looks puffy.
On the ISS astronauts exercise for about **2 hours** a day.
Valeri Polyakov holds the record for the longest single space flight, at 437 days.
Oleg Kononenko spent a total of 1111 days in space on five flights (as of 2025).
In the first few days many suffer from **space sickness**.

abschnitte.text: On Earth, bones and muscles carry our weight all the time. In space this load disappears. So the body loses **bone**, especially in the hips and legs: without countermeasures about 1 to 1.5 per cent per month. The **muscles** become weaker too. That is why astronauts on the ISS exercise for about two hours a day on a treadmill, an exercise bike and a weight machine.

On Earth, gravity pulls blood and other fluid into the legs. In space this **body fluid** shifts towards the head. The face swells up and the legs become thinner. The **spine** changes too: the discs between the vertebrae stretch, and astronauts become a few centimetres taller. After returning, they shrink back to their old height.

The **balance organ** in the inner ear normally tells us where up and down are. In weightlessness it sends unusual signals that do not match what the eyes see. That is why many astronauts feel sick and dizzy in the first few days. This **space sickness** usually wears off after a few days.

From 1994 to 1995 the doctor and cosmonaut **Valeri Polyakov** lived on the space station Mir for a whole 437 days. He studied the effects of long space flights on himself. In the **twin study**, NASA compared the astronaut Scott Kelly, who spent about 340 days on the ISS in 2015 and 2016, with his twin brother Mark on Earth. Researchers studied, among other things, the immune system, gene activity and thinking skills.

In space you are more exposed to **radiation** from space, because the protective atmosphere is missing. Living in a cramped space far away from family and friends is also a strain. For future long journeys to Mars, space medicine still has many questions to solve. Its findings also help on Earth, for example in treating weak bones.

gewusst: In 2024 Oleg Kononenko became the first person to spend more than 1000 days in space.
The bone loss in one month in space is about as great as that of older people with osteoporosis in a whole year.

teile.einleitung: If you look closely, stars shine in different colours: reddish, yellow, white or bluish. The colour reveals how hot a star is on its surface. Red stars are cool, blue ones very hot.
wichtigste: The colour of a star depends on its surface temperature.
The coolest stars shine red, the hottest blue.
From hot to cool, the spectral classes are O, B, A, F, G, K, M.
A class A star such as Vega shines white.
With a spectroscope you split starlight into its colours.
The hottest blue stars are over 30,000 °C hot.

abschnitte.text: When you heat a piece of **iron**, it first starts to glow **red**. As it gets hotter, it glows orange, yellow and finally whitish. It is similar with stars. Their colour depends on their **surface temperature**. The **coolest** stars are **red**, the hottest **blue**. At about 5500 °C, our Sun is yellowish white.

In the constellation **Orion** you can see the difference well. **Betelgeuse** shines reddish, **Rigel** bluish white. So the stars have **different surface temperatures**. Betelgeuse is a cool red supergiant. Rigel is a much hotter star. With binoculars you can see the colours even more clearly.

With a **spectroscope** you split the light of a star into its colours, as in a rainbow. From this you can see at which colour the star gives off the most light. This lets you work out its **temperature**. Dark lines in the spectrum also show which substances are found in the star.

Stars are sorted by temperature into **spectral classes**. From hot to cool they are called **O, B, A, F, G, K, M**. O stars are blue and over **30,000 °C** hot. A class **A** star such as **Vega** shines **white**. The Sun belongs to class G, Betelgeuse to class M. M stars are red and often only about 3000 °C hot.

abschnitte.titel: Why are there no green stars?
abschnitte.text: A star does not shine in just one colour but in many colours at once. Even if it gives off the most green light, a lot of red and blue is added. **Its light mixes to white**. That is why there are no stars that shine green. Our Sun actually shines most strongly in the green range and still looks white.

gewusst: With fire and hot plates it is the same as with stars: blue is hotter than red, even though we often call red “warm”.
With the naked eye you can only see star colours well in bright stars, because our eyes can hardly see colours in the dark.

teile.einleitung: A radio telescope picks up radio waves from space. With it, researchers can see things that remain invisible to ordinary telescopes.
wichtigste: At the beginning of the 1930s, Karl Jansky discovered radio waves from the Milky Way.
Radio telescopes can also observe during the day and when it is cloudy.
Neutral hydrogen gives off radiation at a wavelength of 21 centimetres.
The Chinese radio telescope FAST has a diameter of 500 metres.
The Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico collapsed in 2020.
In 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope made the first image of a black hole.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 1930s, the engineer **Karl Jansky** was looking for sources of interference with radio links. He found a hiss that came from the direction of the **centre of the Milky Way**. That was the beginning of **radio astronomy**. A radio telescope usually consists of a large **dish**. It collects the faint radio waves and directs them onto a receiver.

Radio waves pass through **clouds**, and the Sun hardly disturbs them during the day. That is why radio telescopes can measure almost around the clock. Cold **hydrogen** in space gives off faint radio waves with a wavelength of **21 centimetres**. With them, the spiral arms of the Milky Way could be made visible.

The **Effelsberg** radio telescope in the Eifel in Germany is 100 metres across and one of the largest fully movable ones in the world. It started working in 1972. The 305 metre dish at **Arecibo** in Puerto Rico was the largest in the world for decades. In December 2020, the receiver platform crashed into the dish. Today the Chinese **FAST**, at 500 metres, is the largest radio telescope with a single dish.

Several radio telescopes can be **linked together**. This technique is called **interferometry**. The sharpness of the image then depends roughly on the distance between the antennas. **ALMA** in Chile's Atacama Desert consists of 66 antennas at a height of about 5,000 metres. The **Event Horizon Telescope** linked radio telescopes on several continents into a telescope the size of the Earth. In 2019 it showed the first image of a **black hole**.

gewusst: The black hole in the first image lies at the centre of the distant galaxy M87.
The FAST dish lies in a natural hollow in the province of Guizhou.

teile.einleitung: A space station is a building in space where people can live, and it orbits the Earth. Astronauts often live and do research there for several months. The best known is the International Space Station ISS, where people have lived all the time since the year 2000.
wichtigste: A space station is a place in space where people live and work for a long time.
The ISS has been permanently lived in since the year 2000.
The ISS flies about 400 kilometres above the Earth.
It orbits the Earth about 16 times a day.
The ISS gets its electricity from large solar cells.
From Switzerland you can see the ISS with the naked eye as a bright point of light.
China also runs its own space station called Tiangong.

abschnitte.text: A **space station** is a large spacecraft in which people can live in space for a long time. Unlike a rocket, it stays in **orbit** permanently. The crew is taken there by spacecraft and picked up again. Cargo ships bring food, water, air and materials. The first space station was the Soviet Salyut 1 from 1971, later followed by Skylab from the USA and the Russian station Mir.

The **International Space Station ISS** is a joint project of the USA, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. Building began in 1998, and since November 2000 people have lived on board all the time. It is about the size of a football pitch and is made of many **modules** joined together. The European laboratory is called Columbus. Usually seven people live on the ISS at the same time.

The ISS flies about 400 kilometres above the Earth, which is roughly the distance from Geneva to St Gallen. It races around the Earth at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. It needs only about 90 minutes for one lap, so it orbits the Earth about 16 times a day. The crew therefore sees about 16 sunrises every day. Its electricity comes from huge **solar cells**, whose wings stick out far beyond the station.

On the ISS there is **weightlessness**: everything floats. That is why the astronauts sleep in sleeping bags that are tied down, and drink from pouches. So that their muscles and bones do not become weak, they exercise for about two hours a day. The crew carries out experiments on medicine, plants, materials and physics. Many of these experiments are only possible without gravity.

From Switzerland you can often see the ISS with the naked eye. It appears as a bright, steady **point of light** that crosses the sky in a few minutes and does not blink like an aeroplane. The best time to see it is shortly after sunset or before sunrise, when it is still lit by the Sun. You can check on websites and in apps when it will pass over. The ISS is expected to be brought down on purpose into the Pacific around the year 2030, after which new stations are to follow.

begriffe.erklaerung: A spacecraft where people can live, which stays in space permanently.
A building block of the space station, for example a laboratory or living space.
The state in which people and things in space seem to float.
The path on which the station circles the Earth.

gewusst: On the ISS, the crew's urine is treated and turned back into drinking water.
The ISS is the most expensive structure that humans have ever built.
The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier was never on the ISS, but he flew into space four times on the Space Shuttle.

teile.einleitung: The zodiac is a band of constellations in the sky through which the Sun seems to move over the course of a year. It is divided into twelve signs, almost all of which are named after animals or people.
wichtigste: The zodiac has **twelve** signs, matching the twelve months.
Over the course of a year the **Sun** seems to move through the constellations of the zodiac.
The zodiac includes, for example, **Leo**, but not Orion or the Great Bear.
**Libra**, the Scales, is the only sign that shows an object.
**Capricorn**, the ibex in German, is also the heraldic animal of the canton of Grisons.
Most of the names come from ancient times.

abschnitte.text: The Earth goes around the Sun in one year. Seen from the Earth, the Sun is therefore always in front of different constellations. Its apparent path across the sky is called the **ecliptic**. The constellations along this path form the **zodiac**. The Moon and the planets also move roughly through this band.

The twelve signs are called **Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces**. In German the zodiac is called “Tierkreis”, the circle of animals, because many of them show animals. Libra, on the other hand, shows a device for weighing, the Scales. It is the only sign that does not show a person or an animal.

Many signs tell stories from Greek **legends**. **Gemini**, the Twins, shows two brothers, and its two brightest stars are close together. **Pisces** is two fish joined by a ribbon. **Sagittarius** shows an archer who is half man and half horse. **Aries** is a ram, a male sheep with large curved horns.

abschnitte.titel: A sign with a Swiss link
abschnitte.text: The **ibex** lives in the Alps and climbs skilfully over steep rocks. In German the sign of **Capricorn** is called “Steinbock”, which means ibex. In Switzerland it is the **heraldic animal** of the canton of Grisons. In the 19th century it was wiped out in Switzerland, but today, thanks to reintroduction, it lives in many areas again.

**Astronomy** is the science of celestial bodies. It uses the constellations to divide up the sky. **Astrology**, on the other hand, links the star signs to people's characters, and that is not a science. Because the Earth's axis slowly shifts over thousands of years, the Sun is often in a different constellation on a given date today than it was about 2000 years ago.

gewusst: The Sun also passes through the constellation **Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer**, which is still not counted among the twelve signs of the zodiac.
The word “zodiac” comes from the Greek word for living creatures.

teile.einleitung: Day and night happen because the Earth spins on its own axis like a top. The side that is facing the Sun has day, the other side has night. The Earth needs about 24 hours for one full turn.
wichtigste: The Earth turns once on its own axis in about 24 hours.
It is day on the side facing the Sun and night on the other side.
The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
The Sun does not move around the Earth; it is the Earth that turns.
When it is midday in Switzerland, it is around midnight in New Zealand.
In Switzerland the days are longest in June and shortest in December.
The different lengths of day are caused by the tilted axis of the Earth.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns around its own axis, which goes through the North and South Poles. It needs about **24 hours** for one full turn, which is one day. The Sun only ever lights up one half of the globe. There it is **day**, and on the half facing away it is **night**. Because we turn with it, we notice nothing, even though in Switzerland we are moving at over 1000 kilometres per hour.

The Earth turns from west to east. That is why it looks as if the Sun rises in the **east**, is high in the south at midday and sets in the **west**. In reality the Sun stands still and we turn past it. For a long time people believed that the Sun went around the Earth. It was only in the 16th century that Nicolaus Copernicus described that the Earth turns and travels around the Sun.

Because it is not day everywhere at the same time, the Earth has been divided into **time zones**. Switzerland uses Central European Time. When it is midday here, it is around midnight in New Zealand, on the other side of the Earth. In New York it is only early morning then. In summer Switzerland puts its clocks forward by one hour; this is **summer time**.

The Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees. So in summer the Northern Hemisphere is tilted more towards the Sun, and the days are long. The longest day is around 21 June, the **summer solstice**, with almost 16 hours of daylight in Switzerland. Around 21 December, the **winter solstice**, there are only about 8 to 9 hours. In March and September, day and night are about the same length everywhere.

Near the poles it is even more extreme. In summer the Sun does not set there at all for weeks or months; this is the **polar day** or midnight sun. In winter, on the other hand, it stays below the horizon for a long time; this is the **polar night**. You can experience this well in the north of Norway. At the equator, by contrast, day and night are about the same length all year round.

Plants, animals and people have an **internal clock** that follows day and night. It tells us, for example, when we get tired. Some animals such as owls, bats and hedgehogs are **nocturnal** and look for food in the dark. Many flowers close their blossoms at night. Children need enough sleep at night to grow up healthy and learn well.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line through the North and South Poles, around which the Earth turns.
An area of the Earth where the same clock time applies.
The day with the longest or the shortest daylight of the year.
The time in winter when the Sun does not rise at all near the poles.

gewusst: A day on Earth is very slowly getting longer, because the Moon slows down the Earth's rotation; hundreds of millions of years ago a day had only about 22 hours.
One full turn of the Earth compared with the stars takes only about 23 hours and 56 minutes.
On Venus a day lasts longer than a whole Venus year.

teile.einleitung: A rocket launch is one of the most exciting moments in space travel. With an enormous roar, the rocket lifts off and carries people or satellites into space.
wichtigste: Large rockets launch straight upwards and only tilt to the side later.
The moment the rocket leaves the ground is called lift-off.
Astronauts sit in a capsule on top of the rocket.
A launch is often postponed if there is a thunderstorm.
For an orbit, a rocket needs about 28,000 km/h.
Experts monitor the flight in the control centre.

abschnitte.text: Before the launch, the rocket is filled with fuel on the **launch pad**. Experts check all the systems carefully. In the **control centre**, many people sit at screens and monitor everything. A launch only takes place in suitable weather. If there is a **thunderstorm**, it is often postponed, because lightning could damage the rocket's electronics.

In the **countdown**, people count backwards to zero. Then the engines ignite, and the rocket leaves the pad. This moment is called **lift-off**. Large rockets launch **straight upwards**. That way they leave the dense air as quickly as possible. Only later do they tilt to the side.

The engines burn huge amounts of fuel in a short time. This makes an **enormous roar**. The heat, the noise and the danger of an explosion are very great near the pad. That is why spectators usually stand **several kilometres** away. The astronauts sit in a **capsule** right at the top of the rocket, with the tanks and engines beneath them.

For a satellite or a capsule to circle the Earth, the rocket has to become very fast. For an **orbit** just above the atmosphere, you need about **28,000 kilometres per hour**. That is about thirty times as fast as a passenger aeroplane. On this path, the **orbit**, the satellite then flies around the Earth again and again.

gewusst: European rockets are usually launched from Kourou in French Guiana in South America, close to the equator.
During many launches, a lot of water is sprayed under the pad to dampen the noise and the heat.

teile.einleitung: Planck was a space telescope of the European Space Agency ESA. It measured the oldest light in the universe, the cosmic background radiation, more precisely than ever before.
wichtigste: Planck was an ESA mission with NASA involvement.
The telescope was launched on 14 May 2009 together with the infrared telescope Herschel.
It worked near the Lagrange point L2, about 1.5 million kilometres from the Earth.
There were two instruments on board: LFI and HFI.
The HFI detectors were cooled to about 0.1 kelvin.
Planck was switched off on 23 October 2013.

abschnitte.text: The telescope is named after the German physicist **Max Planck**. It flew into space on an **Ariane 5 rocket** from Kourou in French Guiana, together with the Herschel telescope. Planck was to map the **cosmic background radiation**. This is a faint glow that fills the whole sky and comes from the early days of the universe.

Planck worked near the **Lagrange point L2**. Seen from the Sun, it lies about 1.5 million kilometres behind the Earth. There, the Sun, Earth and Moon are always on the same side. The telescope could turn its back on them and so was hardly disturbed by their heat.

Planck had two instruments. The **LFI** (Low Frequency Instrument) worked with radio receivers, and the **HFI** (High Frequency Instrument) with **bolometers**, very sensitive heat sensors. Together they covered nine frequency bands from 30 to 857 gigahertz. A cooler with helium-3 and helium-4 cooled the bolometers to about a tenth of a kelvin, just above absolute zero. When the coolant was used up, the mission ended in 2013.

Planck's map shows tiny temperature differences in the background radiation. From them you can read what the universe is made of. Ordinary matter such as stars, gas, planets and living things makes up only about **5 per cent**. The rest is **dark matter** and **dark energy**, whose nature is still unknown. Planck also found that, on a large scale, space is **flat** within the accuracy of the measurements.

gewusst: According to the Planck data, the universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
The analysis of the measurements went on until 2018, five years after the telescope was switched off.

teile.einleitung: Space technology is about how to build rockets, satellites and space probes and how to put them on the right path in space. It needs physics, maths and a lot of engineering skill. Even small calculation errors can make a mission fail.
wichtigste: The rocket equation describes the change in speed a rocket can achieve.
A low circular orbit around the Earth needs about 7.9 km/s, the first cosmic velocity.
To escape the Earth completely, you need an escape velocity of about 11.2 km/s.
A Hohmann transfer is an energy-saving elliptical path between two circular orbits.
In a swing-by manoeuvre, a space probe gains speed from a planet.
The geostationary orbit lies about 35,800 km above the equator.
Ion engines have a very high specific impulse but only a very small thrust.

abschnitte.text: The **rocket equation** was set up by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1903. It tells you how much a rocket can change its speed, the so-called **delta-v**. This depends on the exhaust speed of the gases and on the ratio between launch mass and empty mass. You multiply the exhaust speed by the natural logarithm of this mass ratio. A rocket with an exhaust speed of 3000 m/s and a mass ratio of 4 therefore reaches about 4.2 km/s, which is why rockets are built with several stages.

To stop a satellite from falling down, it has to fly sideways very fast. A low circular orbit around the Earth needs about 7.9 km/s, the **first cosmic velocity**. The satellite then keeps falling around the Earth without ever hitting it. To leave the Earth completely from its surface, you need about 11.2 km/s, the **escape velocity**. That is over 40,000 kilometres per hour.

A **Hohmann transfer** is an energy-saving elliptical path that connects two circular orbits and needs only two engine burns. It is named after the German engineer Walter Hohmann, who described it in 1925. This is one way to reach the **geostationary orbit** about 35,800 km above the equator. There a satellite needs exactly one day for one lap and seems to stand still above one point on Earth. In a **swing-by**, a space probe uses the gravity and motion of a planet to gain speed.

How economical an engine is is given by its **specific impulse**, which is often measured in seconds. Chemical engines, for example using hydrogen and oxygen, reach about 450 seconds and provide a lot of thrust. **Ion engines** accelerate electrically charged particles using electricity from solar cells. They have a very high specific impulse but only a very small thrust, roughly as much as the weight of a sheet of paper. In return they can run for months and are well suited to long journeys of space probes.

Spacecraft have to withstand enormous heat, icy cold and strong radiation. When re-entering the atmosphere, a **heat shield** protects capsules from temperatures of well over 1000 degrees. Power usually comes from **solar cells**, and far out in the solar system also from radioactive batteries. Swiss companies and universities contribute too, for example with precision parts, atomic clocks for navigation satellites or instruments from the University of Bern. Every gram counts, because every extra kilo needs more fuel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change in speed that a spacecraft can achieve with its engines.
The speed you need to escape the gravity of a celestial body completely.
An economical transfer path between two circular orbits.
A flyby of a planet to gain speed.
A measure of how economically an engine uses its fuel.

gewusst: The space probes Voyager 1 and 2 used several swing-by manoeuvres to reach the edge of the solar system.
Astronauts on the ISS do not float because there is no gravity there, but because they are constantly falling around the Earth together with the station.
With today's rockets, a journey to Mars on a Hohmann path takes about seven to nine months.

teile.einleitung: In winter the night sky shows some of the brightest stars and most beautiful constellations of the year. Because it gets dark early, you can watch stars in the evening. Warm clothes are a must.
wichtigste: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky and belongs to Canis Major, the Great Dog.
In winter it gets dark early, which is good for stargazing.
Sirius, Betelgeuse and Procyon form the Winter Triangle.
Six bright stars together form the Winter Hexagon.
The Pleiades in Taurus are also called the Seven Sisters.
Aldebaran forms the red eye of the Bull.

abschnitte.text: In winter it gets **dark early**, often before six o'clock in the evening. So you can watch the stars without staying up late. Cold, dry air is often especially clear. Because it is cold outside, you should definitely take **warm clothes**, a hat and gloves. It is best to find a place without street lights.

The best-known winter constellation is **Orion**. You recognise it by three bright stars in a row, the **belt**. At the top left shines the reddish **Betelgeuse**, at the bottom right the bluish **Rigel**. If you extend the belt down to the left, you come to **Sirius** in **Canis Major, the Great Dog**. Sirius is the **brightest star** in the whole night sky.

**Sirius**, **Betelgeuse** and **Procyon** in Canis Minor, the Little Dog, together form the **Winter Triangle**. Even bigger is the **Winter Hexagon**, made of six bright stars: Sirius, Procyon, Pollux, Capella, Aldebaran and Rigel. High in the sky you can see the twin stars **Castor and Pollux** in the constellation Gemini, the Twins. These figures help you to find your way around the sky.

To the upper right of Orion is **Taurus, the Bull**. Its red eye is the bright star **Aldebaran**. The face of the Bull is formed by the star cluster of the **Hyades**. A little further on lie the **Pleiades**, a small, bluish star cluster. They are also called the **Seven Sisters**. With good eyes you can make out six or seven stars in it.

gewusst: Low above the horizon, Sirius often twinkles in many colours, because the restless air swirls its light.
In reality the Pleiades consist of hundreds of stars, but with the naked eye you only see the brightest ones.

teile.einleitung: TRAPPIST-1 is a small, cool star with seven planets that are about the size of the Earth. The system is about 40 light years away and is one of the most exciting targets in the search for Earth-like worlds.
wichtigste: TRAPPIST-1 is an **ultracool red dwarf**.
The system is about **40 light years** away in the constellation **Aquarius**.
**Seven planets**, roughly the size of the Earth, orbit the star.
The innermost planet, TRAPPIST-1 b, needs only about 1.5 days for one orbit.
According to common models, planets e, f and g lie in the **habitable zone**.
The name comes from a small telescope run by the University of Liège in **Belgium**.

abschnitte.text: TRAPPIST-1 is a **red dwarf**, and a particularly cool one. It has only just under a tenth of the mass of the Sun and is hardly bigger than the planet Jupiter. It shines faintly and gives off light mainly in the **infrared**. It cannot be seen with the naked eye, even though at about 40 light years it is very close by astronomical standards.

The planets were discovered with the small telescope **TRAPPIST**. It is run by the University of Liège in Belgium and stands in Chile. The name is also a nod to the Belgian Trappist beers. The researchers found the planets with the **transit method**: when a planet passes in front of the star, the star becomes slightly dimmer for a short time.

The seven planets are called TRAPPIST-1 b to h. They orbit very close to their star. The innermost needs only about **a day and a half** for one orbit. All the planets would fit inside the orbit of Mercury. Neighbouring planets are in simple number ratios such as 8 to 5 or 3 to 2. This **resonance chain** keeps the crowded system stable.

The three middle planets, **e, f and g**, receive about enough radiation for liquid water on their surface to be possible. They are said to lie in the **habitable zone**. The inner planets are probably too hot, and the outermost probably too cold. Whether there really is water on any of the planets is not yet known.

The **James Webb Space Telescope** has studied TRAPPIST-1 closely. In 2023 it measured the heat radiation from the day side of the innermost planet. It was so high that hardly any heat can be spread around. This fits a bare rocky planet **without a thick atmosphere**. The outer planets are still being studied.

gewusst: From a planet around TRAPPIST-1, you could sometimes see the neighbouring planets in the sky looking bigger than our Moon.
A year on the innermost planet lasts only about a day and a half on Earth.

teile.einleitung: A satellite is a body that orbits a planet or moon. Usually the word means artificial satellites, that is, devices built by people in an orbit around the Earth. They give us weather pictures, navigation, television and internet.
wichtigste: A satellite is a body that orbits another celestial body.
The first artificial satellite was Sputnik 1 in 1957.
Geostationary satellites orbit about 36,000 km above the equator.
Navigation satellites such as those of the European system Galileo help you to work out where you are.
The first satellite built entirely in Switzerland was SwissCube, launched in 2009.
In 1993 and 1999 the Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope.
Today several thousand active satellites orbit the Earth.

abschnitte.text: The word **satellite** comes from Latin and means companion. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth. **Artificial satellites** are devices that are carried into space by rockets. So that they do not fall down, they have to orbit the Earth very fast, at low altitude at almost 28,000 kilometres per hour. They then keep falling around the Earth without ever hitting it.

On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put **Sputnik 1** into orbit around the Earth. The shiny ball was about 58 centimetres across and sent out only a beeping signal. Even so, it caused a shock in the West and started the race into space. As early as 1958 the first American satellite, Explorer 1, followed. Today many thousands of active satellites orbit the Earth, a large share of them for internet connections.

Many satellites fly in a **low orbit** a few hundred kilometres up and circle the Earth in about an hour and a half. **Geostationary satellites** orbit about 36,000 km above the equator. There they need exactly one day for one lap and seem to stand still in the sky. That is why satellite dishes for television can be pointed at them permanently. In Switzerland, such dishes point south, because the equator lies to the south.

**Weather satellites** photograph clouds and help with weather forecasts, for example for MeteoSwiss. Navigation satellites such as those of the American GPS or of the European system **Galileo** help you to work out exactly where you are. Communications satellites transmit television, telephone and internet. Earth observation satellites keep watch on glaciers, forests and natural disasters. Space telescopes such as Hubble look into space without being disturbed by the atmosphere.

The first satellite built entirely in Switzerland was **SwissCube**, a cube only 10 centimetres along each edge. Students from EPFL in Lausanne and other universities built it, and it was launched on an Indian rocket in 2009. The Swiss astronaut **Claude Nicollier** flew on the Space Shuttle and in 1993 and 1999 helped to repair the Hubble Space Telescope. Swiss companies supply atomic clocks for the Galileo satellites. A growing worry is **space debris**: old satellites and wreckage that can endanger active satellites.

begriffe.erklaerung: A body that orbits a planet or moon.
An orbit in which a satellite always stays above the same point on the Earth.
A satellite whose signals can be used to work out your location.
Old satellites and pieces of wreckage that orbit the Earth.

gewusst: SwissCube was only meant to work for a few months, but it kept sending data for many years.
A smartphone receives signals from several navigation satellites at the same time to calculate its location.
On clear evenings you can sometimes see satellites as slowly moving points of light in the sky.

teile.einleitung: Starlink is a network of thousands of satellites that provides internet from space. It is run by the American space company SpaceX. It helps in remote places, but it is also criticised.
wichtigste: Starlink is run by the company SpaceX.
Most of the satellites orbit at a height of about 550 kilometres.
The first group of 60 satellites was launched in 2019.
In 2026 there were over 10,000 Starlink satellites in space.
Newer satellites exchange data using laser beams.
Astronomers complain about trails of light on pictures of the sky.

abschnitte.text: **Starlink** provides internet via satellites. It is run by the American company **SpaceX**. At home you need a small antenna that keeps in radio contact with the satellites. This is especially useful in remote places, on ships or in areas without good cables. Because the satellites move quickly across the sky, the antenna keeps switching from one to the next.

Most Starlink satellites orbit at about **550 kilometres** up. This is a **low Earth orbit**. Older internet satellites, on the other hand, are geostationary, almost 36,000 kilometres up. Because Starlink is **much closer to the Earth**, the signals take less time. That is why the internet is faster and responds more quickly, for example in video calls or games.

In **2019** the first group of **60** Starlink satellites was launched. Since then SpaceX has kept putting new ones into space with its Falcon 9 rockets. In **2026** there were **over 10,000**. This means that most of the active satellites in Earth orbit belong to Starlink. Newer satellites exchange data with each other using **laser beams**.

abschnitte.titel: A string of lights in the sky
abschnitte.text: Shortly after a launch, you can sometimes see a **string of bright points of light** in the evening sky. These are freshly launched Starlink satellites that are still flying close behind each other. They reflect sunlight. After a few days they rise higher and spread out.
