Then they are much harder to see.

Many **astronomers** complain about Starlink. The satellites leave **trails of light on pictures of the sky** and also disturb radio telescopes. SpaceX has made some satellites darker to reduce the problem. Others are worried about **space debris**, because so many objects in space make collisions more likely.

gewusst: Old Starlink satellites are deliberately lowered and then burn up in the atmosphere.
Other countries and companies are planning similar satellite networks, so the sky could become even more crowded.

teile.einleitung: Pluto is a small, icy body very far out in the solar system. For a long time it was considered the ninth planet, but since 2006 it has been counted among the dwarf planets.
wichtigste: Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh in the USA.
The name was suggested by eleven-year-old Venetia Burney from England.
Pluto is named after the Roman god of the underworld.
It is smaller than our Moon.
It takes about 248 years to go once around the Sun.
Its largest moon is called Charon.

abschnitte.text: **Clyde Tombaugh** worked at an observatory in the USA. He compared many photos of the night sky that had been taken at different times. In **1930** he found a small point of light that was moving among the stars. That was Pluto. Since its discovery, Pluto has not yet completed one whole lap around the Sun.

The name was suggested by **Venetia Burney**, an eleven-year-old girl from England. She thought of **Pluto**, the Roman god of the underworld. The name was chosen. It fits well, because so far out it is dark and cold. The surface is about minus 230 degrees.

In **2015**, the space probe **New Horizons** flew past Pluto. Its photos showed mountains of ice, plains and a bright area in the shape of a **heart**. Pluto is just under 2,400 kilometres wide, our Moon almost 3,500 kilometres. So Pluto is smaller than the Moon.

Pluto's largest moon is called **Charon**. It is about half as wide as Pluto. The two circle each other like a pair. Besides Charon, Pluto has four smaller moons. Since 2006, Pluto has been considered a **dwarf planet**, because it shares its orbit with many other bodies in the Kuiper Belt.

gewusst: Pluto's orbit is so stretched that at times it is closer to the Sun than Neptune.
Some of Clyde Tombaugh's ashes flew on board New Horizons.

teile.einleitung: Specific impulse shows how economically a rocket engine uses its fuel. The higher it is, the more push the engine gets out of each kilogram of fuel. It is usually given in seconds.
wichtigste: Specific impulse tells you how efficiently an engine uses its fuel.
It is often given in seconds.
Multiplied by the Earth's gravitational acceleration of about 9.81 m/s², it gives the exhaust speed.
Thrust is the mass pushed out per second times the exhaust speed.
In a vacuum the specific impulse is higher than at sea level.
Among common chemical fuels, hydrogen and oxygen reach the highest value.

abschnitte.text: A rocket pushes hot gas out backwards and is pushed forwards as a result. This is **recoil**. The **thrust** in a vacuum is the mass pushed out per second times the **exhaust speed**. If an engine pushes out 100 kilograms of gas per second at 3000 m/s, this gives 300,000 newtons, that is **300 kN**. The faster the gas comes out, the more thrust each kilogram provides.

**Specific impulse** is the effective exhaust speed divided by the Earth's gravitational acceleration of about **9.81 m/s²**. This gives a number in **seconds** that is the same everywhere in the world. Put simply, it shows **how efficiently** an engine uses its fuel. The other way round: 300 seconds times 9.81 m/s² gives an exhaust speed of about **2940 m/s**.

At **sea level**, the air pushes against the jet of exhaust. Part of the force is lost this way. In a **vacuum** there is **no surrounding pressure** pushing against it, so the specific impulse is higher there. Typical **solid-fuel rockets** reach about 250 to 270 seconds at sea level. That is why engines for space often have particularly large nozzles.

Among the common chemical fuels, **liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen** reaches the highest specific impulse. The exhaust gases, mainly water vapour, have a **low molecular mass** and so stream out very fast. The Space Shuttle's main engine, the **RS-25**, reached about **450 seconds** in a vacuum. The European Ariane rocket also uses hydrogen and oxygen.

**Ion engines** accelerate charged particles using electrical energy. They reach a specific impulse of **several thousand seconds**. In return, their thrust is very small, roughly as strong as the weight of a sheet of paper. They are not enough for a launch from the Earth. But in space they can slowly bring space probes up to high speeds over months.

gewusst: A higher specific impulse saves a lot of fuel, which is why the very cold hydrogen tanks, though difficult to handle, are worth it.
Ion engines need so little fuel that some space probes travel with them for years.

teile.einleitung: What exactly is a planet? The International Astronomical Union answered this question in 2006 with an official definition. Since then our solar system has had eight planets.
wichtigste: The International Astronomical Union (IAU) agreed on the definition in Prague in August 2006.
A planet has to meet three conditions.
Since 2006, our solar system has had 8 planets.
Since then, Pluto has been considered a dwarf planet.
Most asteroids and comets are called small solar system bodies.
The definition expressly applies to bodies that circle our Sun.

abschnitte.text: The **International Astronomical Union** (IAU) is the worldwide association of astronomers. It also gives the official names to celestial bodies. At the beginning of the 2000s, bodies about the same size as Pluto were found far out in the solar system, for example **Eris**. So clear rules were needed. In August 2006, the members voted on a definition at their General Assembly in **Prague**.

First, a planet must **circle the Sun**. Second, it must have so much mass that its own **gravity** shapes it into a roughly round ball. Third, it must have **cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit**, in other words be by far the largest body there. The Earth's Moon is round, but it circles the Earth and so is a moon.

The eight planets are **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune**. A body that circles the Sun and is round but has not cleared its orbit is called a **dwarf planet**. These include Pluto, Ceres and Eris. Pluto shares its orbit with many other bodies in the Kuiper Belt.

Anything that is neither a planet nor a dwarf planet nor a moon counts as a **small solar system body**. These include most asteroids, comets and Kuiper Belt objects. The definition expressly speaks of bodies around our Sun. For **exoplanets**, which circle other stars, there are separate working rules.

gewusst: The decision about Pluto was controversial among experts and is still being discussed today.
After its discovery in 1801, Ceres in the asteroid belt was at first considered a planet itself.

teile.einleitung: Atmospheric circulation is the Earth's great, worldwide system of winds. Because the Sun heats the tropics much more strongly than the poles, the air starts to move and carries heat around the globe. This creates trade winds, westerlies and jet streams, which also decide the weather in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Sun heats the Earth more strongly at the equator than at the poles, and this drives the winds.
In the Hadley cell, air rises at the equator and sinks at about 30 degrees latitude.
In the tropics, the trade winds blow at ground level from the north-east and south-east towards the equator.
The Coriolis force deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.
Because of the Ferrel cell and the Coriolis force, westerly winds prevail in Switzerland.
Jet streams are strong bands of wind high up at the boundary between air masses.
The föhn and the bise are well-known local winds in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Sun heats the Earth unevenly: at the **equator** the light falls steeply, at the poles only at a shallow angle. Warm air is lighter and rises, cold air is heavier and sinks. This creates areas of low and high **air pressure**. Air always flows from high to low pressure, and this creates wind. In this way heat is carried from the tropics towards the poles.

In each hemisphere there are three large loops, so-called **circulation cells**. In the **Hadley cell**, warm air rises at the equator, flows towards the pole high up and sinks again at about 30 degrees latitude. Many large deserts such as the Sahara lie there, because sinking air is dry. Between about 30 and 60 degrees lies the **Ferrel cell**, and at the poles the polar cell. This model is simplified, but it shows the basic pattern well.

Because the Earth turns, winds are not steered straight ahead. The **Coriolis force** deflects moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere. That is why the winds near the ground that flow towards the equator blow from the north-east and south-east. These steady winds are called **trade winds**. In the past, sailing ships used them to cross the Atlantic.

Near the equator, the trade winds of both hemispheres flow together. This trough of low pressure is called the **Intertropical Convergence Zone**. There moist, warm air rises, and huge thunderclouds form almost every day. It moves a little north and south with the seasons. This creates **rainy seasons** and dry seasons in many tropical countries.

In the middle latitudes, including Switzerland, mainly **westerly winds** blow. This is because of the Ferrel cell and the Coriolis force. That is why our weather usually comes from the Atlantic. At a height of about 8 to 12 kilometres, at the boundary between cold and warm air, for example at the polar front, strong bands of wind blow, the **jet streams**. They often reach over 200 kilometres per hour, and aeroplanes flying east use them as a tailwind.

As well as the large wind systems there are local winds. The **föhn** is a warm, dry downslope wind on the lee side of the Alps, that is, the side facing away from the wind. It blows, for example, through the Reuss Valley in the canton of Uri and can reach storm force. The **bise** is a cold, dry north-easterly wind that blows through the Central Plateau between the Jura and the Alps as if through a funnel. On Lake Geneva it can become especially strong.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing down on a surface.
An apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation, which deflects winds sideways.
A steady wind in the tropics that blows towards the equator.
A narrow band of very strong wind high up.

gewusst: Because of the jet stream, a flight from New York to Zurich often takes much less time than the flight back.
The Coriolis force decides which way low-pressure systems spin, but not which way the water drains out of a washbasin.
During föhn, it can suddenly become over 15 °C warm in Alpine valleys in winter.

teile.einleitung: A space probe is an uncrewed spacecraft that explores other celestial bodies. It flies to planets, moons, comets or the Sun and sends pictures and measurements back to Earth. Without space probes, we would know hardly anything about what other worlds look like.
wichtigste: Space probes are uncrewed spacecraft for exploring space.
They fly past celestial bodies, orbit them or land on them.
Voyager 1 is the human-made object furthest from the Earth.
In 2015, New Horizons was the first probe to fly past the dwarf planet Pluto.
NASA's rover Perseverance landed on Mars in February 2021.
The Parker Solar Probe has come closer to the Sun than any other human-made object.
The CaSSIS camera from the University of Bern photographs Mars from orbit.

abschnitte.text: A **space probe** is a spacecraft without people on board that studies celestial bodies beyond the Earth's orbit. It carries cameras and measuring devices, which are called **instruments**. It sends its data by radio to Earth, where large antennas receive them. Some probes only fly past, others orbit a planet as an **orbiter**. Still others land, and robots that can drive around are called rovers.

Space probes are often travelling for many years. To save fuel, they gain speed from planets in **swing-by manoeuvres**. Far away from the Sun they use radioactive batteries instead of solar cells. The further away a probe is, the longer its radio signals take. That is why probes have to do many things on their own.

The twin probes **Voyager 1** and Voyager 2 were launched in 1977 and visited the outer planets. Today Voyager 1 is the human-made object furthest from the Earth and has reached interstellar space. In 2015, **New Horizons** was the first probe to fly past the dwarf planet Pluto and showed a heart-shaped plain of ice. The Cassini probe explored Saturn from 2004 to 2017. In 2014 the European probe Rosetta set down the lander Philae on a comet.

Mars is the target of a particularly large number of probes. In February 2021, NASA's rover **Perseverance** landed in Jezero Crater, where it is collecting rock samples. From orbit, the **CaSSIS** camera from the University of Bern on the European probe Trace Gas Orbiter photographs the surface of Mars in colour. NASA's **Parker Solar Probe** has come closer to the Sun than any other human-made object. A heat shield protects it from the enormous temperatures.

Switzerland is a member of the European Space Agency **ESA** and helps to build many probes. The University of Bern has developed instruments for missions such as Rosetta, BepiColombo to Mercury and the Jupiter mission JUICE. The probe **CHEOPS**, which studies exoplanets, was built under the leadership of the University of Bern. Swiss companies also supply parts such as structures and precision mechanics. So ideas from Switzerland are part of many space missions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A space probe that orbits a celestial body.
A part of a mission that touches down on a celestial body.
A robot vehicle that drives around on another celestial body.
A measuring device or camera on board a probe.

gewusst: On board the Voyager probes there is a golden record with pictures, music and greetings from Earth.
The radio signals from Voyager 1 take almost a whole day to reach the Earth.
The Parker Solar Probe is the fastest object ever built by humans.

teile.einleitung: A solar flare is a sudden, violent burst of radiation on the Sun. Experts also simply call it a **flare**. In a few minutes it releases huge amounts of energy, which can have effects as far as the Earth.
wichtigste: A solar flare is a short, bright burst of radiation on the Sun.
The energy comes from twisted magnetic fields above active regions of the Sun.
Flares are divided by their X-ray brightness into the classes A, B, C, M and X.
Each class is ten times stronger than the one before; X flares are the strongest.
The light from a flare reaches the Earth after just over eight minutes.
Strong flares can disrupt shortwave radio on the day side of the Earth.

abschnitte.text: Above **sunspots** and other active regions, the Sun's magnetic fields are strongly twisted and stretched like a rubber band. A great deal of energy is stored in them. In **magnetic reconnection**, the field lines suddenly join up in a new way. This releases the stored energy all at once. It heats the gas, speeds up particles and produces radiation ranging from radio waves to X-rays.

The strength is measured with the American **GOES satellites**. They record **soft X-rays** in the range from 0.1 to 0.8 nanometres. In order of increasing strength, the classes are called A, B, C, M and X. Each class is ten times stronger than the one before, so an X1 flare is ten times stronger than an M1 flare. A number from 1 to 9 gives the strength within the class more precisely.

A solar flare is a short event. The brightness usually rises steeply within a few minutes. Then it fades away again over minutes to hours. Large events can last several hours. Because light covers about 150 million kilometres at 300,000 kilometres per second, we only see a flare just over **8 minutes** after it starts.

The X-rays from a strong flare hit the **ionosphere**, an electrically charged layer high in the atmosphere. It becomes more strongly charged and then swallows short waves that would otherwise be reflected. This can cause **shortwave radio** to fail on the day side of the Earth. On the ground we are well protected by the atmosphere.

After strong flares, very fast **protons** from the Sun can arrive. This is called a solar particle event. Outside the protective magnetic field of the Earth, these particles clearly increase the **radiation exposure**. Astronauts then have to go to better shielded areas of their spacecraft. That is why researchers watch the Sun around the clock.

gewusst: The first solar flare was observed in 1859 by the Englishman Richard Carrington, when a bright flash of light lit up on the Sun.
In a few minutes a large flare releases more energy than all of humanity uses in many years.

teile.einleitung: Atmospheric stability describes how the temperature of the air changes with height. It decides whether rising air keeps rising and thunderstorms form, or whether the air stays calm.
wichtigste: The temperature gradient of the surrounding air is compared with the adiabatic gradient.
If the temperature falls by more than 1 °C per 100 m, the air is absolutely unstable.
If the gradient lies between the moist and dry adiabatic rates, it is conditionally unstable.
In absolutely stable air, a parcel that has been lifted sinks back.
Heap clouds are typical of unstable air.
The stratosphere is very stable, because there the temperature rises with height.

abschnitte.text: A rising parcel of air cools down: by about **1 °C per 100 m** if it is unsaturated. Whether it keeps rising depends on its surroundings. If the parcel is warmer than the air around it, it is lighter and keeps rising. If it is colder, it sinks back. The **ICAO standard atmosphere** assumes an average of **0.65 °C per 100 m** in the troposphere.

If the temperature falls, for example, by **1.2 °C per 100 m**, that is more than the dry adiabatic rate. A lifted parcel always stays warmer than its surroundings. The air is **absolutely unstable**. Parcels of air keep rising by themselves, and **heap clouds** (cumulus) form, even **thunderstorms**. One measure of this is **CAPE**, the convective available potential energy.

If the gradient of the surrounding air lies between the **moist and the dry adiabatic** rates, the air is called **conditionally unstable**. Unsaturated air is then stable. But saturated air cools more slowly and becomes unstable. So whether clouds pile up depends on the **humidity**.

In **absolutely stable** air, a lifted parcel is colder and heavier than its surroundings. It sinks back to where it started. In doing so it can swing up and down around this position, at the **Brunt-Väisälä frequency**. The **stratosphere** is very stable. There **ozone** absorbs UV radiation and warms the upper layers. Because warm air lies above cold air, mixing is suppressed.

gewusst: During a temperature inversion in winter, warm air lies above cold air, and in the Swiss Central Plateau a layer of low fog often stays for weeks.
Thunderclouds can grow up to the top of the troposphere and spread out there like an anvil.

teile.einleitung: A day is not just a day: astronomers distinguish between a solar day and a sidereal day. The solar day is based on the Sun, the sidereal day on the distant stars. The sidereal day is almost four minutes shorter.
wichtigste: A mean solar day lasts 24 hours.
A sidereal day lasts about 23 hours and 56 minutes.
The solar day is longer because the Earth moves on along its orbit around the Sun.
A year has one more sidereal day than solar days.
A star rises about 4 minutes earlier each night.
A sundial shows the true local time according to the position of the Sun.

abschnitte.text: A **solar day** is the time from one midday to the next, that is, until the Sun is at its highest again. On average this is exactly **24 hours**. A **sidereal day** is the time until a distant star is back in the same place in the sky. It lasts only about **23 hours and 56 minutes**. **Sidereal time**, which observatories use, is based on this rotation.

While the Earth turns once, it also moves on a little along its **orbit around the Sun**. So every day it has to turn a little more before the Sun is back in the south. This small extra bit adds up to about **4 minutes**. Over a whole year it adds up to one full turn. That is why a year has **one more sidereal day** than solar days.

Because the sidereal day is shorter, every star rises about **4 minutes earlier** each night. In a month that adds up to about two hours. That is why you see different constellations in the evening sky in winter than in summer. After one year the sky looks the same again at the same time of day.

A **sundial** shows the **true local time** according to the position of the Sun. But the length of true solar days varies slightly, because the Earth's orbit is an ellipse and the Earth's axis is tilted. So our clocks run on an even **mean solar time**. The difference between the two is called the **equation of time**. Over the course of the year it reaches up to about a quarter of an hour.

If two places are one **degree of longitude** apart, their local time differs by **4 minutes**. Switzerland stretches from Geneva in the west to the Val Müstair in the east. So there the Sun is in the south more than a quarter of an hour earlier than in Geneva. So that the same clock time still applies everywhere, Switzerland uses **Central European Time**.

gewusst: Before there were standard time zones, almost every town had its own local time.
A full turn of 360 degrees in 24 hours means 15 degrees per hour, so 1 degree in 4 minutes.

teile.einleitung: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, AMOC for short, is a huge system of currents in the Atlantic. It carries warm water north and cold deep water south, and in this way affects Europe's climate.
wichtigste: In the far North Atlantic, for example in the Labrador Sea, water sinks into the depths.
Volume flows in the ocean are measured in sverdrups.
Since 2004, an average of about 17 sverdrups has been measured at 26.5° north.
The current makes winters in north-western Europe milder.
Fresh water from Greenland can weaken it.
The IPCC expects it very likely to weaken in the 21st century.

abschnitte.titel: A conveyor belt in the ocean
abschnitte.text: Warm, salty surface water flows north. In the far North Atlantic, for example in the **Labrador Sea**, it cools down strongly and becomes heavy. It sinks into the depths and forms **North Atlantic Deep Water**, which flows south. In the 1980s the scientist **Wallace Broecker** made the picture of the **great conveyor belt**, which spreads heat and salt between the oceans, widely known.

Volume flows in the ocean are measured in **sverdrups**. One sverdrup is one million cubic metres per second. The unit is named after the Norwegian oceanographer **Harald Sverdrup**. All the rivers of the world together carry only about one sverdrup. Since **2004**, a chain of instruments right across the Atlantic at **26.5° north** has been measuring all the time. On average it is about **17 sverdrups**, with big changes from year to year.

In the north the current gives off heat to the air. **Westerly winds** carry this warmth to Europe. That is why **winters in north-western Europe are milder** than you would expect for its position. But south of Greenland there is a region of sea that has cooled down against the global trend, the **cold blob**. It is often explained by a weaker overturning circulation, though other causes are also discussed.

When ice melts in **Greenland**, more **fresh water** gets into the North Atlantic. It lowers the **salt content** and therefore the **density** of the surface water. Lighter water does not sink so easily, and the driving force becomes weaker. As early as **1961**, **Henry Stommel** showed with a simple box model that the current can have two stable states and can tip between strong and weak.

The sixth report of the **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change IPCC** expects it **very likely to weaken** in the 21st century. With medium confidence it does not expect a sudden collapse before 2100. But such a collapse cannot be ruled out completely. That is why the current continues to be watched closely.

gewusst: The AMOC carries many times the amount of water of all the Earth's rivers put together.
The Gulf Stream is part of this great system of currents.

teile.einleitung: A supernova is the gigantic explosion of a star. For a short time it can shine as brightly as a whole galaxy with billions of stars. Supernovae produce many chemical elements, which later make up new stars, planets and even us humans.
wichtigste: A supernova is the explosion of a star at the end of its life, or of a white dwarf.
In massive stars the core collapses as soon as it is made of iron, because fusing iron no longer gives energy.
About 99 per cent of the energy of a core-collapse supernova is carried away by neutrinos.
Type Ia supernovae are used as standard candles to measure great distances.
The Crab Nebula is the remains of a supernova that was observed in 1054, among other places in China.
SN 1987A exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
The last supernova in the Milky Way seen with the naked eye was SN 1604, Kepler's Supernova.

abschnitte.text: A **supernova** is one of the most powerful explosions in the universe. A star that could perhaps hardly be seen before suddenly shines billions of times brighter. After weeks to months it fades again. The name comes from the Latin word nova, meaning new, because people used to believe that a new star had appeared. What is left is an expanding cloud of gas, a **supernova remnant**.

Very massive stars build up heavier and heavier elements in their core, up to **iron**. But fusing iron no longer gives energy. So the core can no longer hold up against its own weight and collapses in a fraction of a second. This produces a **neutron star** or a black hole, and the outer layers are blown away. About 99 per cent of the energy released is carried away by tiny, almost invisible particles, the **neutrinos**.

Experts tell supernovae apart by their **spectrum**. Type II supernovae show hydrogen lines, type I do not. Type II is caused by the core collapse of a heavy star that still has its outer layer of hydrogen. Type Ia forms differently: a **white dwarf** in a binary star system sucks material from its partner until it reaches the Chandrasekhar limit and explodes completely.

Type Ia supernovae almost always reach a similar brightness. That is why they are used as **standard candles**: if you compare how bright they really are with how bright they look to us, you can calculate their distance. In this way distances of billions of light years can be measured. With this method researchers discovered in 1998 that the universe is expanding faster and faster. This was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011.

In the year 1054 Chinese astronomers observed a new star that could even be seen in the daytime. Its remains are the **Crab Nebula** in the constellation Taurus. In 1572 Tycho Brahe described a supernova, and in 1604 Johannes Kepler observed the last supernova in the Milky Way seen so far with the naked eye. In 1987 **SN 1987A** exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a neighbouring galaxy. For the first time, neutrinos from a supernova were caught.

Supernovae fling many elements that the star has made out into space, such as oxygen, silicon, calcium and iron. Some heavy elements are only made during the explosion itself. New stars and planets form from this material. So the iron in our blood and the calcium in our bones partly come from stars that exploded long ago. That is why people say we are made of **stardust**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The gigantic explosion of a star, which shines extremely brightly for a short time.
A tiny, almost massless particle that passes through almost everything.
An object in the sky with a known brightness, which can be used to measure distances.
The glowing cloud of gas that is left after the explosion.

gewusst: At the centre of the Crab Nebula, a neutron star spins about 30 times a second.
In a galaxy like the Milky Way, a supernova explodes roughly every 50 to 100 years, but most are hidden behind dust.
The red giant star Betelgeuse in Orion will explode as a supernova at some point, but probably not for many thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: A spaceport is a place from which rockets take off into space. It has everything needed for a rocket launch: halls, launch pads and control centres.
wichtigste: Rockets take off into space from a **spaceport**.
The oldest spaceport is **Baikonur** in Kazakhstan. From there Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space in 1961.
The **Kennedy Space Center** is in Florida. The Moon rockets were launched from there.
Spaceports near the **equator** make use of the boost from the Earth's rotation.
The fuel is only filled into the rocket shortly before launch.
Switzerland does not have its own spaceport.

abschnitte.text: A spaceport is much more than a launch pad. In huge **assembly halls**, the rockets are put together from their parts. Then they are slowly taken to the **launch pad**. In the **control centre**, experts watch the launch on many screens. There are also fuel depots, workshops, roads and often an airfield of its own.

Many rockets fly with liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen. These substances are extremely cold and must be kept well cooled, or they evaporate. Other fuels are poisonous or catch fire easily. That is why the tanks are only filled in the last few hours before launch. During refuelling, everyone has to keep a large safe distance.

At the **equator**, the ground moves fastest as the Earth turns. If a rocket launches eastwards from there, it gets this boost for free and needs less fuel. That is why the European spaceport is in **Kourou** in French Guiana, close to the equator. Many spaceports are also on a coast. That way the rockets fly over the sea, and falling parts do not hit any houses.

**Baikonur** lies in the steppe of Kazakhstan and is used by Russia. The first satellite, Sputnik, and Yuri Gagarin were launched from there. The **Kennedy Space Center** in Florida was the launch site of the Apollo Moon flights and the Space Shuttles. **Tanegashima** is on an island in the south of Japan and is said to be one of the most beautiful spaceports. China and India also have their own launch sites.

Switzerland does not have a spaceport. But it is a founding member of the European Space Agency **ESA**. So Swiss satellites are launched, for example, from Kourou or from the USA. The Swiss research satellite **CHEOPS** flew into space from Kourou in 2019.

gewusst: The rocket assembly building at the Kennedy Space Center is one of the largest buildings in the world.
Liquid hydrogen is colder than minus 250 degrees Celsius.

teile.einleitung: The corona is the outermost layer of the Sun's atmosphere. It is a very thin gas, but over a million degrees hot. With the naked eye you can only see it during a total solar eclipse, as a bright halo of rays.
wichtigste: The corona is the outer atmosphere of the Sun.
It is much hotter than the Sun's surface; exactly why is not yet fully understood.
The corona is about a million times fainter than the Sun's disc.
With the coronagraph invented by Bernard Lyot, you can observe it without an eclipse.
The solar wind streams out of the corona into space.
In 2021 the Parker Solar Probe was the first space probe to fly through the corona.

abschnitte.text: The word **corona** means wreath or crown. The corona is about a million times **fainter** than the bright disc of the Sun. Normally the Sun completely outshines it. Only when the Moon completely covers the disc in a **total solar eclipse** can you see the shimmering halo. It reaches far out into space.

One part of the light is called the **K corona**. Here free **electrons** scatter the light from the Sun's surface, the **photosphere**. On top of this comes light scattered by dust further out. In the past, people saw a puzzling green line at 530.3 nanometres in the spectrum. They suspected an unknown element, “coronium”. Later it turned out that it is produced by **highly ionised iron atoms** that have lost many electrons.

The Sun's surface is about 5500 degrees hot, but the corona is over a million degrees. How the corona gets heated so strongly is an open question. It is called the **coronal heating problem**. Researchers suspect that magnetic fields and waves carry energy upwards. Because the gas is so hot, it shines in the **X-ray range**. There, the corona can be observed well even in front of the Sun's disc.

Around 1930 the Frenchman **Bernard Lyot** developed the **coronagraph**. In it, a small disc covers the Sun, creating an artificial eclipse. This makes it possible to study the corona on any clear day. It works best on high mountains with clean air. Today satellites also carry coronagraphs.

The **solar wind** constantly streams out of the corona into space. In **coronal holes** the magnetic field lines are open, and particularly fast solar wind escapes there. On X-ray images these areas look dark. In 2021 NASA's **Parker Solar Probe** was the first space probe to fly through the corona.

gewusst: The gas of the corona is so thin that it gives off only a little heat despite being over a million degrees.
The green coronal line puzzled researchers for about 70 years, until iron was recognised as the cause.

teile.einleitung: A planet is a large, round celestial body that circles a star and does not shine by itself. We live on a planet, the Earth. Eight planets circle our Sun, and thousands more have already been found around other stars.
wichtigste: A planet circles a star and does not shine by itself.
The word planet comes from Greek and means wanderer.
Our solar system has eight planets.
We live on the planet Earth.
The path of a planet around the Sun is called its orbit.
Since 2006, Pluto has been considered a dwarf planet.
Some planets can be seen without a telescope, like bright stars in the sky.

abschnitte.text: A **planet** is a celestial body that circles a star, is roughly round because of its own gravity and has cleared its neighbourhood of other bodies. This is how the International Astronomical Union defined it in 2006. Planets do not shine by themselves like stars but reflect the light of their star. The word comes from the Greek “planetes”, which means **wanderer**. Even in ancient times, people noticed that these points of light wander about among the stars.

Eight planets circle our Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The four inner ones are small **rocky planets** with a solid surface. Jupiter and Saturn are huge **gas planets**, and Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants. Jupiter is the largest planet, Mercury the smallest. A well-known German memory aid is “Mein Vater erklärt mir jeden Sonntag unseren Nachthimmel” (My father explains our night sky to me every Sunday); the first letters of the words stand for the planets in German.

The path along which a planet circles the Sun is called its **orbit**. It is a slightly oval ellipse, as Johannes Kepler found out at the beginning of the 17th century. The time for one whole lap is a year on that planet. The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year lasts. Mercury needs only about 88 days, but Neptune about 165 Earth years.

Pluto was discovered in 1930 and was considered the ninth planet for a long time. Then other bodies of similar size were found far out in the solar system. That is why Pluto was declared a **dwarf planet** in 2006. It is round, but it has not cleared its orbit of other bodies. Other dwarf planets include, for example, Ceres in the asteroid belt and Eris.

abschnitte.titel: Planets in the sky and elsewhere
abschnitte.text: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn can be seen without a telescope; they look like **bright stars**. A planet usually twinkles less than a star. Planets that circle other stars are called **exoplanets**. The first exoplanet around a Sun-like star was discovered by the Swiss Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz in 1995 at the University of Geneva. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019, and today over 5,000 exoplanets are known.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path along which one celestial body circles another.
A round celestial body that circles the Sun but has not cleared its orbit.
A planet that circles a star other than the Sun.
A planet with a solid surface of rock.

gewusst: After the Sun and the Moon, Venus is the brightest object in the night sky and is called the evening star or morning star.
All the planets of the solar system would just about fit side by side in the average distance between the Earth and the Moon.
The names of the planets almost all come from Roman gods; only the Earth's does not.

teile.einleitung: Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space. In June 1963 the Soviet cosmonaut flew around the Earth for almost three days in the spacecraft Vostok 6.
wichtigste: On **16 June 1963** Tereshkova became the first woman to fly into space.
Her spacecraft was called **Vostok 6**.
Her radio call sign was **“Chaika”**, which means seagull.
She went around the Earth **48 times** in almost three days.
Before that she worked in a **textile factory**.
Her hobby, **parachuting**, helped her to be chosen.

abschnitte.text: Valentina Tereshkova was born in the Soviet Union in 1937. She worked in a **spinning mill**, a textile factory. Alongside this she trained as a technician. From 1959 she was a keen **parachutist**. This was important, because the cosmonauts on the Vostok flights had to be able to land by parachute at the end.

On **16 June 1963** Tereshkova was launched on **Vostok 6**. It was the last spacecraft in the Vostok series. At the same time, **Vostok 5** was also in space with a cosmonaut on board. Tereshkova stayed in space until 19 June, almost three days. During this time she orbited the Earth **48 times**, each lap taking about an hour and a half.

Every cosmonaut had a **radio call sign**. Tereshkova's call sign was “**Chaika**”, which means seagull. She reported to the ground station under this name. Her sentence “I am Chaika” became famous in the Soviet Union.

abschnitte.titel: The only one for a long time
abschnitte.text: After Tereshkova, no woman flew into space for a long time. Only **19 years** later, in 1982, did the Soviet cosmonaut **Svetlana Savitskaya** follow. In 1983 **Sally Ride** became the first American woman in space. Today many women work as astronauts, including on the space station ISS.

gewusst: Tereshkova was only 26 years old at the time of her flight.
To this day she is the only woman who has flown into space alone in a spacecraft.

teile.einleitung: A shooting star is a bright streak of light that darts across the night sky for a brief moment. But it has nothing to do with a star: it is a tiny particle from space that burns up in the Earth's atmosphere.
wichtigste: In scientific language a shooting star is called a **meteor**.
The particle itself is called a **meteoroid**; it is usually smaller than a grain of sand or a pebble.
The particle races into the air so fast that it glows and burns up.
Shooting stars usually light up at a height of about 80 to 120 kilometres.
A shooting star is usually over after about a second.
You can see shooting stars all year round on any clear night.
They are best seen in a dark place without lights.

abschnitte.text: Countless small chunks of rock and metal fly around in space. Many of them come from comets or asteroids. Such a particle is called a **meteoroid**. When it hits the Earth, we see a trail of light in the sky, the **meteor**. If a larger piece reaches the ground, it is called a **meteorite**.

The particles are unbelievably fast, many kilometres per second. When they race into the Earth's atmosphere, the air in front of them is strongly **squashed** and becomes very hot. This makes the particle glow and burn up. Because it is so fast, even a grain of sand shines brightly. This happens about 100 kilometres above us, much higher than aeroplanes fly.

Every day, many small particles hit the Earth. That is why you can see shooting stars on any clear night, in winter just as in summer. But on certain nights there are many more. Then the Earth crosses a trail of dust left behind by a comet. This is called a **meteor shower**. A well-known one is the **Perseids** in August.

Shooting stars are often faint. Bright light from street lamps outshines them. That is why they are best seen in the countryside or in the mountains, where the sky is dark. The **full Moon** also makes the sky bright, and then you see fewer shooting stars. You do not need a telescope: you lie down comfortably and simply look at the sky for a while.

Many people silently make a wish when they see a shooting star. This is an old **custom**. You have to be quick, because the trail of light is usually gone after a second. According to the custom, you should keep the wish to yourself.

gewusst: The German word for shooting star, “Sternschnuppe”, comes from the old idea that a star was trimming its wick like a candle; “Schnuppe” is the burnt end of a candle wick.
Even a particle smaller than a grain of sand can shine as a bright shooting star.

teile.einleitung: A water rocket is a simple rocket that you can build yourself. It is made of a plastic bottle with water and air. When you pump air into it, the bottle shoots up into the air.
wichtigste: A water rocket is often built from a **plastic bottle**.
You pump air into it with a **bicycle pump**.
The bottle is only **partly** filled with water.
At launch the **water sprays downwards** and the bottle flies upwards.
**Fins** make sure the rocket flies straight.
At launch you must keep **a safe distance**.

abschnitte.text: A **plastic drinks bottle** is good for a water rocket. It is light and holds the air pressure well. At the bottom end you stick on **fins**, for example made of cardboard. They keep the rocket stable so that it flies straight and does not wobble. Often a soft tip is put on top.

You fill the bottle only **partly** with water. The rest must leave room for the **air**. Then you stand the bottle upside down on a launcher, with the opening pointing **downwards**. With a **bicycle pump** you push more and more air into it. The pressure in the bottle rises.

When the rocket is released, the squashed air pushes the water out downwards with great force. This makes the bottle shoot upwards. This is called **recoil**: what is pushed downwards pushes the rocket upwards. Real rockets fly on the same principle; they push out hot gases.

The more air you pump in, the greater the **pressure**. The water is then pushed out more strongly, and the rocket flies higher. The amount of water matters too. If there is too little water, there is hardly any thrust. If there is too much, there is not enough room for the compressed air.

The bottle shoots off very fast and can **hurt** someone. That is why you only launch outside in an open space and keep **a safe distance**. Nobody may lean over the rocket. Do not pump too much, so that the bottle does not burst. It is best to build a water rocket together with adults.

gewusst: You get wet: at launch the water often rains back down on the launcher.
With water rockets, pupils learn the same principle in lessons that large space rockets use to fly.

teile.einleitung: In space tourism, people fly into space who are not professional astronauts and who pay for the flight themselves. For some years now, private companies have been offering such flights. But they are very expensive and only possible for a few people.
wichtigste: The first paying **space tourist** was Dennis Tito in 2001.
According to a widely used definition, space begins at a height of 100 km, at the **Kármán line**.
On short flights, the guests experience a few minutes of **weightlessness**.
In 2021, with **Inspiration4**, a crew without professional astronauts orbited the Earth for the first time.
During Polaris Dawn in 2024, private individuals stepped out into open space for the first time.
Important companies are **Blue Origin**, **Virgin Galactic** and SpaceX.

abschnitte.text: In 2001 the American **Dennis Tito** flew to the International Space Station ISS in a Russian Soyuz capsule. He paid about 20 million dollars for it and is regarded as the first space tourist. After him, a few other wealthy private individuals flew to the ISS in the same way. They had to train for months beforehand.

There is no clear boundary between air and space, because the air simply gets thinner and thinner as you go up. The **Kármán line** at a height of 100 km is often taken as the boundary. It is named after the engineer Theodore von Kármán. In the USA, people are sometimes counted as astronauts from about 80 km. Many tourist flights go just above these boundaries.

Jeff Bezos's company **Blue Origin** flies guests on the **New Shepard** rocket. The capsule climbs over 100 km high and lands under parachutes. At **Virgin Galactic**, a carrier aircraft takes a spaceplane up high, which then fires its rocket engine. In this way Richard Branson reached a height of about 86 km in July 2021. On such flights the passengers float weightless at the top for **a few minutes**.

In September 2021, during **Inspiration4**, four civilians flew around the Earth for three days in a SpaceX capsule. With the mission they also raised money for a children's hospital. In September 2024, during **Polaris Dawn**, private individuals stepped out of the capsule into open space for the first time. Such flights show that space travel is no longer just a matter for countries.

A flight costs hundreds of thousands to many millions of francs, and there are only a few seats. That is why space tourism has so far only been possible for very few people. Supporters hope that flights will get cheaper over time and push technology forward. Critics point to the high costs and the burden that rocket launches place on the environment.

gewusst: In July 2021 Jeff Bezos himself flew into space on his New Shepard rocket.
The Kármán line is about ten times higher than passenger aeroplanes fly.

teile.einleitung: A rocket is a flying machine that moves forwards by the recoil of hot gases streaming out. Because it needs no air to fly, it is the only vehicle that can get into space. Rockets carry satellites, space probes and people into space.
wichtigste: A rocket pushes hot exhaust gases out downwards and so flies upwards.
This principle is called recoil.
Rockets also work in the vacuum of space.
In 1957, a rocket carried the first satellite, Sputnik 1, into space.
The huge Saturn V took astronauts to the Moon.
Europe's large rockets are called Ariane.
Before launch, people count backwards to zero in the countdown.

abschnitte.text: In a rocket, **fuel** burns together with a source of oxygen. This produces very hot **exhaust gases**, which shoot out downwards from a nozzle at high speed. In reaction, the rocket is pushed upwards. You can try out this **recoil** with a balloon: if you let it go without tying it up, it whizzes away. Isaac Newton already described this principle in the 17th century as the law of action and reaction.

A large rocket usually consists of several **stages** sitting on top of each other. When the fuel of a stage is used up, it is dropped so that the rocket becomes lighter. Right at the top sits the **payload**, for example a satellite or a space capsule. Most of a rocket is fuel tank. Some rockets use liquid hydrogen and oxygen, others solid fuel, as in a large firework rocket.

About 800 years ago, gunpowder rockets were already used in China. In the 20th century, pioneers such as Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, Robert Goddard and Hermann Oberth researched space travel with rockets. In 1957, a Soviet rocket put the first satellite, **Sputnik 1**, into orbit. In 1961, Yuri Gagarin became the first person to fly into space. The American **Saturn V** was over 110 metres tall and took astronauts to the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

Europe's large rockets are called **Ariane** and are launched from the Kourou spaceport in French Guiana in South America. The newest version is the Ariane 6, which flew for the first time in 2024. Switzerland is a member of the European Space Agency **ESA**, and Swiss companies build, for example, the payload fairing at the tip of the Ariane. Today there are also private companies such as SpaceX, whose rocket stages land again and can be reused.

Before launch, people count backwards to zero in the **countdown**. This way everyone involved knows exactly how much time is left until lift-off. During this time, tanks are filled and many systems are checked. If something is not right, the countdown is stopped or the launch is postponed. By the way, the idea of counting backwards comes from the German science fiction film “Frau im Mond” (Woman in the Moon) from 1929.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that pushes a rocket forwards when gases stream out backwards.
A part of a rocket with its own engine, which is dropped after use.
What a rocket is meant to carry into space, such as a satellite.
Counting backwards to the launch.

gewusst: For an orbit around the Earth, a rocket needs a speed of almost 28,000 kilometres per hour.
By far the largest part of a rocket's weight at launch is fuel.
Rockets often launch towards the east, because that way they take advantage of the momentum of the Earth's rotation.

teile.einleitung: At sunrise the Sun appears on the horizon in the morning and the day begins. This happens every day because the Earth turns. When the Sun rises depends on the season and on the place.
wichtigste: Sunrise is in the morning, when the Sun appears on the horizon.
We see the Sun rise because the Earth turns once a day on its own axis.
The horizon is the line where sky and earth seem to touch.
The time just before, when it slowly gets light, is called dawn.
In Switzerland the Sun rises earliest in summer.
On a high mountain you see the Sun rise earlier than down in the valley.

abschnitte.text: In fact it is not the Sun that moves, but the **Earth**. It **turns** once a day on its own axis. In the morning the place where we live comes round again to the side facing the **Sun**. To us it then looks as if the Sun is rising. The Sun rises roughly in the **east** and sets in the **west**.

The **horizon** is the line where the sky and the land or sea seem to **meet**. That is where we see the Sun rise and set. By the sea or on a wide plain, the horizon is flat. In Switzerland, **mountains** often hide the horizon. Then you only see the Sun once it is above the mountains.

Even **before sunrise** the sky slowly gets light. This time is called **dawn**. At sunrise the sky often glows **red and orange**. This is because the light of the low Sun has to travel a long way through the air. On the way the blue light is scattered to the side, and mainly red light reaches us.

abschnitte.titel: Early in summer, late in winter
abschnitte.text: In **summer** the days are long. So in Switzerland the Sun rises early in the morning and sets late in the evening. In June it rises before 6 o'clock. In **winter** the days are short. In December the Sun does not rise until after 8 o'clock. On a **high mountain** you can see further over the horizon, so you see the Sun a little earlier there than in the valley between the mountains.

The **cockerel** often crows very early in the morning, around sunrise. That is why it is seen as a morning bird. Many other birds also start to sing at dawn. This is called the **dawn chorus**. For many animals, sunrise is the sign that the day is beginning.

gewusst: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach the Earth, so at sunrise we see the Sun as it was 8 minutes earlier.
Astronauts on the space station see about 16 sunrises in a single day.

teile.einleitung: A Cherenkov telescope observes very high-energy gamma rays from space. This radiation does not reach the ground, but it creates short bluish flashes of light in the air. The telescopes catch exactly these flashes with large mirrors.
wichtigste: **Cherenkov radiation** is produced when charged particles move faster than light does in that material.
**Pavel Cherenkov** received the Nobel Prize for it in 1958, together with Frank and Tamm.
The bluish glow in the water of research reactors is Cherenkov light.
A flash of light lasts only a few **billionths of a second**.
In 1989 the **Whipple telescope** was the first to detect TeV gamma rays from the Crab Nebula.
The new observatory **CTAO** is being built on La Palma and in Chile.

abschnitte.text: In a vacuum, nothing is faster than light. But in air or water, light is a little **slower**. A charged particle can fly faster than light there. Then it creates a **cone of light**, rather like a supersonic aeroplane creates a bang. This glow is mainly blue. You can see it, for example, as a bluish glow in the water pool of a research reactor.

In 1934 the Soviet physicist **Pavel Cherenkov** observed the bluish glow in liquids that were exposed to radioactive radiation. **Ilya Frank** and **Igor Tamm** provided the theoretical explanation. In 1958 the three of them received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** together. The radiation is named after Cherenkov.

When a very high-energy gamma ray hits the atmosphere, it creates an **air shower** of many fast particles. These produce Cherenkov light. The flash is extremely short and lasts only a few **nanoseconds**, that is, billionths of a second. That is why the telescopes need large mirrors and very fast, sensitive **cameras**. From the shape of the flash you can tell whether it comes from gamma rays or from other particles.

In 1989 the 10-metre **Whipple telescope** in Arizona was the first to detect gamma rays in the TeV range from the **Crab Nebula**. The **H.E.S.S.** system stands on the Khomas Highland in **Namibia** and observes the southern sky with the centre of the Milky Way. More telescopes, such as MAGIC, stand on the Canary Island of **La Palma**.

The **FACT** telescope on La Palma, in which **ETH Zurich** is involved, was the first to test a camera with **silicon photomultipliers**, from 2011. These semiconductor light sensors are tougher and can even measure in moonlight. The big new observatory **CTAO** is being built at two sites: on La Palma for the northern sky and in the Atacama Desert in Chile for the southern sky. Together there are to be over 60 telescopes there.

gewusst: With these telescopes, the Earth's atmosphere itself is part of the measuring instrument.
The name FACT stands for “First G-APD Cherenkov Telescope”.

teile.einleitung: The radial velocity method is used to find planets around other stars. It measures how a star wobbles slightly to and fro because of the pull of its planet.
wichtigste: A planet and its star both circle a common centre of gravity.
The movement of the star shifts its spectral lines through the Doppler effect.
When the star moves towards us, the lines shift towards blue.
The period of the measured curve shows the orbital period of the planet.
Without the tilt of the orbit, the method gives only a minimum mass for the planet.
Massive planets on tight orbits are the easiest to find.

abschnitte.text: A planet pulls on its star with its gravity. That is why both circle a **common centre of gravity**. The star moves in a small orbit as it does so. From the Earth you can see it moving alternately a little towards us and away from us. This speed along the line of sight is called the **radial velocity**.

When a star moves towards us, its light waves are squeezed. The **spectral lines** shift towards the blue end; this is called **blueshift**. When it moves away, they shift towards red. The shift is tiny: at 30 metres per second, a line at 500 nanometres shifts by only 0.00005 nanometres. This needs very precise **spectrographs**.

The measurements give a curve. Its **period** shows the orbital period of the planet. Using Kepler's third law, the size of the orbit follows from this. If the curve is not an even sine curve, the orbit is **elliptical**. Because only the movement along the line of sight is measured, without the tilt of the orbit you get only a **minimum mass** for the planet.

In 1995, **Michel Mayor** and **Didier Queloz** from the University of Geneva used this method to find the planet **51 Pegasi b**. It was the first planet discovered around a Sun-like star. It is a gas giant on a very tight orbit. For this discovery, the two received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** in 2019.

The heavier and closer a planet is, the more strongly it pulls on the star. That is why **massive planets on tight orbits** are the easiest to find. Jupiter moves our Sun at about 12 to 13 metres per second, which can be measured with good instruments. The Earth moves the Sun at only about **9 centimetres per second**. Such a signal is extremely hard to measure.

gewusst: The Earth's signal in the Sun's movement is over a hundred times weaker than Jupiter's signal.
Jupiter is about a thousand times lighter than the Sun and can still be detected well.

teile.einleitung: The transit method is used to search for planets around other stars, called exoplanets. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star becomes a tiny bit dimmer for a short time. This tiny drop in brightness can be measured.
wichtigste: You measure the brief **drop in brightness** of a star when a planet passes in front of it.
The depth of the transit gives the **radius** of the planet.
Together with the mass, the **average density** can be calculated.
A transit can only be seen if we are looking almost exactly at the **edge of the orbit**.
Transits that come early or late reveal other planets.
According to plans in 2026, ESA's mission **PLATO** is due to launch at the beginning of 2027.

abschnitte.text: When a planet passes in front of its star, it covers a small part of the **star's disc**. The star then looks slightly dimmer for a few hours. If this happens again and again regularly, it points to a planet. The time between two transits is its **orbital period**. The dimming is often tiny: if the Earth passed in front of the Sun, the Sun would only become about 0.008 per cent dimmer for observers far away.

The depth of the transit depends on the ratio of the **cross-sectional areas** of planet and star. If you know the star's radius, this gives you the **radius of the planet**. If the mass is worked out with another method, you can calculate the **average density**. Mass divided by volume shows whether a planet is made mainly of rock or of gas.

A transit can only be seen if the orbit lies almost exactly in our **line of sight**. For most systems this is not the case. The probability is roughly the star's radius divided by the radius of the orbit. For an Earth twin around a Sun twin, it is only about **0.5 per cent**. That is why you have to watch a great many stars at the same time.

Neighbouring planets pull on each other with their **gravity**. As a result, transits come slightly early or late. From these **transit timing variations**, further planets can be discovered and even their masses worked out. In **transmission spectroscopy**, researchers study the starlight that passes through the planet's atmosphere during a transit. Gases such as water vapour swallow certain wavelengths and so give themselves away.

From space, brightness can be measured especially precisely. NASA's **Kepler** space telescope found thousands of exoplanets with the transit method. It was followed by **TESS**, which searches almost the whole sky. ESA's mission **PLATO** is to follow hundreds of thousands of bright stars with 26 cameras. Its aim is rocky planets in the habitable zone of Sun-like stars.

gewusst: Most of the exoplanets known today were discovered with the transit method.
The planets of the TRAPPIST-1 system were also found with the transit method.

teile.einleitung: The Alps are still rising today, by just over a millimetre a year. Even so, they are not getting steadily higher, because erosion carries away almost as much rock again.
wichtigste: Parts of the Swiss Alps are rising today by up to about 1.5 mm a year.
The uplift is strongest in Valais and the Grisons.
A large part comes from the melting of the Ice Age glaciers.
Behind this is the principle of isostasy.
Erosion removes about as much as the mountains rise.
Under the Central Alps the crust is about 50 kilometres thick.

abschnitte.text: The **national survey** has long been measuring very precisely how the land moves. For this it uses repeated **precision levelling** and **GNSS measurements**, that is, satellite positioning. In the Central Alps, parts are rising by **up to about 1.5 mm a year**. The uplift is strongest in **Valais** and the **Grisons**, especially around Brig and Chur. The Central Plateau and the Jura hardly rise at all.

The Earth's crust floats on the stiff, slow-moving mantle, rather like an **iceberg** in water. This principle is called **isostasy**. If a load is removed, the crust slowly rises back up. In the Ice Age, thick glaciers pressed down on the Alps. According to a study from **2016**, the **melting of these glaciers** can explain a large part of today's uplift. Since then the crust has slowly been springing back.

Under the Central Alps the Earth's crust has thickened into a **mountain root**. There it is about **50 kilometres** thick, while under the Central Plateau it is only about 30 kilometres. This light root holds up the mountains like a **float**. When rock is removed at the top, the root rises a little.

Rivers, glaciers, **rockfalls** and **weathering** constantly remove rock. About as much as the mountains rise. That is why uplift and **erosion** roughly balance each other, and the Alps are not getting steadily higher. Through uplift and erosion, rock that was once buried deep comes back to the surface. This is called **exhumation**.

You can measure when a rock cooled down on its way up. In **apatite fission track dating**, you count tiny tracks left behind in the mineral apatite by the decay of **uranium**. These tracks only survive below about **100 °C**. From this you can work out when a rock came close to the surface.

gewusst: Over 1000 years, an uplift of 1 mm a year adds up to a whole metre.
Today you can touch high-pressure rocks in the Alps that once lay many kilometres deep.

teile.einleitung: Dwarf planets are round celestial bodies that orbit the Sun but are too small to count as proper planets. The best-known dwarf planet is Pluto, which was regarded as the ninth planet until 2006.
wichtigste: Five **dwarf planets** are officially recognised: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake (as of 2025).
Astronomers set the rules for this in Prague in **2006**.
A dwarf planet has not cleared its orbit of other chunks.
**Ceres** orbits between Mars and Jupiter and was discovered in 1801.
At just under 2400 km, **Pluto** is the widest dwarf planet.
Haumea is long like an egg, because it spins very fast.

abschnitte.text: In **2006** astronomers from the International Astronomical Union met in Prague. There they decided what a planet is. A planet orbits the Sun, is roughly round and has **cleared its orbit**, which means it is clearly the largest body there. A **dwarf planet** meets the first two points but not the third. Since then Pluto has no longer counted as a planet.

The Italian **Giuseppe Piazzi** discovered Ceres on 1 January 1801. At first Ceres was even thought to be a planet. At about 940 kilometres, Ceres is the largest body in the **asteroid belt** between Mars and Jupiter. The space probe Dawn visited Ceres from 2015 and found bright patches of salt on the surface.

Pluto was discovered in 1930 and orbits far out beyond Neptune. At just under **2400 kilometres**, it is the widest known dwarf planet, but it is smaller than our Moon. Its largest moon is called Charon. In 2015 the space probe **New Horizons** flew past Pluto and showed mountains of ice and a large bright plain.

**Eris** was discovered in 2005 and is almost the same size as Pluto. Its discovery led to the question of what a planet really is. **Haumea** spins once on its axis in just under four hours and is therefore stretched out like an egg. **Makemake** also orbits far out beyond Neptune. All three are very cold and far from the Sun.

A great many icy bodies orbit beyond Neptune. Researchers suspect that some of them could also be dwarf planets. But they are so far away and so faint that their size and shape are hard to measure. That is why only five have been officially recognised so far.

gewusst: Eris is a little smaller than Pluto but has more mass.
Pluto needs about 248 years for one lap around the Sun.

teile.einleitung: In the space station, astronauts float through the rooms. Pens, drops of water and tools do not fall down either. This state is called weightlessness.
wichtigste: In the space station nothing falls down: everything floats.
The space station is constantly falling around the Earth, so the astronauts do not feel their weight.
In weightlessness a drop of water becomes a ball.
In space your back gets a few centimetres longer.
Astronauts have to exercise every day so that their muscles and bones stay strong.
Tools are fastened down so that they do not float away.

abschnitte.text: The space station circles high above the Earth. There the Earth's **gravity** is still almost as strong as on the ground. But the station is constantly **falling**, and it is moving sideways so fast that it keeps **falling around the Earth**. Everything inside it falls at exactly the same speed. That is why the astronauts **do not feel their weight** and float. This is called **weightlessness**.

If you let go of a **pen** in the space station, it does not fall down. It simply stays floating in the air. **Water** pulls itself together into round **balls** that drift through the room. Loose **tools** would float away. That is why the astronauts fasten everything with **Velcro**, straps or cords.

In weightlessness there is really **no up and no down**. You can work on the ceiling just as well as on the floor. You cannot walk. The astronauts **push themselves off** **handles** with their hands and feet and float on. To wash, they use **damp cloths** and shampoo that does not need rinsing out, because a shower would spread drops everywhere.

Without weight, the **vertebrae** in your back no longer press so hard on each other. That is why an astronaut gets a few centimetres **taller** in space. At the same time, **muscles** and **bones** need hardly any strength. Without training they would become weak. That is why astronauts **exercise every day**, for example on a treadmill with straps or on a weight machine.

You can be weightless for a short time on Earth too. In **parabolic flights**, an aeroplane flies steeply upwards and then down again in an arc. During the arc, the people on board float for about 20 seconds. This is how astronauts train and researchers carry out experiments. On a roller coaster, too, you sometimes feel this tingling for a moment.

gewusst: At the height of the space station, gravity is still about nine tenths as strong as on the ground.
After returning to Earth, the astronauts shrink back to their normal height.

teile.einleitung: An orbit is the path on which a celestial body or a satellite circles another one. The Moon circles the Earth, and the Earth circles the Sun. Gravity is always at work.
wichtigste: A satellite is **constantly falling**, but flies sideways so fast that it misses the Earth.
A low Earth orbit needs about **7.9 km/s**.
The Earth and the Moon circle their **common centre of mass**.
On average the Moon is about **384,000 km** from the Earth.
**GPS satellites** orbit at a height of about 20,200 km.
The **Hohmann transfer** is an energy-saving transfer path.

abschnitte.text: **Gravity** also acts in orbit. So a satellite is always falling towards the Earth. But it flies sideways so fast that the Earth's surface **curves away** beneath it as it falls. In this way it keeps falling around the Earth. For a circular orbit just above the Earth you need about **7.9 km per second**. This is called the first cosmic velocity.

The Moon orbits the Earth at an average distance of about **384,400 km**. That is about 30 Earth diameters. Strictly speaking, the Earth and the Moon both circle their **common centre of mass**. Because the Earth has much more mass, this point is still inside the Earth, about 4700 km from the Earth's centre.

The space station **ISS** and the Hubble telescope fly only a few hundred kilometres up. **GPS satellites** orbit at about 20,200 km and go around the Earth about twice a day. Television satellites fly even higher, at about 36,000 km. There they need exactly one day for one lap and seem to stand still above one point. This is called **geostationary**.

In a **polar orbit**, a satellite flies over the North and South Poles. The Earth keeps turning beneath it. In this way it can gradually observe the whole surface of the Earth. Many weather satellites and Earth observation satellites use such orbits.

Even a few hundred kilometres up there is still very thin **air**. It slowly slows satellites down. Without a boost they sink and finally burn up. To move from one circular orbit to a higher one, people often use the **Hohmann transfer**. In 1925 Walter Hohmann described this half-ellipse that connects two circular orbits.

gewusst: Astronauts in the ISS float because they are constantly falling around the Earth together with the station.
Most orbits are not perfect circles but ellipses, as Johannes Kepler found out.

teile.einleitung: Large rockets consist of several parts built on top of each other. These parts are called rocket stages, and they are dropped one after the other during the flight.
wichtigste: A rocket made of several stages on top of each other is called a multistage rocket.
Each stage has its own tanks and engines.
When a stage is empty, it is dropped, and the rocket becomes lighter.
At launch, the lowest stage fires first.
Extra rockets on the sides are called boosters.
Today some first stages land upright again and are reused.

abschnitte.titel: Stages on top of each other
abschnitte.text: In a **multistage rocket**, several rocket parts are built on top of each other. Each **stage** has its own tanks and its own engines. The **lowest stage** is the largest and most powerful. It fires first at launch and lifts the whole rocket off the ground. Right at the top sits the **payload**, for example a satellite or a capsule with astronauts.

When a stage is empty, it is **dropped**. The rocket then has less weight to carry and can become faster. After separation, the next stage fires its own engine, and the rocket flies on without a break. The **top stage** flies furthest and takes the payload all the way to its destination. Without stages, today's rockets could hardly reach orbit.

Many rockets have extra rockets on their sides, the **boosters**. They give extra thrust at launch and are dropped after they have burned out. Many rockets fly over the **sea** after launch. There, empty stages can fall into the water without any danger to people.

A rocket stage is very expensive. That is why today some companies let the first stage **land upright again**, for example the company SpaceX with the **Falcon 9** rocket. On the way back, the stage fires its engines again and slows down. If it lands safely, it can be **reused** for another flight.

gewusst: The Moon rocket Saturn V had three stages and was over 100 metres tall.
Some stages land on floating platforms in the middle of the sea.

teile.einleitung: The orbital period is the time a celestial body needs for one full lap around another. The Earth needs one year to go once around the Sun. The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its lap takes.
wichtigste: At about 88 days, **Mercury** has the shortest orbital period.
**Venus** needs about 225 days, **Mars** about 687 days.
**Jupiter** needs about 12 years, **Saturn** about 29.5 years.
**Uranus** needs about 84 years, **Neptune** about 165 years.
Measured against the stars, the Moon needs about **27.3 days** for one orbit.
The orbital period measured against the fixed stars is called the **sidereal period**.

abschnitte.text: To measure an orbital period, you need a fixed point of reference. Often the **fixed stars** are used. The time until a celestial body is back in front of the same stars is called the **sidereal period**. The word comes from the Latin “sidus”, star. For the Earth this is one year, just over 365 days.

Measured against the stars, the Moon needs about **27.3 days** for one orbit of the Earth. This is the **sidereal month**. But from full moon to full moon it takes a little longer, about 29.5 days. The reason: during this time the Earth has moved a bit further around the Sun. So the Moon has to travel a little more before it is in the same position relative to the Sun again.

**Mercury** is the planet closest to the Sun and needs only about **88 days** for one orbit. So a Mercury year is shorter than a quarter of a year on Earth. **Venus** needs about 225 days. **Mars** is further out than the Earth and needs about **687 days**, almost two Earth years.

**Jupiter** needs about 11.9 Earth years for one lap. So each year it moves on by roughly one constellation of the zodiac. **Saturn** needs about 29.5 years, **Uranus** about 84 years, roughly a human lifetime. **Neptune** is so far out that it needs about **165 years**. Since its discovery in 1846 it has only gone around the Sun about once.

abschnitte.titel: Further away, longer on the way
abschnitte.text: The further a planet is from the Sun, the **longer** its path. It also moves **more slowly**, because the Sun's pull is weaker. Johannes Kepler described this relationship in his **third law**. With it you can calculate a planet's distance from the Sun from its orbital period.

gewusst: A person living on Mercury would have a birthday after only about 88 days.
Since Neptune was discovered, only about one single Neptune year has passed.

teile.einleitung: The solar wind sail was an experiment by the University of Bern that was set up on the Moon. It caught particles of the solar wind so that they could be studied on Earth. On Apollo 11 it was even set up before the American flag.
wichtigste: The solar wind sail was led by the Bern physicist Johannes Geiss.
It was made of a thin sheet of aluminium foil.
In 1969 Buzz Aldrin set it up even before the US flag.
On Apollo 11 it was the only experiment that was not American.
It was set up on the Moon on five Apollo missions.
In Bern, researchers measured helium, neon and argon from the solar wind in it.

abschnitte.text: The physicist **Johannes Geiss** from the **University of Bern** wanted to know exactly what the solar wind is made of. On Earth this stream of particles does not arrive, because of the atmosphere and the magnetic field. But on the Moon it hits the ground without being slowed down. So Geiss suggested catching the particles there with a sail. NASA included the idea in the Apollo missions.

On 21 July 1969 **Buzz Aldrin** set up the sail on the Moon, even **before the US flag**. It was the **only experiment on Apollo 11 that was not American**. The sail looked like a small flagpole with a shiny sheet of foil. On Apollo 11 it stayed up for about **77 minutes**. Then the foil was rolled up and taken back.

The sail was made of a very thin sheet of **aluminium foil**. The fast particles of the solar wind drilled a little way into the foil and got stuck in it. After the measurement the foil was **rolled up and brought back to Earth**. In Bern, the researchers got the trapped atoms out again in the laboratory and identified them.

The Bern researchers measured the **noble gases helium, neon and argon** from the solar wind. They also worked out how much of the different kinds of these atoms, the **isotopes**, there are. This reveals a lot about what the Sun is made of. These values still help us today to understand how the solar system formed.

The solar wind sail flew on **five** Apollo missions: on Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15 and 16. On the later flights it stayed up longer, so more particles were collected. For Swiss space research the experiment was a great success. Since then the University of Bern has taken part in many space missions.

gewusst: The sail was roughly the size of a narrow bath towel, about 1.4 metres long and 30 centimetres wide.
The Bern experiment stood on the Moon before the astronauts put up their own flag.

teile.einleitung: Apparent magnitude tells you how bright a star or planet looks from the Earth. It is measured in magnitudes. The scale is old and works backwards: smaller numbers mean brighter stars.
wichtigste: Apparent brightness is given in magnitudes, abbreviated mag.
The smaller the number, the brighter the star looks; very bright objects have negative values.
Under a dark sky you can see stars down to about 6 mag with the naked eye.
5 magnitudes correspond to exactly a factor of 100, one magnitude to about a factor of 2.5.
In ancient times Hipparchus already divided the stars into six classes of brightness.
Absolute magnitude tells you how bright a star would be from a distance of 10 parsecs.

abschnitte.text: The Greek astronomer **Hipparchus** divided the stars into six classes in **ancient times**. He counted the brightest stars as **first magnitude** and the faintest visible ones as **sixth magnitude**. Today's scale is based on this. Apparent brightness is given in **magnitudes**, abbreviated **mag**. In German it is also called “Grössenklasse”, which means size class.

The **smaller** the magnitude number, the **brighter** the star looks. Very bright objects even have **negative values**. Today the scale is precisely defined: **5 magnitudes** correspond to exactly a **factor of 100**. So a star of 1 mag is 100 times brighter than one of 6 mag. A single magnitude corresponds to the fifth root of 100, about a **factor of 2.5**.

At about **minus 26.7 mag**, the **Sun** is the brightest object in the sky. The **full Moon** reaches about **minus 12.7 mag**. Next comes **Venus**: in the evening or morning sky it is the brightest object after the Sun and the Moon. It is close, and its clouds reflect sunlight strongly. That is why it is also called the **evening star** or **morning star**. The brightest star in the night sky is **Sirius**, at about minus 1.5 mag.

Under a very **dark sky** you can see stars down to about **sixth magnitude** with the naked eye. For fainter stars you need **binoculars** or a telescope. In towns and cities you see far fewer stars, because artificial light brightens the sky. This is called **light pollution**. In the Swiss mountains the sky is often much darker than in the Central Plateau.

Apparent brightness does not depend only on how strongly a star shines. It also depends on its **distance**. A faint star nearby can look brighter than a powerful one far away.
