To compare stars fairly, there is **absolute magnitude**. It tells you how bright a star would look from a distance of **10 parsecs**, which is about 32.6 light years.

gewusst: A first-magnitude star is about 2.5 times brighter than a second-magnitude one, but 100 times brighter than a sixth-magnitude one.
Large space telescopes can see objects that are many billions of times fainter than the faintest stars the naked eye can make out.

teile.einleitung: Tycho Brahe was a Danish astronomer who lived in the 16th century. Without a telescope, he measured the sky more precisely than anyone before him. His measurements later helped Johannes Kepler to find the laws of planetary motion.
wichtigste: Tycho Brahe was born in **1546** in Scania, which belonged to **Denmark** at the time.
On the island of **Ven** he built the observatory **Uraniborg**.
In 1572 he observed a bright new star in the constellation **Cassiopeia**.
He measured with large **angle-measuring instruments**, because the telescope did not exist yet.
In a duel he lost part of his **nose**.
He died in **Prague** in **1601**.

abschnitte.text: Tycho Brahe was born in 1546 in **Scania**, which belonged to Denmark at the time but is part of Sweden today. He came from a **noble** family. As a young man he was already fascinated by the sky. As a student, in 1566, he lost a piece of his nose in a **sword duel**. After that he wore a replacement nose made of metal.

In 1572 Tycho saw a very bright star suddenly appear in the constellation **Cassiopeia**. Today we know it was a **supernova**, the explosion of a star. At that time people believed that the sky of the fixed stars never changed. With his measurements, Tycho showed that things can change there too. In 1577 he studied a large **comet** and proved that it was further away than the Moon.

The Danish king gave Tycho the island of **Ven**. There he built the observatory **Uraniborg**, named after Urania, the muse of astronomy. The telescope did not yet exist in his lifetime. Tycho measured with huge **quadrants** and other large angle-measuring instruments. With them he worked out the positions of stars and planets more precisely than anyone before him.

In Tycho's time people argued about whether the Earth or the Sun was at the centre. Tycho combined both ideas in his own **model of the universe**. The Earth stays still at the centre, and the **Sun goes around the Earth**. But the other planets go around the Sun. Today we know that all the planets, including the Earth, go around the Sun.

Later Tycho moved to the court of **Emperor Rudolf II** in Prague. There the young **Johannes Kepler** worked with him. Tycho died in Prague in 1601. Afterwards Kepler used Tycho's precise measurements, especially those of Mars. In this way he found out that the planets travel around the Sun on **ellipses**.

gewusst: The supernova of 1572 is still called “Tycho's Supernova” after him.
A large crater on the Moon bears the name Tycho.

teile.einleitung: Rudolf Wolf was an important Swiss astronomer of the 19th century. He studied sunspots and founded the Federal Observatory in Zurich. His sunspot relative number is still being continued today.
wichtigste: Rudolf Wolf was born in 1816 in Fällanden in the canton of Zurich and died in 1893.
He worked first in Bern and later in Zurich.
In 1849 he developed the Wolf number, a measure of sunspots.
He worked out the length of the sunspot cycle as about 11 years.
In 1852 he recognised the link between sunspots and changes in the Earth's magnetic field.
He founded the Federal Observatory in Zurich and also ran the ETH library.

abschnitte.text: **Rudolf Wolf** was born in **1816** in **Fällanden** near Zurich. He studied maths and astronomy. At first he worked as a teacher in **Bern** and ran the small observatory there. Later he became professor of astronomy in **Zurich**, at the university and at the Polytechnic, today's **ETH Zurich**. He died in Zurich in **1893**.

In **1849** Wolf developed a measure for the number of sunspots, the **Wolf number** (relative sunspot number). You count the **groups of spots** and the **individual spots**. The relative number is 10 times the number of groups plus the number of spots. With 3 groups that have 12 spots altogether, this gives 30 plus 12, so **42**. This number is still kept up worldwide today.

Wolf also analysed **old observations** from earlier centuries. In this way he was able to show that the number of sunspots rises and falls regularly. He worked out the length of this **cycle** as about **11 years**. In **1852**, at the same time as other researchers, he recognised that the **Earth's magnetic field** changes in the same rhythm as the sunspots.

Wolf founded the **Federal Observatory** in Zurich. The building was designed by the famous architect **Gottfried Semper**. Wolf ran the observatory as its first director from **1864** until his death in 1893. Alongside this he was also head of the **ETH library**. He collected many books and instruments on the history of astronomy.

Wolf was also a Swiss pioneer in **meteorology**, the science of weather. He chaired the **Swiss Meteorological Commission**. It set up a network of weather stations throughout Switzerland. Later Wolf was the first director of the **Central Meteorological Institute**, from which today's Federal Office of Meteorology, MeteoSwiss, developed.

gewusst: The sunspot relative number is still also called the “Wolf number” after him today.
Wolf also wrote books about the history of astronomy and about well-known Swiss scientists.

teile.einleitung: Phobos and Deimos are the two small moons of Mars. They are irregularly shaped, almost like potatoes. Phobos is so close to Mars that it goes around it faster than the planet turns.
wichtigste: Asaph Hall discovered the two moons of Mars in August 1877.
The names mean “fear” and “terror”.
Both moons are irregularly shaped like potatoes.
At just over 22 kilometres, Phobos is almost twice as big as Deimos.
Phobos goes around Mars in less than 8 hours and rises in the west.
The largest crater on Phobos is called Stickney.

abschnitte.text: The American astronomer **Asaph Hall** found the two moons in **August 1877** with a large refracting telescope in **Washington**. He discovered **Deimos** first, and **Phobos** a few days later. The moons are very small and close to bright Mars. That is why they were so hard to find.

In Greek legend, **Phobos** and **Deimos** are sons of the god of war **Ares**. The Romans called this god **Mars**. The names mean **fear** and **terror**. The word Phobos is also found in the word **phobia**, which describes a strong fear.

The two moons of Mars are too small for their own **gravity** to shape them into spheres. That is why they look like lumpy **potatoes**. **Phobos** measures just over **22 kilometres** on average, and **Deimos** only about **12 kilometres**. On Phobos lies the crater **Stickney**, about **9 kilometres** across. Compared with the size of the moon, it is huge. It is named after the maiden name of Asaph Hall's wife.

**Phobos** goes around Mars in about **7 hours and 39 minutes**. That makes it faster than Mars turns once on its axis. So, seen from the ground on Mars, it moves backwards across the sky: it rises in the **west** and sets in the **east**. Deimos is further away and takes a little more than one Martian day for one orbit.

Phobos comes a little **closer** to Mars every year. The planet's tidal forces are slowly slowing it down. In a few tens of millions of years, it will probably **break apart** and form a **ring** around Mars, or **crash** onto Mars. Where the two moons originally came from has not yet been settled for certain.

gewusst: Phobos is so small that a person would weigh hardly anything on it.
Seen from Mars, Deimos looks only like a bright star.

teile.einleitung: An observatory is a building where people watch the sky with telescopes. There researchers and visitors look at stars, planets and the Moon.
wichtigste: In German, an observatory is also called a “Sternwarte”, meaning star watch; the other word is **observatory**.
The most important instrument is a large **telescope** under a dome.
The dome can be turned and opened.
Public observatories are usually open on clear evenings.
Large observatories are often built far away from towns, because it is darker there.
In Zurich the **Urania Observatory** stands right in the middle of the city.

abschnitte.text: In German an observatory is called a “Sternwarte”, and also an **observatory**. The word comes from the Latin word for observing. Inside there is a large **telescope**. With it you can see things that are too faint or too small for the naked eye. You should not confuse an observatory with a **planetarium**: there an artificial starry sky is projected onto a dome.

Many observatories have a round roof, the **dome**. It protects the telescope from rain, wind and dust. In the dome there is a slit that can be opened. Because the dome can be turned, the telescope can look at the sky in any direction. This means you can follow a star as it moves across the sky.

You can only see stars when it is dark. That is why **public observatories** usually open in the evening when the sky is clear. When it is cloudy, the observing is often cancelled. In Switzerland there are many such observatories run by clubs. There you can look through the telescope yourself, for example at the rings of Saturn or the craters of the Moon.

The **Urania Observatory** in Zurich opened in 1907. It stands on a tower in the middle of the city. High in the Alps, on the **Jungfraujoch**, stands the research station with the **Sphinx** observatory, at over 3500 metres. There experts do research on the weather, the air and the sky. At high altitude the air is thinner and clearer.

In towns and cities, lamps make the night sky bright. This is called **light pollution**. That is why large research observatories are built far away from towns, often on high mountains. There it is darker, and there is less restless air above the telescope. Some of the largest observatories in the world are in the desert of Chile.

gewusst: The Urania Observatory in Zurich is over a hundred years old and yet stands in the middle of a big city.
The Sphinx on the Jungfraujoch is one of the highest research stations in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Saturn's ring system is the largest and brightest in the solar system. It is made up of several main rings named with letters, and it is kept in shape by small moons.
wichtigste: The main rings have letters such as A, B, C, D, E, F and G, given in the order in which they were discovered.
The B ring is the brightest and most massive ring.
The main rings are over 100,000 kilometres wide but usually only tens of metres thick.
In 1610 Galileo thought the rings were two companion bodies; Huygens recognised the ring and described it in 1659.
Shepherd moons such as Prometheus and Pandora keep rings like the F ring in shape.
All four gas planets have rings, but Saturn's are the most striking.

abschnitte.text: Saturn's rings are named with **letters** from A to G. The letters were given in the **order of discovery**, not according to their position. That is why from the inside out they go D, C, B, A, F, G and E. The **B ring** is the brightest and contains the most material. It lies between the faint **C ring** and the **A ring**. Between the B ring and the A ring there is a dark gap, the **Cassini Division**.

Together the main rings are **over 100,000 km** wide. Their thickness is usually only about **10 to 100 metres**. Compared with their width, this makes them thinner than a sheet of paper. The ring particles are mostly made of **water ice** and range from grains of dust to chunks the size of a house. They all orbit the planet in almost the same plane.

In **1610** **Galileo Galilei** pointed his telescope at Saturn. It was too weak to show the rings clearly. So Galileo believed that Saturn had **two large companions**, one on the left and one on the right. Only the Dutchman **Christiaan Huygens**, with a better telescope, recognised a flat ring. He described it in a book in **1659**.

Some small moons orbit at the edge of the rings or right in the middle of them. They are called **shepherd moons** because they keep the ring particles together as a shepherd keeps his sheep together. They steer the particles with their **gravity**. In this way the moons **Prometheus** and **Pandora** accompany the narrow **F ring** and keep its edges sharp.

The space probe **Cassini** explored Saturn from 2004 to 2017. In its last months, during the **“Grand Finale”**, it flew 22 times through the narrow gap between the innermost rings and the planet. It collected measurements that nobody had been able to make before. On **15 September 2017** Cassini burned up in Saturn's atmosphere. **Jupiter**, **Uranus** and **Neptune** also have rings, but they are much darker and narrower.

gewusst: The outermost, very faint E ring is fed by ice particles that spray into space from the small moon Enceladus.
The Cassini Division is so wide that the Moon would fit inside it.

teile.einleitung: Rocket fuel provides the energy that a rocket uses to fly into space. Because there is no air there, a rocket takes everything needed for burning with it.
wichtigste: A rocket has to take oxygen with it, because there is no air in space.
Many large rockets burn hydrogen and oxygen.
This produces water vapour.
Liquid hydrogen has to be cooled to about minus 253 °C.
Hard fuel is called solid propellant.
About nine tenths of a rocket's launch weight is fuel.

abschnitte.text: For something to burn, **oxygen** is needed. An aircraft engine takes it from the air. But in space there is no air. That is why a rocket has its own **oxygen tank**. The fuel and the oxygen together are often called a **propellant pair**.

Many large rockets burn **liquid hydrogen** and **liquid oxygen**. This gives a very powerful combustion, for example in the European **Ariane**. Hydrogen and oxygen combine to form water, which comes out of the nozzle as **water vapour** because of the heat. Hydrogen only becomes liquid at about **minus 253 degrees**. That is why the tanks have to be very well insulated.

The first stage of the Moon rocket **Saturn V** burned **kerosene** together with liquid oxygen. Kerosene is also the fuel of jet aircraft. It is easier to store than hydrogen, because it does not have to be cooled so much. Many rockets still use kerosene in their first stage today.

There is also **solid propellant**. It is a hard mass in the rocket tube. Once it has been ignited, it burns to the end and cannot be switched off. Many **boosters** of large rockets use solid propellant. **Firework rockets** on 1 August, the Swiss National Day, work in the same way: they are powered by **gunpowder**, which burns quickly.

abschnitte.titel: Lots of energy, lots of care
abschnitte.text: A rocket is above all a huge tank. About **nine tenths** of its launch weight is fuel. Rocket fuel contains a great deal of energy. A small mistake can lead to a fire or an **explosion**. That is why strict attention is paid to safety when fuelling.

gewusst: Liquid oxygen is pale blue and has to be cooled to about minus 183 °C.
The white clouds at the launch of a hydrogen rocket consist largely of water vapour.

teile.einleitung: The Perseids are a stream of shooting stars that you can see every year in summer. Around 12 August, a particularly large number of streaks of light flash across the night sky. All you need is your own eyes and a dark place.
wichtigste: The Perseids are a meteor shower with the most shooting stars around 12 August.
They seem to come from the constellation Perseus, hence the name.
The dust comes from the comet Swift-Tuttle.
An old name is the “Tears of St Lawrence”.
You usually see the most in the second half of the night.
In a very dark place, up to about 100 an hour are possible.

abschnitte.text: A **comet** called **Swift-Tuttle** has lost a lot of **dust** along its orbit around the Sun. This trail of dust stays behind in space. Every year in August, the Earth flies through it. The dust grains are usually only the size of grains of sand. They race into the **atmosphere** at high speed and burn up high above. We see this as **shooting stars**.

All the shooting stars of the Perseids seem to come from the same direction in the sky. This point lies in the **constellation Perseus**. That is why they are called the **Perseids**. An old name is the **Tears of St Lawrence**: the feast day of St Lawrence is around 10 August. The shooting stars fall at exactly this time.

The Perseids are active from about mid July to the end of August. There are most shooting stars around **12 August**. It is best to watch in the **second half of the night**. After midnight the constellation Perseus is higher in the sky, and you usually see more. On the best night, in a very dark place, you can count up to about **100 shooting stars an hour**. In towns there are far fewer.

You need **no telescope** for the Perseids. Shooting stars dart quickly across the whole sky, so it is best to watch with the **naked eye**. A place far from street lamps is ideal, for example in the mountains or in the countryside. Lie down on a blanket or a deckchair and wait about 20 minutes until your eyes have got used to the dark. A bright moon can outshine the fainter shooting stars.

gewusst: The comet Swift-Tuttle takes about 130 years to go once around the Sun.
The dust particles of the Perseids hit the atmosphere at about 59 kilometres per second.

teile.einleitung: Albedo tells you how much light a surface reflects. It is important for the Earth's climate, because bright surfaces reflect sunlight and dark ones absorb it.
wichtigste: Albedo is the share of light reflected, from 0 to 1.
The Earth has an average albedo of about 0.3.
When the Sun is high, open sea has an albedo of only about 0.06.
Clouds contribute most to the reflection.
Sahara dust lowers the albedo of snow and speeds up melting.
Albedo is measured with an albedometer.

abschnitte.text: The word **albedo** comes from the Latin “albus”, white. An albedo of 0 means that all the light is absorbed. An albedo of 1 means that all of it is reflected. Fresh **snow** is very bright and has a high albedo. An open **sea surface**, on the other hand, is very dark: when the Sun is high, its albedo is only about **0.06**.

The Earth reflects about **30 per cent** of sunlight back into space, so its albedo is about **0.3**. **Clouds** contribute most to this. They cover about two thirds of the Earth and are bright from above. A worked example: on average **340 W/m²** reach the Earth. 70 per cent is absorbed, so 340 times 0.7, which gives **238 W/m²**.

When **Sahara dust** lies on the snow, the snow becomes darker. It absorbs more solar radiation and melts earlier in the year. In the Swiss Alps, parts of glaciers are covered with white **fleece** sheets in summer, for example at the Rhône Glacier. The sheets reflect sunlight and insulate the ice. This means much less melts on small areas, but they do not stop the **shrinking of the glaciers**.

In snowy northern regions, dark **conifers** stick up out of the snow and swallow a lot of light. If the forest is cut down, a bright snowfield remains. Through albedo this can have a cooling effect. But at the same time **CO2** is released, which causes warming. Experts have to weigh both effects against each other.

An **albedometer** consists of two radiation sensors. One points upwards and measures the incoming light. The other points downwards and measures the reflected light. The **ratio** of the two values gives the albedo. For the whole Earth, albedo is measured with satellites today.

gewusst: When sea ice melts, dark water is revealed, which absorbs more heat and speeds up the melting even more.
The Moon has an albedo of only about 0.12; it is actually as dark as asphalt.

teile.einleitung: Triton is Neptune's largest moon and one of the strangest moons in the solar system. It orbits its planet backwards and has geysers that shoot nitrogen high up.
wichtigste: Triton has a diameter of about **2700 kilometres**.
It orbits Neptune in a **retrograde** way, that is, against the planet's direction of rotation.
It was probably **captured** by Neptune.
In 1989 **Voyager 2** was the only probe to fly past Triton.
At about **minus 235 degrees**, it is one of the coldest places ever measured in the solar system.
It was discovered in 1846, only **17 days** after Neptune.

abschnitte.text: Neptune was discovered on 23 September 1846. On 10 October 1846, only **17 days** later, the Englishman **William Lassell** found the moon Triton. Triton is by far the largest moon of Neptune. It contains well over 99 per cent of the mass of all Neptune's moons together.

Triton orbits Neptune in a **retrograde** way, that is, against the planet's direction of rotation. It is the only large moon in the solar system that does this. A moon that forms together with its planet normally orbits in the same direction. That is why researchers suspect that Triton was once a separate body from the **Kuiper Belt**. Neptune probably **captured** it.

In August 1989 **Voyager 2** flew past Neptune and Triton. To this day it is the only probe that has been there. It took the first close-up pictures and discovered dark **geysers**: plumes of nitrogen gas and dust shoot up to about 8 kilometres high. Such features are also called **cryovolcanoes**, that is, ice volcanoes.

Voyager 2 measured about 38 kelvin on Triton, which is about **235 degrees Celsius below zero**. A large area is covered with hollows and ridges. It looks like the skin of a **cantaloupe melon** and is therefore called cantaloupe terrain. The surface is covered with frozen nitrogen.

Because of its retrograde orbit, Triton is very slowly losing height. In a few billion years it will probably come very close to Neptune. Then the planet's **tidal forces** could tear it apart. The pieces might then form a **ring** around Neptune.

gewusst: Triton is one of the few bodies in the solar system on which active eruptions have been observed.
Many experts think Triton is a close relative of the dwarf planet Pluto.

teile.einleitung: Auroras are glowing bands and arcs in the night sky. You see them mainly in the far north and south, but sometimes even in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Auroras form when particles from the Sun hit the Earth's atmosphere.
In the north the aurora is also called the northern lights, in the south the southern lights.
You can only see auroras at night.
In Norway and other countries in the far north, they can often be seen in winter.
They often move like curtains blowing in the wind.
In May 2024, after a strong solar storm, auroras could even be seen in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Sun constantly flings tiny, electrically charged particles into space: the **solar wind**. The Earth's **magnetic field** deflects these particles and guides many of them to the poles. There they hit the air high up. The particles of air are excited and give off light. This is how the **aurora** forms.

The colours depend on which gases are glowing. **Oxygen** usually glows green, and red at great heights. **Nitrogen** gives bluish and violet tones. The lights often form bands and arcs that move like **curtains in the wind**. Auroras glow much higher up than aeroplanes fly.

An aurora in the far north is also called the **northern lights**, and in the south the **southern lights**. Good places for watching them are, for example, **Norway**, Finland, Iceland or Canada. You see them best in **winter**, because the nights there are long and dark. In summer it is almost light even at night in the far north, so you can hardly see them.

Auroras are not as bright as the Sun, which is why you only see them at **night**. In Switzerland they are very rare. Only during particularly strong **solar storms** does the glow reach so far south. In **May 2024** there was such a storm, and many people saw reddish auroras over Switzerland.

gewusst: Mobile phone cameras often show auroras more colourfully than you see them with the naked eye.
Other planets such as Jupiter and Saturn also have auroras.

teile.einleitung: A leap year has one day more than an ordinary year, namely 366 days. The extra day is 29 February. This keeps the calendar in step with the seasons.
wichtigste: A solar year lasts about 365 days and almost 6 hours, more precisely about 365.2422 days.
In a leap year, 29 February is added.
Leap years can be divided by 4; century years only if they can also be divided by 400.
In 45 BC Julius Caesar introduced a leap day every four years.
In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar.
In the Swiss Confederation, most Catholic cantons changed over in 1584, most Protestant ones in 1701.

abschnitte.text: The Earth does not take exactly 365 days for one lap around the Sun. A **solar year** lasts about **365.2422 days**, roughly 365 days and almost 6 hours. Without a correction, the calendar would shift by these hours against the **seasons** every year. After a few centuries Christmas would then fall in autumn. That is why a **leap day** is added every few years.

In a leap year **February has 29 days instead of 28**, and the year then has **366 days**. A year is a leap year if it can be divided by **4**. **Century years** are only leap years if they can also be divided by **400**. That is why **1900 was not** a leap year, **but 2000 was**. From 2001 up to and including 2100 there are **24** leap years, because 2100 is not one. The next leap year after 2026 is **2028**.

In **45 BC** **Julius Caesar** introduced the **Julian calendar**. He simply added a leap day every four years. This made the calendar year 365.25 days long on average. That is slightly **too long**, by about 11 minutes a year. Over the centuries this error added up to about ten days.

**Pope Gregory XIII** had the calendar reformed in **1582**. This introduced the rule for **century years**. To bring the calendar back in line with the seasons, **ten days** were left out. Thursday **4 October 1582** was followed directly by Friday **15 October**. This calendar is called **Gregorian**, and we still use it today.

In the **Swiss Confederation**, not all cantons changed over at the same time. Most **Catholic cantons** adopted the new calendar in **1584**. Most of the **Protestant cantons** did not follow until **1701**. In the **Grisons**, the changeover dragged on until **1812**. So for a long time, neighbouring places used different dates.

gewusst: If you were born on 29 February, you only have a birthday on your real birthday every four years.
The Gregorian calendar only drifts one day away from the solar year after about 3000 years.

teile.einleitung: Rosetta was a space probe of the European Space Agency ESA. It flew for ten years to reach a comet and then accompanied it for two years. Its small lander Philae was the first device to land on a comet.
wichtigste: Rosetta was launched in March 2004 and reached the comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014.
The comet is often called “Chury” for short and looks like a rubber duck.
In November 2014 the lander Philae became the first device to touch down on a comet.
The University of Bern led the instrument ROSINA, which studied the comet's gases.
In September 2016 Rosetta was allowed to sink slowly onto the comet, ending the mission.
The name comes from the Rosetta Stone, which helped to decipher Egyptian writing.

abschnitte.text: Rosetta was launched on a European rocket in **March 2004**. The way to the comet was very long, because the probe had to match its path and its speed. To do this it flew past the Earth several times and past Mars once, gaining speed each time. On the way it visited two asteroids. After **ten years** it reached its target in **2014**.

The target was the comet **Churyumov-Gerasimenko**. Because the name is so long, people often just say **Chury**. The comet is only a few kilometres in size. It is made of **two parts** joined together, which is why it looks like a **rubber duck**. Comets are chunks of ice, dust and rock from the early days of the solar system.

Rosetta carried a small lander called **Philae**. In **November 2014** it separated from the probe and touched down on the comet. This was the **first landing on a comet**. Because the anchoring devices did not work as planned, Philae **bounced** twice before it came to rest. Even so, it sent important measurements back to Earth.

**Switzerland** is a member of ESA and took part in Rosetta. Researchers at the **University of Bern** led the instrument **ROSINA**. It studied the **gases** that streamed into space around the comet. This revealed what substances the comet is made of. The University of Bern has long experience with instruments like this in space.

In **September 2016** the researchers let Rosetta **sink** slowly onto the comet. This ended the mission. The probe is named after the **Rosetta Stone**. This ancient stone carries the same text in several scripts and helped people to decipher **Egyptian hieroglyphs**. The probe was meant to help unlock the secrets of comets in the same way.

gewusst: On its journey Rosetta slept for about two and a half years to save energy, and woke up again in 2014.
The name Philae also comes from Egypt: on a Nile island of that name, an obelisk with inscriptions was found that helped with deciphering.

teile.einleitung: The asthenosphere is a soft layer in the upper mantle of the Earth. The rigid plates of the lithosphere glide on it, and over long periods of time it can flow slowly.
wichtigste: The name comes from the Greek “asthenés”, weak.
The asthenosphere lies about 100 to 300 km deep.
The rock is mostly solid, but close to its melting point.
In measurements it shows up as a zone of slower earthquake waves.
Scandinavia is rising because the crust is springing back after the Ice Age.
The term was introduced by Joseph Barrell in 1914.

abschnitte.text: The Greek **“asthenés”** means powerless or weak. The **asthenosphere** is mechanically softer than the rigid **lithosphere** above it, which includes the Earth's crust and the uppermost mantle. It lies about **100 to 300 km** deep. Under oceans it begins at about 80 km, under continents deeper. Its lower boundary is not sharp.

The rock of the asthenosphere is mostly **solid**. But its temperature is just below its **melting point**, and in places there is a little melted rock. So over very long periods it can slowly **flow**. Its **viscosity**, or stickiness, is about 10²⁰ Pa·s. Honey is about 10 Pa·s, so the asthenosphere is unimaginably stickier.

Earthquake waves reveal what the inside of the Earth is like. In the asthenosphere they become slower, especially the **S waves**. This is called the **low-velocity zone**, the zone of reduced wave speed. It points to softer, partly melted rock.

In the Ice Age, a thick sheet of ice pressed the lithosphere of Scandinavia down into the yielding asthenosphere. After the ice melted, mantle rock slowly flows back and the land rises. This is called **isostasy**. Around the **Gulf of Bothnia**, the uplift today is up to almost **1 cm a year**. This uplift is also used to calculate the viscosity of the asthenosphere.

The term was introduced in **1914** by the American geologist **Joseph Barrell**. From **gravity measurements** he concluded that there is a soft layer beneath a rigid shell. In this way he was able to explain how mountains float in balance. Later the asthenosphere became important for the theory of **plate tectonics**.

gewusst: On the coast of the Gulf of Bothnia the land is measurably growing out into the sea, and old harbours are now inland.
The Alps are also partly rising because the load of the Ice Age glaciers has disappeared.

teile.einleitung: A rotation curve shows how fast stars and gas in a galaxy orbit the centre, depending on their distance. From it you can read how the mass in the galaxy is distributed. It was these very curves that gave an important clue to dark matter.
wichtigste: The rotation curve plots the orbital speed against the distance from the centre.
If the mass were only where stars shine, the speed further out would have to fall off as 1 divided by the square root of r.
In spiral galaxies, however, an almost flat curve is observed further out.
Vera Rubin and Kent Ford made flat rotation curves widely known in the 1970s.
They are measured using the Doppler effect, far out often with the 21 cm line of neutral hydrogen.
Most experts explain the flat curves with dark matter, while the MOND theory uses a changed law of gravity.

abschnitte.text: For a **rotation curve** you measure how fast stars and gas orbit the centre of a galaxy at different distances. You plot this **orbital speed** against the **radius**. For a circular orbit: v squared times r divided by G gives the **mass inside the orbit**. With v equal to 230 km/s and r equal to 8.2 kiloparsecs, you get about **100 billion solar masses** for the Sun's orbit.

abschnitte.titel: Expected: as in the solar system
abschnitte.text: In the solar system, almost all the mass sits in the Sun. There v equals **the square root of GM divided by r**: the planets get slower and slower further out. At four times the radius, the speed is only **half as great**. If in a galaxy, too, the mass were mainly where the stars shine, the curve would have to drop like this further out. This pattern is called **Keplerian**.

In fact, in **spiral galaxies** the speeds stay almost **constant** far beyond the visible edge. So the curve is **flat**. In the 1970s the astronomer **Vera Rubin**, together with **Kent Ford**, measured the rotation of the Andromeda Galaxy and many other spiral galaxies. Their results made **dark matter** a central topic. As early as 1933, the Swiss astronomer **Fritz Zwicky** had suspected invisible mass in galaxy clusters.

It is measured using the **Doppler effect**. If you see a disc galaxy from the side, one side is turning towards us and the other away from us. The spectral lines of one side are therefore **blueshifted**, those of the other **redshifted**. Far out, people often use the **21 cm line** of neutral hydrogen. This gas reaches much further out than the stars.

Most experts interpret the flat curves with a **halo of dark matter** that surrounds the galaxy. This matter gives off no light but acts through its gravity. Another idea is **MOND**, **Modified Newtonian Dynamics**. Mordehai Milgrom proposed it in **1983**. According to it, gravity acts more strongly at very small accelerations than Newton described.

gewusst: According to today's estimates, the Milky Way contains much more dark matter than visible matter.
As early as 1933 Fritz Zwicky coined the term “dark matter” for the invisible mass.

teile.einleitung: In redshift, the light of a celestial body is shifted to longer wavelengths, towards the red end of the spectrum. It reveals how galaxies move and how the universe is expanding. There are several causes for it.
wichtigste: The redshift z is the increase in wavelength divided by the rest wavelength.
The observed wavelength is (1 + z) times the rest wavelength.
Cosmological redshift is caused by the expansion of space.
Light climbing out of a strong gravitational field shows a gravitational redshift.
From 1912 Vesto Slipher was the first to measure the speeds of spiral nebulae.
The Andromeda Galaxy shows a blueshift because it is moving towards us.
The cosmic background radiation has a redshift of about 1100.

abschnitte.text: The **redshift z** is defined like this: observed wavelength minus original wavelength, divided by the **original wavelength**. z is a number **without a unit**. The other way round: the observed wavelength is **(1 + z) times** the rest wavelength. The **H-alpha** line lies at 656.3 nm in the laboratory. In a galaxy with z equal to 0.1, it is measured at about **721.9 nm**.

If a light source moves away from us, its waves are stretched. If it comes towards us, they are squashed, which is called **blueshift**. For small z, approximately **v equals c times z**. For z equal to 0.02, this gives about **6000 km/s**. The **Andromeda Galaxy** is approaching the Milky Way and therefore shows a blueshift.

From **1912** **Vesto Slipher** measured the spectra of spiral nebulae at the Lowell Observatory. Most of them were **redshifted**. His data later became an important basis for **Hubble's law**: the further away a galaxy is, the more strongly its light is shifted. The cause is the **expansion of space**. While the light is travelling, space expands, and the light waves expand with it.

According to the **general theory of relativity**, light loses energy when it climbs out of a strong **gravitational field**. This makes its wavelength longer. This is called **gravitational redshift**. It can be measured, for example, in the light of **white dwarfs** or of stars that fly close past a black hole.

The greater the redshift, the longer the light has been travelling. The **cosmic background radiation** comes from the time when the universe was about **1100 times smaller** than today. That is why its redshift is about **1100**. For very distant galaxies, visible and ultraviolet light slips into the **infrared**. The Lyman-alpha line at 121.6 nm appears at **1216 nm** for z equal to 9.

gewusst: That is why the James Webb Space Telescope observes mainly in the infrared: this way it can see the galaxies with the greatest redshifts.
The Andromeda Galaxy is one of the few galaxies whose light is blueshifted.

teile.einleitung: Stars do not all look the same. If you split their light into a spectrum, typical dark lines appear. Stars are divided into spectral classes according to these lines, which mainly reveal their temperature.
wichtigste: From hot to cool, the spectral classes are called O, B, A, F, G, K and M.
The classes L, T and Y are even cooler than M.
A digit from 0 to 9 divides each class into subclasses.
The Sun has the spectral type G2V.
Annie Jump Cannon classified hundreds of thousands of stars at Harvard.
In 1925 Cecilia Payne showed that stars are made mainly of hydrogen and helium.

abschnitte.text: With a **spectroscope** you split the light of a star into its colours. In it you can see dark **spectral lines**. They form because atoms in the star's atmosphere swallow certain light. Which lines are strong depends mainly on the **temperature**. In this way stars can be sorted by their spectrum.

abschnitte.titel: O, B, A, F, G, K, M
abschnitte.text: From hot to cool, the main classes are called **O, B, A, F, G, K, M**. O stars are blue and very hot, M stars red and cool. In class **A** the **Balmer lines** of hydrogen are strongest. In cool M stars, molecules such as **titanium oxide** form, which produce broad bands. The red supergiant **Betelgeuse** belongs to class M. The classes **L, T and Y** are cooler still; they are mostly brown dwarfs.

The Sun has the spectral type **G2V**. The letter G is the main class. The digit **2** is the **subclass within G**: each class is divided into steps from 0 to 9, with 0 being the hottest. The Roman numeral **V** is the luminosity class. It shows that the Sun is a normal star on the **main sequence**, a so-called dwarf star.

Around 1900 a group of women at the Harvard University observatory worked on star spectra. **Annie Jump Cannon** sorted the spectra of several hundred thousand stars. She put the classes into the order that is usual today. Her system is still used. Many people remember the order with the English saying “Oh Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me”.

For a long time people thought that stars were made of similar things to the Earth. In her doctoral thesis in **1925**, **Cecilia Payne** showed that the differences in the spectra come mainly from temperature. Stars are made mostly of **hydrogen and helium**. At first many experts did not believe her. Today her result is one of the foundations of astronomy.

gewusst: The strange order O, B, A came about because the classes were first sorted alphabetically and later re-sorted by temperature.
Most of the stars near us are small, red M stars that cannot be seen with the naked eye at all.

teile.einleitung: The Pleiades are a small, eye-catching group of stars in the constellation Taurus. They are also called the Seven Sisters, and they were already depicted thousands of years ago.
wichtigste: The Pleiades are an open star cluster.
With the naked eye you can see about 6 to 9 stars, but several hundred belong to it in total.
They are about 440 light years from the Earth.
At about 125 million years, they are very young.
They are named after the seven daughters of Atlas from Greek legend.
In Switzerland you can see them well in the evening in autumn and winter.

abschnitte.text: The Pleiades are a loose group of young stars, an **open star cluster**. They lie in the constellation **Taurus**. Depending on the viewing conditions and your eyes, you can make out 6 to 9 stars with the naked eye, and many more with binoculars. At least 400 members are known. If you count faint stars and close pairs too, there are probably over 1,000.

Measurements by the **Gaia** satellite give a distance of about 135 parsecs, which is about **440 light years**. So the light we see today has been travelling for about 440 years. The Pleiades are about **125 million years** old. Our Sun is over thirty times older. Their brightest stars shine hot and bluish.

In Greek legend, the Pleiades were the seven **daughters of the Titan Atlas** and Pleione. The brightest stars bear their names. On the **Nebra sky disc** from Germany, which is about 3,600 years old, a group of seven gold dots very probably shows the Pleiades. It is considered one of the oldest pictures of the sky in the world.

In Switzerland, the Pleiades rise in the east in the evening in **autumn**. In **winter** they are high in the sky in the evening. They look like a small, blurry patch of stars. With **binoculars** you can make out many more stars. In long-exposure photos you can see bluish shimmering dust around the stars.

gewusst: The Japanese name for the Pleiades is “Subaru”, and a car brand is named after it.
The Pleiades are among the nearest open star clusters, which is why they are so easy to see.

teile.einleitung: Perseverance is a NASA rover that has been driving around on Mars since 2021. It is looking for traces of past life and collecting rock samples. Its name means persistence or endurance.
wichtigste: Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater on Mars on 18 February 2021.
Long ago there was a lake in the crater.
The rover weighs about 1 tonne and drives on six wheels.
It is looking for traces of past life.
It puts selected rock samples into small tubes.
The MOXIE experiment made oxygen from the Martian air.
Its electricity comes from a radioisotope battery with plutonium.

abschnitte.text: Perseverance was launched in summer 2020 and landed in **Jezero Crater** on **18 February 2021**. Long ago there was a **lake** there, into which a river flowed. At the end of the landing, a kind of flying crane hovered above the ground and lowered the rover gently on ropes. Cameras filmed the landing, so that people could watch it on Earth later.

abschnitte.titel: A rover like a small car
abschnitte.text: Perseverance weighs about **1,025 kg** and is about the size of a small car. It drives on **six wheels** made of aluminium and so can get over stones and sand. It has many cameras, a robotic arm with tools and even microphones. Its electricity comes from a **radioisotope battery**: radioactive **plutonium** decays in it and produces heat, from which electricity is made, even at night and in dust storms.

Perseverance is mainly looking for **traces of past life**. It studies rock from the old **lake basin**. Traces of tiny living things could be preserved there, if they ever existed. It drills into selected samples and seals them in small **tubes**. These may later be brought to Earth by another mission.

The Martian air consists mainly of **carbon dioxide**. The **MOXIE** experiment split it and obtained **oxygen** from it. It was a test for the future: people on Mars could make air to breathe or fuel for the journey home in this way.

The name was suggested by a pupil from the USA in a **competition**. **Perseverance** means endurance or persistence. On board was a small helicopter called **Ingenuity**. In April 2021 it became the first aircraft to fly under its own power on another planet.

gewusst: With Perseverance's microphones, sounds from the surface of Mars, such as the wind, were heard for the first time.
Instead of the planned five flights, Ingenuity managed many dozens of flights.

teile.einleitung: Mount Etna is a mighty volcano on the island of Sicily in Italy. It is the highest active volcano in Europe and erupts very often. Even so, many people live on its slopes.
wichtigste: Etna stands on Sicily, an island that belongs to Italy.
It is the highest active volcano in Europe.
Etna is over 3000 metres high, and its exact height changes with eruptions.
It is one of the most active volcanoes in the world and erupts almost every year.
The large city of Catania lies at the foot of Etna.
In Sicily, Etna is also called Mongibello.
Famous pistachios grow on the western slope near Bronte.

abschnitte.text: Etna is a **stratovolcano**: it is built up of many layers of lava and ash that have piled on top of each other during eruptions. It has several summit craters and many smaller side craters on its flanks. Smaller and larger **eruptions** happen very often, sometimes several times a year. Glowing lava spurts up into the air or flows slowly down the slope. That is why researchers watch the mountain around the clock with measuring instruments.

Etna is over 3000 metres high, making it the highest active volcano in Europe. Its height is not always the same: during eruptions new rock is added, while in other places the summit collapses. Because it is so high, there is often **snow** at the top in winter. There are even ski areas on Etna, so you can ski on a volcano and see the sea at the same time.

At the foot of Etna lies **Catania**, one of the largest cities in Sicily. In a big eruption in 1669, lava flowed right into the city. Despite the danger, many people live in the villages around the mountain. The local people often simply call it “the mountain” or **Mongibello**. This old name combines a Latin and an Arabic word, both of which mean “mountain”.

Weathered lava and ash form very **fertile soil**. That is why grapevines, oranges, lemons and olives grow on the slopes of Etna. Particularly famous are the green **pistachios** from the area around the small town of Bronte on the western slope. They are a speciality and are used in ice cream, pastries and sweets.

The ancient Greeks already knew Etna well. In their legends, the blacksmith god Hephaestus had his workshop under the mountain, and the fire came from his forge. Today Etna is a popular place for trips, and you can go part of the way up by cable car. Since 2013 the mountain has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Etna is so active that it is one of the best-studied volcanoes in the world.
In winter you can ski on an active volcano and look out over the Mediterranean at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Sagittarius A* is the supermassive black hole at the centre of our Milky Way. It has about four million times as much mass as the Sun. Research on it was honoured with the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020.
wichtigste: Sagittarius A* lies in the constellation Sagittarius, in the direction of the centre of the Milky Way.
Its mass is about 4 million solar masses.
Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2020 for proving it.
The star S2 orbits it in about 16 years and came very close to it in 2018.
Stars near Sagittarius A* are observed in the infrared because dust swallows visible light.
Sagittarius A* shines faintly because at the moment it is swallowing only a little matter.

abschnitte.text: **Sagittarius** is the Latin name of the constellation of **the Archer**. The **centre of the Milky Way** lies in this direction. In **1932** **Karl Jansky** was studying interference in radio communications and found radio waves coming from the constellation Sagittarius. With this he founded **radio astronomy**. The very small, bright radio source **Sagittarius A*** itself was not discovered until 1974.

Between us and the centre there are dense **clouds of dust** in the disc of the Milky Way. They swallow visible light almost completely. **Infrared light** gets through the dust much better. That is why the stars near Sagittarius A* are observed mainly in the infrared. Over decades, two research groups followed the **orbits of the stars** around the centre in this way.

The star **S2** is particularly important. It has a semi-major axis of about **1000 AU** and needs about **16 years** for one lap. According to **Kepler's third law**, in AU, years and solar masses: M equals a cubed divided by T squared. This gives about **4 million solar masses**. In **2018** S2 came within about 120 AU of the black hole and reached about **7650 km/s**, almost 3 per cent of the speed of light.

When S2 flew past in 2018, the **GRAVITY collaboration** measured the **gravitational redshift**. The light lost energy as it climbed out of the gravitational field, exactly as the **general theory of relativity** predicts. In **2020** **Reinhard Genzel** and **Andrea Ghez** received the Nobel Prize in Physics for proving the black hole. The other half of the prize went to **Roger Penrose**.

The **Schwarzschild radius** of Sagittarius A* is about **12 million km**. It grows in proportion to the mass: with twice the mass it would be twice as large. The brightness of a black hole comes from heated gas falling into it. At the moment only very **little gas** flows around Sagittarius A*, so it shines much more faintly than a **quasar**. In **2022** the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first picture of its shadow.

gewusst: Sagittarius A* is about 26,000 light years away from the Earth.
For the 2022 picture, radio telescopes all over the Earth worked together like one single giant telescope.

teile.einleitung: Stars do not last forever: they are born, shine for millions to billions of years and then die. Stellar evolution describes this life of a star, from its birth in a cloud of gas to its end as a white dwarf, neutron star or black hole. How a star lives and dies depends mainly on its mass.
wichtigste: Stars form in cold clouds of gas and dust.
Stars spend most of their lives on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium.
Heavy stars live much shorter lives than light ones, because they use up their fuel faster.
The Sun belongs to spectral class G2.
In the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, luminosity is plotted against surface temperature.
In the end the Sun will become a white dwarf.
A white dwarf can have at most about 1.4 solar masses; this is the Chandrasekhar limit.

abschnitte.text: Stars form in huge **molecular clouds** of gas and dust, for example in the Orion Nebula. When part of the cloud becomes denser, it contracts under its own gravity and heats up. This creates a **protostar**. When the temperature in the core reaches about 10 million degrees, nuclear fusion begins. Then a real star has been born.

Around 1910 Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell arranged the stars in a diagram. In the **Hertzsprung-Russell diagram**, luminosity is plotted against surface temperature. Most stars lie on a band, the **main sequence**. At the top right are the giants, at the bottom left the white dwarfs. The Sun is a main sequence star of **spectral class G2**.

On the main sequence, stars fuse hydrogen into helium in their core. Stars like the Sun do this mainly through the **proton-proton chain**. In much more massive stars, most of the energy comes from the **CNO cycle**, in which carbon, nitrogen and oxygen act as helpers. Heavy stars use up their fuel much faster. The lifetime scales roughly with the mass to the power of minus 2.5: if the Sun lives about 10 billion years, a star with 10 solar masses lives only about 30 million years.

When the hydrogen in the core is used up, the core contracts and gets hotter, while the outer layers swell up greatly. The star becomes a **red giant**. At about 100 million degrees, the **triple-alpha process** begins in the core: three helium-4 nuclei fuse into carbon-12. Much of the carbon in our bodies was made in stars in this way. Very heavy stars then go on to make oxygen, silicon and finally iron.

At the end, stars like the Sun shed their outer layers. This glowing shell of gas is called a **planetary nebula**. What is left is the hot core as a **white dwarf**, about the size of the Earth but very dense. A white dwarf can have at most about 1.4 solar masses; this **Chandrasekhar limit** was calculated by Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar around 1930. The Sun will go this way in about 5 billion years.

Stars with more than about eight solar masses come to a spectacular end. When their core is made of iron, it can no longer gain energy through fusion and collapses in a fraction of a second. The star explodes as a **supernova**. What is left is a **neutron star** or, for particularly heavy stars, a black hole. The elements flung out later form new stars and planets.

begriffe.erklaerung: The long, calm stage in a star's life when it fuses hydrogen into helium.
An old, greatly swollen star with a cool, reddish surface.
The small, very dense remains of a Sun-like star.
An extremely dense remnant of a star, only about 20 kilometres across.

gewusst: A teaspoon of material from a white dwarf would weigh several tonnes on Earth.
The lightest stars, red dwarfs, live so long that not a single one has died in the whole age of the universe so far.
When the Sun becomes a red giant, it will probably swallow Mercury and Venus.

teile.einleitung: A reflecting telescope collects the light of distant stars with a curved mirror instead of a lens. Almost all the large telescopes in the world are reflecting telescopes. Switzerland also takes part in such giant telescopes.
wichtigste: In 1668 Isaac Newton built one of the first usable reflecting telescopes.
The main mirror is curved inwards like a bowl.
Unlike lenses, mirrors do not produce coloured edges.
The main mirror of the James Webb Space Telescope is made of 18 gold-coated segments.
ESO's Extremely Large Telescope will have a mirror of about 39 metres.
Switzerland has been a member of ESO since 1982.

abschnitte.text: The **main mirror** of a reflecting telescope is **curved inwards like a bowl**. It collects the light and focuses it at one point, the **focal point**. The larger the mirror, the more light it catches. This means you can also see very faint and distant objects. A mirror has a big advantage: it produces **no coloured edges** like the ones that appear with simple lenses.

The English natural scientist **Isaac Newton** built one of the first usable reflecting telescopes in **1668**. He wanted to avoid the coloured edges of lens telescopes. In his design, a small, slanted **secondary mirror** directs the light **sideways to the eyepiece**. That is where you look in. This simple design is still popular with amateur astronomers today.

A single huge mirror would be **too heavy** and very hard to make. That is why the largest mirrors today are made of many separate **segments**. Computers keep them in exactly the right shape. The **James Webb Space Telescope** has a main mirror made of **18** six-sided segments. They are coated with **gold**, because gold reflects infrared light very well.

The **European Southern Observatory ESO** runs large telescopes in the desert of Chile. There the air is very dry and clear. ESO is building the **Extremely Large Telescope** with a main mirror of **about 39 metres** (as of 2025). It will be the largest telescope for visible light in the world. **Switzerland** has been a member of ESO since **1982**.

The **Observatory of the University of Geneva** runs its own reflecting telescope with a diameter of 1.2 metres at La Silla in Chile. It is named after the Basel mathematician **Leonhard Euler**. With the **Euler Telescope**, researchers mainly search for planets around other stars. Geneva is world famous in this field.

gewusst: Newton's first reflecting telescope had a mirror only about three centimetres across.
The layer of gold on the mirrors of the James Webb Telescope is wafer-thin: only about 48 grams of gold in total.

teile.einleitung: Proxima Centauri is the star closest to our Sun. Even so, it is so faint that you can only see it with a telescope.
wichtigste: Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf.
It has only about an eighth of the Sun's mass.
It is about 4.2 light years away from us.
It belongs to the Alpha Centauri system, a triple system.
Robert Innes discovered it in 1915.
In 2016, the planet Proxima b was discovered.

abschnitte.text: Proxima Centauri is a **red dwarf**. This is a small, cool star that shines reddish. It has only about 12 per cent of the Sun's mass, about an **eighth**. Red dwarfs are the most common stars in the Milky Way. Although Proxima is so close, it is far too faint for the naked eye; you need a **telescope**.

“Proxima” is Latin and means **“the nearest”**. The name fits, because it is the closest of all stars to us; its light takes about **4.2 years** to reach us. The Scottish astronomer **Robert Innes** discovered it in South Africa in 1915. Later it turned out that it is the nearest star after the Sun.

Proxima circles the two stars **Alpha Centauri A and B** at a great distance. Together they form a **triple system**. Proxima is also a **flare star**: strong outbursts of radiation keep happening on its surface. Then its brightness suddenly rises sharply.

In 2016, researchers found the planet **Proxima b**. It orbits its star at a distance where liquid water might be possible. Whether there really is water there is not known. Proxima's strong outbursts of radiation could harm the planet. That is why it is being studied further.

Proxima Centauri lies in the constellation **Centaurus** in the southern sky. From Switzerland it never rises above the horizon. So you can never see it here, not even with a telescope. For that you have to travel further south, for example to the southern hemisphere.

gewusst: Even with the fastest space probes of today, a journey to Proxima would take tens of thousands of years.
Red dwarfs like Proxima live much longer than the Sun because they use up their supply very sparingly.

teile.einleitung: There is a solstice twice a year. In June we have the longest day in Switzerland, in December the shortest. People have celebrated these special days since ancient times.
wichtigste: There is a solstice twice a year.
The summer solstice around 21 June brings the longest day.
The winter solstice around 21 December brings the shortest day.
Winter begins with the winter solstice.
After the winter solstice the days get longer again.
Stonehenge in England is lined up with the solstice.

abschnitte.text: The Earth's axis is tilted. So on its way around the Sun, sometimes the Northern Hemisphere and sometimes the Southern Hemisphere is tilted more towards the Sun. At the **solstice**, the Sun at midday is at its highest or lowest. After that it “turns back” in its course. This happens **twice** a year.

The **summer solstice** is around **21 June**. Then we have the **longest day** of the year and the shortest night. At midday the Sun is higher than at any other time. After that the days slowly get shorter again. In the Southern Hemisphere, for example in Australia, it is exactly the other way round.

The **winter solstice** is around **21 December**. Then Switzerland has the **shortest day** of the year. According to the astronomical calendar, **winter** begins with it. From now on the days get **longer** again. At first you hardly notice, but from January it becomes clear.

Many people celebrate the solstice. Around the summer solstice, **St John's fires** are lit in some areas. They are named after John the Baptist, whose feast day is on 24 June. There are also old customs with light around the winter solstice, because from then on the days get brighter again.

**Stonehenge** in England is a huge stone circle from the Stone Age. It is built so that the Sun rises at a particular spot at the summer solstice. At the winter solstice it sets on the opposite side. So the people of that time watched the sky very closely. Even today many visitors come at the solstice.

gewusst: On the longest day the Sun shines in Switzerland for about 16 hours, on the shortest only about 8 to 9 hours.
Far in the north, for example in Lapland, the Sun does not set at all around the summer solstice.

teile.einleitung: A planetarium shows the starry sky on a large dome. This lets you look at stars and planets in any weather and at any time of day.
wichtigste: The starry sky is projected onto a dome shaped like half a sphere.
The first projector for a modern dome planetarium was built by the company Carl Zeiss in Jena.
It was designed by the engineer Walther Bauersfeld.
It was built for the Deutsches Museum in Munich and first shown in 1923.
The Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne has had a planetarium since 1969.
Modern planetariums use fulldome projection.

abschnitte.text: In the past, a planetarium was a **mechanical model**. With cogwheels, small balls turned around a sun and showed the movement of the planets. In the Dutch town of Franeker, Eise Eisinga built such a model into the ceiling of his living room in the 18th century. It is considered the oldest planetarium in the world that still works.

Oskar von Miller, the founder of the **Deutsches Museum** in Munich, wanted to show the starry sky in the museum. The company **Carl Zeiss** in Jena took on the job. The engineer **Walther Bauersfeld** designed a projector that throws points of light onto a dome. He also developed a particularly light way of building the dome. In 1923 the projector was shown for the first time.

The **Swiss Museum of Transport** in Lucerne has had a planetarium since 1969. It is the largest planetarium in Switzerland. Many school classes visit it to learn more about stars, planets and space travel. The shows present, for example, what the sky over Switzerland looks like on a particular night.

A planetarium is **independent of the weather and the time of day**. It can show the sky for any time, any date and any place on Earth, even the sky of the southern hemisphere. Modern planetariums often use **fulldome projection**: several video projectors put together one picture across the whole dome. This also makes it possible to show flights through space.

gewusst: The dome imitates the vault of the sky, which is why in a planetarium you feel almost as if you were under the open sky.
In a planetarium you can show in a few minutes how the sky changes over a whole year.

teile.einleitung: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest in our solar system. It is famous for its magnificent, bright rings of ice and rock. Although it is huge, it is so light that it would float in a gigantic bathtub.
wichtigste: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun.
After Jupiter, it is the second largest planet.
Saturn is famous for its large, bright rings.
The rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock.
Its largest moon is called Titan.
Saturn has a lower density than water.
It is a gas planet without a solid surface.

abschnitte.text: Saturn has a diameter of about 120,000 kilometres, almost ten times that of the Earth. It is a **gas planet** and consists mainly of hydrogen and helium. It has no solid surface that you could land on. Because it spins on its axis in only about 10.5 hours, it is clearly flattened at the poles. It is named after **Saturn**, a Roman god of sowing.

Saturn's bright **rings** have a diameter of about 270,000 kilometres, but are usually only a few tens of metres thick. They are made of countless chunks of **ice** and rock, from grains of dust to blocks the size of a house. Galileo Galilei was the first to see them in 1610, but he did not yet understand what they were. Only in 1655 did Christiaan Huygens correctly describe that Saturn is surrounded by a ring. Jupiter, Uranus and Neptune have rings too, but much fainter ones.

Saturn has the lowest **density** of all the planets. It is even lower than the density of water. So in theory Saturn would float in a huge bathtub. Even so, it has about 95 times as much mass as the Earth. At its North Pole it has a strange six-sided swirl of clouds, the so-called **hexagon**.

Saturn has a great many moons: well over a hundred are known. The largest is called **Titan** and is even bigger than the planet Mercury. Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, and it has lakes of liquid methane. The moon **Enceladus** shoots fountains of water vapour into space, and under its icy crust lies an ocean. Titan was discovered by Christiaan Huygens in 1655.

From 2004 to 2017 the space probe **Cassini** orbited Saturn and took hundreds of thousands of pictures. In 2005 it set down the European landing probe **Huygens** on Titan, the first landing in the outer solar system. At the end, Cassini was deliberately crashed into Saturn. Saturn can be seen even without a telescope as a bright, yellowish dot. With just a small telescope you can make out its rings from Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge planet that consists mainly of gases and has no solid surface.
How much mass there is in a certain space, that is, how heavy something is for its size.
Saturn's largest moon, which has a thick atmosphere.
Many chunks of ice and rock that orbit a planet in a flat disc.

gewusst: About every 15 years we look from the Earth exactly at the edge of the rings, and then they almost seem to disappear.
On Saturn a year lasts almost 30 Earth years.
Saturn's rings are slowly losing material and could be gone in many millions of years.

teile.einleitung: Solar neutrinos are tiny particles produced by nuclear fusion inside the Sun. They fly almost unhindered through everything, including the Earth and us. Research on them has led to several Nobel Prizes.
wichtigste: Electron neutrinos are produced by fusion in the Sun's core.
Neutrinos leave the Sun almost unhindered and so reveal what is happening in the core.
Every second, about 65 billion solar neutrinos pass through every square centimetre.
The Homestake experiment found only about a third of the expected neutrinos.
Neutrino oscillation, a change in the type of particle, solved this puzzle.
In 2020 Borexino detected neutrinos from the CNO cycle for the first time.

abschnitte.text: In the core of the Sun, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium. This produces **electron neutrinos**. Light takes a very long time to fight its way out of the dense interior. Neutrinos, on the other hand, hardly react with matter and **leave the Sun almost unhindered**. After just over eight minutes they reach the Earth. In this way they bring direct news from the Sun's core.

Every second, about **65 billion** solar neutrinos pass through every square centimetre on Earth. Even at night they fly right through the whole Earth. We feel nothing of this. Because they so rarely collide with matter, you need huge **detectors**, which are often deep underground. There they are protected from other radiation from space.

From the 1960s, the American **Raymond Davis** built a large tank of **tetrachloroethene**, a cleaning fluid, in a mine in South Dakota. When a neutrino hits a chlorine atom, an argon atom is produced, which can be counted. But Davis found only **about a third** of the predicted neutrinos. This puzzle was called the solar neutrino problem. Davis received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2002.

There are three types of neutrino. On the way they can change their type; this is called **neutrino oscillation**. Davis could only measure electron neutrinos, which is why so many were missing. The Canadian **Sudbury Neutrino Observatory**, using heavy water, confirmed the change of type in 2001 and 2002. It also shows that neutrinos have a tiny mass. This was awarded the Nobel Prize in 2015.

A small part of the Sun's energy comes from the **CNO cycle**, in which carbon, nitrogen and oxygen act as helpers. The **Borexino** experiment in the Gran Sasso laboratory in Italy, deep under a mountain, detected neutrinos from this cycle for the first time in 2020. This proved that this process really does take place in the Sun.

gewusst: Most solar neutrinos would even pass through a wall of lead about a light year thick.
In the Homestake tank only a few argon atoms were produced each week, yet Davis still reliably fished them out.

teile.einleitung: A planet trail is a footpath along which the solar system has been rebuilt at a greatly reduced size. As you walk, you feel how huge the distances in space are.
wichtigste: A well-known planet trail in Zurich runs from the Uetliberg to the Felsenegg.
It is a billion times smaller than the real thing.
One metre on the path stands for a million kilometres in space.
The Sun there is a ball 1.39 metres across.
The Earth is just over a centimetre in size and stands about 150 metres from the Sun.
The whole trail takes about two hours.

abschnitte.text: On a **planet trail**, models of the Sun and the planets stand along a footpath. Sizes and distances are reduced to the same **scale**. There are several such trails in Switzerland. Particularly well known is the planet trail on the **Uetliberg** near Zurich. It runs from the Uetliberg to the **Felsenegg**, and the walk takes about two hours.

On the Uetliberg, everything is made **a billion times** smaller. So one metre of path stands for a million kilometres. The Sun is a yellow ball 1.39 metres across, just under one and a half metres. The Earth is just under 13,000 kilometres wide. In the model it becomes a ball of about 1.3 centimetres, the size of a **marble**.

The real Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun. In the model that is about **150 metres**. Neptune, the outermost planet, is about 4.5 billion kilometres from the Sun. On the planet trail you have to walk about **4.5 kilometres** for this. That is why a planet trail needs so much space.

On the trail you quickly notice that the planets are **much smaller** than the Sun. Even Jupiter, the largest planet, would be only about 14 centimetres in the model. Between the planets, on the other hand, there are long stretches with nothing at all. This shows how **empty** space is.

gewusst: Light takes about eight minutes to travel from the Sun to the Earth; on the planet trail you walk the same distance in about two minutes.
At the same scale, the nearest star after the Sun would be about 40,000 kilometres away, about once around the Earth.

teile.einleitung: Quasars are among the brightest objects in the universe. They are the glowing centres of distant galaxies, in which matter is falling into a huge black hole.
wichtigste: The word quasar comes from “quasi-stellar radio source”.
In 1963, Maarten Schmidt showed with the quasar 3C 273 that quasars are very far away.
The energy comes from matter falling into a supermassive black hole.
A quasar can outshine its whole host galaxy.
Most quasars are very far away because they were more common in the early universe.
In 1979, Q0957+561 was discovered as the first gravitationally lensed quasar.

abschnitte.text: In the 1950s and 1960s, objects were found that looked like **stars** in telescopes but gave off strong **radio waves**. They were called “quasi-stellar radio sources”. This gave rise to the word **quasar**. Later it turned out that many quasars do not give off strong radio waves at all, but the name stuck.

In 1963, **Maarten Schmidt** studied the light of the quasar **3C 273**. He recognised familiar lines of hydrogen that were strongly shifted to longer waves. This **redshift** of 0.158 means that 3C 273 is moving away from us at about 47,000 kilometres per second. So it lies far beyond our Milky Way. That made it clear: quasars must be unimaginably bright.

At the centre of a quasar sits a **supermassive black hole**. Gas collects in an **accretion disc** around the hole and heats up enormously through friction. A large part of the energy is given off as radiation. In this way a quasar can outshine all the stars in its galaxy many times over. If it changes its brightness within a day, the glowing region is at most about one **light day** across.

Looking into the distance means looking into the **past**. About 10 billion years ago, quasars were much more common, because more gas was flowing into the centres of galaxies. The quasar **J0313-1806**, found in 2021, appears as it was about 670 million years after the Big Bang. Its black hole has about 1.6 billion solar masses.

In 1979, the **double quasar Q0957+561** was discovered. It appeared as two almost identical quasars close together. In reality it is a single quasar. A galaxy between it and us bends its light onto two paths with its gravity. This is called a **gravitational lens**.

teile.einleitung: The rocket engine is the motor of a rocket. It pushes hot gases out backwards with great force and so drives the rocket forwards.
wichtigste: In the combustion chamber, the propellants mix and burn.
The gases there become about 3,000 °C hot.
The hot gases stream out backwards through the nozzle.
The force with which the engine pushes the rocket forwards is called thrust.
By swivelling the nozzle, a rocket can change its direction.
Small thrusters turn and steer spacecraft in space.

abschnitte.text: In the **combustion chamber**, the propellants mix and burn. This produces temperatures of about **3,000 degrees**, hotter than molten lava. The hot gases stream out through the **nozzle**. The nozzle is like a large funnel and directs the gases backwards. In a rocket, the main engine usually sits **right at the bottom** at the tail.

A rocket engine works on the **principle of recoil**. The gases are pushed out backwards with great force, and the rocket is pushed forwards as a result. You know this from a balloon that the air is escaping from. The force is called **thrust**. The greater the thrust, the more strongly the rocket is accelerated. Because the rocket does not push against the air, this also works in the vacuum of space.

Many engines can be **tilted** a little. Then the thrust pushes at a slight angle, and the rocket changes direction. Spacecraft also have small **thrusters**. They give short bursts. With them, a spacecraft can be turned in space or steered very precisely up to a **space station**.

An engine constantly needs a fresh supply of fuel. When the fuel is used up, nothing more can burn. The engine **shuts down** and gives no more thrust. The rocket then flies on at the speed it has reached, until gravity or another engine changes it again.

gewusst: The first stage of the Saturn V had five huge engines.
The nozzle of a large rocket engine is often bigger than a person.
